Houthi missile strike on Yemen camp kills 50 security recruits, local authorities say

BBC News Mon, 19 Oct 2026 16:20:51 GMT

More than 50 security personnel have been killed and 200 injured in a Houthi missile strike on a camp in Yemen's central province of Shabwa, local authorities say.

A spokesman for the Saudi-backed Yemeni armed forces said the Iran-backed group launched three ballistic missiles at al-Alam camp near Ataq city, which was being used as a training centre for recruits to the security forces and police.

The head of Yemen's Presidential Leadership Council, Rashad al-Alimi, condemned what he called the "criminal attack" and promised a "firm response".

The Houthis' military spokesman said they had targeted "Saudi enemy concentrations".

Yemen's devastating civil war has flared up in recent months.

At the start of October, pro-government forces launched a major offensive that aims to retake territory in western Yemen that is controlled by the Houthis.

With air support from a Saudi-led coalition of Arab states, they managed to regain control of territory on the Red Sea coast that overlooks the strategically important Bab al-Mandab Strait, which the Houthis captured in a surprise assault in September.

However, fierce fighting is continuing there, as well as around the besieged government-controlled city of Taiz, and to the north in Marib and al-Jawf provinces.

The Houthis have also responded to the Saudi air strikes by launching missiles and drones at airports, energy facilities and military bases in neighbouring Saudi Arabia.

Monday's attack in Shabwa is one of the deadliest reported since the start of the escalation.

Shabwa province's media office said in a statement that ballistic missiles struck the Martyr Ahmed al-Sulaimani Training Centre, where recruits from several provinces were undergoing training to be members of the internal security forces. According to a preliminary assessment, 53 were killed and more than 200 injured, it added.

A video posted on social media appeared to show several bodies scattered across the ground.

Shabwa's deputy governor, Fahad al-Khalifi, told AFP news agency that hospitals in the province were overwhelmed and had been forced to transfer the most seriously wounded to neighbouring Hadramout and Aden, where the government is based. Some of them were in a critical condition, he said.

Information Minister Moammar al-Eryani said the attack constituted a war crime because the internal security forces training centre was not a military target.

He also accused the Houthis of "attempting to fabricate a false media victory, boost the morale of its collapsing elements, and cover up the defeats and setbacks it is suffering across various combat axes".

The Houthis' military spokesman, Yahya Sarea, said in a statement that the missiles targeted a gathering of "Saudi enemy" forces at al-Alam camp, which he said was run by Saudi officers.

There was no immediate comment from Saudi authorities.

In a separate development, Houthi-run media reported that a Saudi air strike on a home in the Sahar district of the Houthi-controlled northern province of Saada on Sunday killed at least 10 people and injured 23 others, many of them women and children.

According to the Houthi-run health ministry in north-western Yemen, a total of 141 people had been killed in Saudi strikes over the past seven weeks.

The government's health ministry, meanwhile, said last week that at least 1,282 people had been killed in the conflict across Yemen since 6 August.

In Saudi Arabia, at least 19 people have been killed in Houthi attacks targeting the kingdom's airports since the beginning of October.

Yemen has been devastated by a civil war that began in 2014, when the Houthis ousted the government from the capital, Sanaa. The conflict escalated in 2015, after the Saudi-led coalition intervened in an attempt to restore the government's rule.

A four-year-old informal ceasefire began to unravel in July, when the Houthis announced a "maritime embargo" against Saudi Arabia and began missile and drone attacks on Saudi airports, oil facilities and tankers in the Red Sea.

The Houthis said they were retaliating for what they call a Saudi blockade of their territory, as well as an air strike on Sanaa airport that they blamed on the kingdom.

Obama blasts federal probe of congresswoman Ilhan Omar as 'so appalling'

BBC News Mon, 19 Oct 2026 16:16:51 GMT

Barack Obama has said congresswoman Ilhan Omar is under federal criminal investigation simply because she's an outspoken critic of the President Donald Trump.

"The full weight of the federal government is being brought down on a law-abiding elected official because she has dared to criticize the president," the former US president wrote on X, calling the probe "so appalling".

The White House defended the inquiry, saying the justice department was "focused on restoring law and order".

Last week, homeland security agents searched the Minnesota Democrat's Washington DC home as part of an investigation into her immigration status. Born in Somalia, Omar moved to the US with her family as a child.

US media outlets have reported that the probe is tied to her American citizenship and whether she lied about her age when she arrived in the US in 1995.

Questions have been raised about whether the age listed on Omar's citizenship application differed from her actual birth date.

Obama said in his X post on Sunday that her father became a naturalised citizen when she was 17, and not yet legally an adult, which then gave her citizenship.

"Now the Administration is actively trying to deport Congresswoman Omar, seemingly based solely on the unsubstantiated theory that she was actually 18 when her father was naturalized, and therefore is not a citizen," he wrote.

"If this becomes the new normal," he added, "there's no reason to believe it will stop with her - or that future presidents, in either party, won't do the same."

According to the US Citizenship and Immigration Services, a child born outside of the US automatically becomes a citizen when he or she has at least one parent who is a citizen by birth or naturalisation, or he or she is under the age of 18, and is a lawful permanent resident living in the custody of a citizen parent.

White House spokeswoman Lauren Bis denied the investigation was politically motivated.

"Unlike Joe Biden, President Trump has not weaponized the Department of Justice against his political foes," she said in an emailed statement to the BBC.

"The Department is focused on restoring law and order and keeping Americans safe."

Trump has often argued that federal criminal investigations against him as he campaigned for re-election were politically motivated.

The investigation into Omar could lead to the justice department seeking to "denaturalise" her, or revoke her citizenship. It would have to prove there were material lies in the naturalisation process.

In 2023, Republicans removed Omar from the House Foreign Affairs Committee for comments and tweets she made about Israel, which drew bipartisan criticism.

Omar has said that Trump has targeted her for years with "baseless lies and smear campaigns" and called the investigation "the latest escalation in his campaign of political intimidation".

But Trump has said the investigation had "nothing to do" with him, while describing Omar as a "terrible person" and a "complainer".

Federal agents reportedly seized her phone, computers, notebooks and passport in the raid a week ago.

Her lawyers have demanded the government return her belongings, CBS News, the BBC's US partner, has reported, arguing in a letter sent on Friday that the seizure of property had violated restrictions put in place by a judge to protect her work as a federal lawmaker.

The lawyers also alleged agents did not duly notify Omar or the House of Representatives general counsel that a search would be taking place and kept her from contacting her attorney for more than an hour, according to CBS.

Democrats characterised the raid as the president attempting to interfere with the legislative branch of government. Republicans, meanwhile, have said Omar should be treated the same as anyone else under the law.

When Obama first ran for president, and throughout his two terms in the White House, Trump repeatedly raised questions about his citizenship, asserting he was not born on American soil and was disqualified from serving in office. Obama released two records proving he had been born in Hawaii.

Obama did not mention that history in his X post on Sunday.

Are free-scoring Brighton genuine title contenders?

BBC News Mon, 19 Oct 2026 14:52:01 GMT

This video can not be played

'Why not?' - 'Breathtaking' Brighton in title race says Dublin

When Jack Hinshelwood unapologetically smashed home Brighton and Hove Albion's fifth goal of the game against bitter rivals Crystal Palace on Sunday, it completed a fourth straight Premier League win for the high-flying Seagulls - with an aggregate scoreline of 15-0.

Hinshelwood's volley from two yards out to wrap up a 5-0 victory was in stark contrast to his team-mate Diego Gomez's audacious effort from the halfway line that put Brighton two up in just the seventh minute of the A23 derby.

Fabian Hurzeler's free-scoring side have arguably been the most entertaining top-flight team to watch this season, but they have backed up their attacking flair with a robust defence. No team has scored more and no team has conceded fewer goals.

After seven games, they sit third on 16 points behind reigning champions Arsenal and table-toppers Manchester City, who have a 100% record. But can the Seagulls maintain their momentum and mount a serious title challenge?

"Why not?"

That's the opinion of Match of the Day pundit Dion Dublin, who played in Manchester United's 1992-93 title-winning side. "Because what we've seen of them this season is just togetherness, harmony... the manager's making good decisions.

"[Pascal] Gross is leading the line in regards to what goes on on the pitch and what is the right kind of way they want to play. And everybody's chipping in with goals. The look a very, very frightening team at the moment."

Shades of Barca and Beckham - Brighton aim to maintain superb start

How Brighton attract and develop the best young players ahead of their rivals

Timely recognition or long overdue? How Gross is proving all-time bargain

Brighton are the Premier League's leading goalscorers this season

In the summer of 2025, Brighton lost their top scorer Joao Pedro to Chelsea, and history repeated itself this year when the Blues lured veteran forward Danny Welbeck to Stamford Bridge.

Once again, however, the Seagulls' enviable data-led recruitment model, aided by club owner Tony Bloom's close links to Jamestown Analytics, appears to have found a promising replacement.

Having been used primarily as a substitute last season, Greece striker Charalampos Kostoulas has been entrusted to spearhead the attack, and the 19-year-old has repaid the faith shown in him by Hurzeler with three league goals and two assists.

Only Lamine Yamal has more goal involvements among teenagers in Europe's top five leagues this season.

Kostoulas has a strong supporting cast including Hinshelwood, Yasin Ayari, Malick Yalcouye and Maxim de Cuyper, not to mention a rejuvenated Pascal Gross pulling the strings from a deeper position.

With 11 league scorers already - while also being the beneficiaries of three own goals - Hurzeler's men are sharing the load impressively. As well as being the division's top scorers, Brighton have had the most shots on target and sit second for xG, shots and big chances.

In the top five European leagues, only Barcelona, with 39 goals from nine La Liga matches, have more domestic league goals than Brighton.

Equally as encouraging is how well they have coped defensively despite the loss of centre-back Jan Paul van Hecke and midfield anchorman Carlos Baleba. Luka Vuskovic looks to be a tremendous acquisition from Tottenham Hotspur, and he has helped the Seagulls, who remain unbeaten at home, record a league-high five clean sheets.

The rapid rise of a former art dealer to Europe's hottest young manager

There are only seven previous instances of a team scoring 23 or more goals after seven games of a Premier League season. All bar one have gone on to finish in the top three, with Manchester City winning the title in 2011-12 and 2022-23.

The outlier? Kevin Keegan's Newcastle United team of 1994-95, who faded and finished sixth. Comparisons have already been drawn between that side, dubbed 'The Entertainers', and the swagger of the current Brighton squad.

With that in mind, Alan Wares co-host of the Albion Roar podcast suggested that perhaps a Champions League place, rather than a full-blown title challenge, might be a more realistic aim.

"I think with the Premier League being seven games in and the other matches we've already played, I think the dream for us is sustainability. I wouldn't go for a target, just as high as possible," said Alan.

"The club is really wanting to qualify for Champions League at the end of the season but yes, we've made a good start - are we title contenders? It's way too early to consider that. I would say that, at the moment, is fantasy stuff. But every football fan's got to have their dream and our point is, why not?

"If we can continue this, and that is the main point we've got to look at, if we can be sustainable in what we're doing and what we achieve, then yes. Why not? Go for the sky, see what happens."

With Conference League football to juggle, it seems improbable Brighton's squad can last the pace with the likes of Arsenal for the duration of the season. Leicester City, the last outsiders to lift the title, do provide some hope. They were eighth with 12 points after seven games of their memorable 2015-16 triumph.

There is a chance Brighton's final league position could be affected by matters off the pitch.

Last month, an independent commission found Manchester City guilty of all charges related to serious breaches of the Premier League's financial rules over a nine-season period.

City are appealing against the verdict, meaning the severity and timing of any punishment - which could take the form of a points deduction - remain unknown.

Brighton have the chance to give City a fright when they travel to the Etihad on Halloween - one of four successive away games in all competitions - and the league table may well present a very different picture by the time November's international break comes around.

For now, Brighton are exactly where they deserve to be. And they're having great fun in the process.

Tennis star Svitolina says emotional toll of Ukraine war led to Monfils separation

BBC News Mon, 19 Oct 2026 14:20:03 GMT

Ukrainian tennis star Elina Svitolina has announced the end of her marriage with French former tennis player Gaël Monfils, citing the emotional impact of the war in her country.

The 32-year-old, who is ranked number six in the world, wrote in a heartfelt post on Instagram about the effect the conflict and "what the war has done to me inside".

"This is the most difficult thing I have ever had to share," she wrote, saying "I need to find my way back to myself". Svitolina said she felt she could not do that within her marriage.

She said her husband Monfils, 40, "listened" and "respected what I need with a strength and grace I will never forget".

"Some battles happen deep inside you, and no amount of love from someone else can win them for you," the four-time Grand Slam semi-finalist wrote.

It was "the hardest thing I have ever had to tell the person I love", Svitolina said.

"Everyone knows how much Ukraine means to me," Svitolina, who grew up in Odesa, said.

Ukraine's Black Sea port city has been heavily bombed by Russia throughout the war.

Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.

"What you didn't see were the sleepless nights, the doubts, and the feeling of slowly losing myself."

The tennis power couple married in 2021 and have one child together - a four-year-old daughter called Skai.

Svitolina said her daughter "will always come first", adding "our marriage is ending, but our family is not".

Monfils, a former world number six, was expected to play the final tournament of his career at next month's Paris Masters in an emotional farewell.

However, the two-time Grand Slam semi-finalist's retirement was effectively confirmed last week when he appeared on the International Tennis Integrity Authority's list of retired players.

Once a player removes themselves from anti-doping protocols, they are not eligible to compete in professional tournaments.

Monfils, who won 13 titles on the ATP Tour, is preparing to start a new career in finance after joining a Swiss wealth management firm.

Australian MP critically injured after being hit by car in apparent attack

BBC News Mon, 19 Oct 2026 14:09:54 GMT

Australian MP Helen Haines is critically ill in hospital in Melbourne after being hit by a car in what Prime Minister Anthony Albanese says may have been a deliberate attack.

The independent MP, 65, was struck outside her constituency office in Wangaratta, in the state of Victoria, on Monday afternoon.

A man, 43, from the nearby town of Tarrawingee was detained at the scene by a passerby and police say a knife was found in the car.

Police are investigating whether it was an "intentional act" but say they do not believe there is an "ongoing threat to the community".

Political leaders have expressed shock and dismay, with Albanese saying "there is no place for violence in a democracy".

While Albanese said it was too early to understand the motive behind what had happened, he did say the political temperature had been rising in Australia.

His Home Affairs Minister Tony Burke backed up that statement with figures showing that reports of threatening or harassing behaviour towards politicians had risen from 951 to 1,067 in the past year.

Haines was hit by a white Toyota Landcruiser at 15:35 (04:35 GMT) outside her office on Murphy Street in Wangaratta, police say.

The town, which has a population of around 30,000, is a few hours north-east of Melbourne.

A witness told Australian broadcaster ABC they had heard a bang and seen a woman pinned between two cars.

Haines was initially taken to a hospital in Wangaratta but later moved to Melbourne by helicopter.

After being subdued and detained by the passerby, the suspect was arrested by police.

Announcing that counter terror police were involved in the investigation, the prime minister said: "This wasn't an accident. There was a deliberate act, it would appear."

In a statement, Victoria Police said: "At this stage, police are investigating as to whether this was an intentional act.

"It is not known yet if the parties are known to each other... The investigation remains ongoing."

Although not necessarily a household name across Australia, in the political sphere Helen Haines is both well-known and well regarded as an anti-corruption campaigner.

There has been an outpouring of messages from politicians and party leaders across the breadth of the political spectrum. In an age of increasingly divisive politics, she is seen by many as a unifying force.

The independent MP has only been a federal parliamentarian for a relatively short time, having been elected in 2019. However, in that time she has become an influential advocate for integrity in politics.

Haines proposed legislation for a national anti-corruption watchdog in 2021, and has been credited for driving the creation of the National Anti-Corruption Commission under Labor in the previous parliamentary term.

She currently sits on the parliamentary committee responsible for its oversight.

Haines has often banded together with other key independents on issues that include climate action and gender equality.

Allegra Spender, another independent MP who has collaborated with Haines, called her "the best of us".

An Australian parliamentary report warned last year that threats and physical attacks had increased "significantly over the past decade".

A threat assessment by the Australian Security Intelligence Organisation - the country's equivalent of MI5 in the UK - warned last year that the risk of politically motivated violence was "already flashing red".

Albanese became emotional as he talked about Haines in a live television interview on ABC's 7:30.

He appeared close to tears when asked whether he and his colleagues talked among themselves about the threats and risks they face.

"Yes," he replied, adding: "My concern at this point in time is for one, one of my colleagues."

He described Haines as having "integrity". In other political reaction:

Apu returns to The Simpsons with new voice after race row

BBC News Mon, 19 Oct 2026 13:22:24 GMT

The Simpsons character Apu has returned to the show voiced by a new actor, after almost a decade away amid accusations of racial stereotypes.

Apu Nahasapeemapetilon - to give the much-loved shopkeeper his full name - re-appeared in Sunday's episode on US network Fox, titled The Revengening, but now voiced by India-born, US-raised actor Sunil Malhotra.

The character has been seen but not heard around Springfield since the October 2017 episode The Serfsons, and his big return to action had reportedly been a closely guarded secret.

Malhotra said in a statement posted on Instagram that it feels like a reclamation. "It truly is his homecoming," he said.

The character, who has been part of the long-running American animation series since 1990, was previously voiced by a white actor, Hank Azaria, putting on a heavy Indian accent.

Indian-American comic Hari Kondabolu made a documentary in 2017, titled the Problem With Apu, saying the character - a South Asian convenience store clerk - was founded on racial stereotypes.

The following year, an episode of The Simpsons addressed the controversy surrounding the Indian character for the first time, making a nod to the accusations but some viewers found it insufficient.

Others defended the show and said all its characters were stereotypes.

Azaria first announced he was stepping down from the role in 2020, and he later told Dax Shepherd's Armchair Expert podcast: "Part of me feels like I need to go around to every single Indian person in this country and personally apologise."

Speaking to Variety ahead of the weekend's latest episode, Azaria's replacement Malhotra explained: "When my agent called me about a Simpsons audition, I knew exactly what role it was for, and the idea actually made my stomach sink.

"But admittedly, part of me was also curious. It had been eight years since Apu had spoken on the show, and it got me thinking: Did the writers' room look different now?"

The Grey's Anatomy and The Legend of Korra actor continued: "Could they bring him back in a way that acknowledged and apologised for past mistakes?

"Could I make the character my own, and reclaim him in some way? And could they achieve all of that in an unmistakably Simpsons way that didn't disappoint fans?"

After years of Apu having become a mere background character, Malhotra said he spoke with showrunner Matt Selman and co-executive producer Cesar Mazariegos about how they could make the returning fans' favourite more culturally appropriate for 2026.

"It was the beginning of a deeply collaborative experience that I hope is equally satisfying for long-time fans of The Simpsons and for other South Asian kids who, like me, stopped watching at some point along the way."

Apu's wife, Manjula, will now be voiced Janina Gavankar - who previously appeared in Apple TV's The Morning Show - taking over from Jan Hooks and Tress MacNeille.

In Apu's haunting comeback episode, a man in a "Daft Monk" Halloween costume - a play on French electro duo Daft Punk - appears to be accidentally killed over and over again by Springfield residents.

A year on he returns to wreak his revenge.

Eventually he summons everyone to the Springfield City Hall, takes off his helmet and reveals himself to be Apu.

He then shares his story of having been nearly killed dozens of times, before winding up on The Island of Forgotten Garbage, where he was healed by Dr Nick.

"I am the man you left for dead. I am the one you pretended never existed," he declares.

Just as he is about to set the city hall ablaze, Marge Simpson - serving as a thinly-veiled mouthpiece for the producers - intervenes, telling him: "Apu, we're so sorry we left you for dead. Believe me, we wanted to do the right thing."

Her famous bratty son Bart adds: "But we were so scared, and just didn't know what to do."

Bart's father Homer then offers to sacrifice himself to save the rest of the town, reminding viewers of how important Apu has been to the town.

"You were on our bowling teams, our barbershop quartets, our dad rock cover bands," said Homer.

"We took you for granted. I took you for granted."

The episode will be made available for viewers in the UK to watch on Disney+ next week.

Kylie Jenner's debut at Victoria's Secret Fashion Show in $50m bra sparks mixed reaction

BBC News Mon, 19 Oct 2026 13:16:22 GMT

Reality TV star Kylie Jenner has sparked mixed reaction after making her Victoria's Secret Fashion Show debut in a $50m (£37m) bra.

The make-up mogul surprised the crowd at the lingerie giant's annual show on Sunday while wearing the famed Fantasy Bra, which was made of 18-carat gold and 4,410 diamonds, according to the designer.

The Fantasy Bra has been a key feature of the show over the years and wearing it is typically seen as an honour and defining moment for the chosen model.

The Kardashians star, 29, being selected to wear the piece delighted some fans, while many others criticised the brand for not giving the opportunity to a veteran supermodel.

Social media and marketing expert Joel Marlinarson says the moment was well-engineered and generated "a lot of conversation" on what it means for the "future of modelling and social media".

"Of course Kylie represents a new era of celebrity where brands are prioritising who's going to bring the most eyeballs, as opposed to who fits the cookie cutter definition of a model," he tells BBC Newsbeat.

Marlinarson says young viewers have a connection with Jenner having grown up watching her on social media and through her reality show with her Kardashian sisters.

However, he says there will be a section of the audience who remembers "the iconic Naomi Campbell era of fashion" who might see Jenner being given this moment as a "betrayal of what they know".

"Ultimately, this represents this new era of marketing where brands, particularly Victoria's Secret and legacy brands, they don't want to take risks," he says.

"They want to bring in somebody who they know is going to generate eyeballs, who's going to generate those headlines and who can consistently raise a crowd and that's exactly what Victoria's Secret has done."

Some fans cheered on Jenner in the comments of a video shared on Victoria's Secret Instagram page unveiling the dramatic look.

While many others branded it as "pure disrespect to real models" and questioned why she was picked out of a "room full of talented models".

One said the show has "gone from iconic glamour to an influencer circus" and they felt "social media clout and performative inclusivity have replaced real modeling talent, elegance, and runway presence".

Chief creative officer at Victoria's Secret, Adam Selman, told Vogue that Jenner was picked for being a "cultural powerhouse".

"Kylie really extends beyond fashion, beyond culture, beyond TV, beyond one singular thing," he adds.

"That's the exact same thing that we do.

"Like, the show is so big, it's true entertainment, and I think that she is a great catalyst for that."

British model Summer Nesbeth tells Newsbeat that she feels Victoria's Secret choosing Jenner was their attempt to keep up with young fans.

"She's an influencer with a lot of power and we are in the social media age," says the 25-year-old, who has walked the runway at New York Fashion Week.

The lingerie brand's catwalk show was scrapped after its 2018 edition drew low ratings, as well as criticism that it was sexist, outdated and lacked diversity.

It returned in 2024, with a promise to "celebrate all women" and featured more a diverse range of talent, including Ashley Graham's appearance as a plus-sized model.

Victoria's Secret created this year's Fantasy Bra in collaboration with jewellery brand Jacob & Co, who said it was the "most valuable" one ever created and took 15 artists more than 1,000 hours to create.

Nesbeth believes the focus on the bra shows "how detached we are".

"People can't eat, people can't afford to keep their lights on," she says.

"I think there's a lot of things to say about where we're focussing our attention and where we're putting our money."

BBC Newsbeat has contacted Victoria's Secret.

The portraits that helped bring the lost Aberfan children home

BBC News Mon, 19 Oct 2026 05:28:02 GMT

For almost 60 years, many of Aberfan's lost children have watched over living rooms, hallways and family gatherings across the village.

Some were painted from faded school photographs. Others were shaped by the memories of grieving parents, who wrote letters to an artist describing the children they had lost: the colour of their eyes, their favourite clothes, the flashes of personality that made them unique.

The portraits arrived in the years after one of Wales' darkest days. And for many families, they became far more than paintings.

In a new BBC programme, Unseen: The Aberfan Portraits, some have shared their paintings and spoken about how the art helped them grieve.

"It brought her back to life," said Denise Morgan, whose younger sister Annette was among those who died in the Aberfan disaster.

On 21 October 1966, a coal tip collapsed above the village. The torrent of slurry engulfed Pantglas Junior School and nearby homes, killing 144 people including 116 children.

The disaster remains woven into everyday life in Aberfan. It is felt most strongly in the memorial garden on the site of the fallen school, and among the white arched monuments of the cemetery.

But it is also felt in the empty places left behind at family tables, in childhood bedrooms which were suddenly occupied by one child instead of two, and in the portraits that came to represent those who never grew up.

Jeanette Keane has fond memories of her sister Edwina.

"It was just such an idyllic childhood really," she said. "She was very quiet and gentle. She had a mischievous streak as well."

The morning of the disaster remains painfully vivid, as Jeanette recalled how Edwina quickly returned home before the school day had begun.

"She came running back and she said, 'Mammy, I forgot to give you a kiss'," Jeanette said. "And so my mother gave her a kiss.

"My mother always said that, at that time, she wanted to keep her home.

"And my mother rued that day for the rest of her life. She just wished she'd listened to herself."

Jeanette's father found eight-year-old Edwina trapped beneath the wreckage.

"She was alive," Jeanette said, but it was a heartbreaking situation.

"He couldn't get her out because the roof would have fallen in.

"The men all said, 'Teddy, you can't and my father laid by the side of her, held her hand and she suffocated."

The trauma echoed through the years that followed the disaster.

"It explains to me why we used to hear him walking back and fore in the corridor at night, banging his head on the wall," Jeanette said.

"It wasn't a very happy life afterwards. Everything changed."

Denise Morgan was attending a different school when word began to spread that something terrible had happened in Aberfan, where her little sister Annette was in class.

"They didn't really give us any details," she said. Racing off the train, the devastation was clear.

"When we looked across to Aberfan, we could just see this black mass."

As rescue efforts began, families across the village waited for news. Some of the memories remain too painful to revisit.

For the surviving siblings, that sense of loss seemed to arrive in the most ordinary moments.

"We always slept together," said Jeanette. "And suddenly I was alone."

Denise remembered the same absence.

"We shared a bed... and then she was gone."

The scale of grief was impossible to escape.

"In our street, five children were lost in 25 houses," Denise said.

"Four children died in my street," Jeanette recalled.

In an era when grief was rarely discussed openly, many survivors were left to process the tragedy alone.

Hundreds of miles away in Llandudno, Conwy county, one man was following events in Aberfan on television and in the newspapers.

Artist William Richardson had no connection to Aberfan, with his skills being used most often on the pier where he sketched caricatures of visitors and celebrities performing in town.

But he was deeply affected by what he saw. According to his children, Jean and Ken, he felt compelled to do something for the bereaved families who had lost their sons and daughters.

"He saw it on the news and he was so moved by it, he decided to paint them," Jean said.

"He just wanted to give something back, to show he cared," added Ken.

Richardson never sought payment or recognition. Instead, he began creating portraits of children killed in the disaster, working from school photographs and detailed descriptions supplied by parents.

"The parents would write to him and tell him about the children," Jean said. "What colour their eyes were, their hair, what they wore."

"They even sent bits of fabric so he could get it right," Ken added.

Jean said her father wanted to capture more than their appearance.

"He'd ask about their personalities, so he could build that into the painting."

Over the years, Richardson is believed to have produced about 100 portraits. As the collection grew, so too did his connection with families in Aberfan.

For his children, the portraits became a constant presence.

"We were surrounded by them for years," said Jean. "All these faces.

"It's like looking back at old friends now."

"We couldn't believe the likeness," Denise said. "That was her.

"It brought her back to life."

Jeanette remembered the effect on her parents when Edwina's portrait arrived.

"I remember my father crying when the painting came," she said. "If they could have hugged it, they would have."

The portraits soon became part of daily life in homes across the village.

"She was there at Christmas, at parties, always in the room," Denise said of Annette's painting.

"In our street, every house had one."

For survivors, such as Gaynor Madgwick, who escaped from Pantglas Junior School when the tip collapsed, the images served another purpose.

"They start conversations," she said. "People begin talking about their children again."

For families who had struggled to find the words, the portraits offered a way to keep memories alive.

"You walked in and their presence was there," Gaynor said.

Jeanette agreed: "It was very, very important to us. It felt like she was always with us while it was there."

As the generation directly affected by Aberfan grows older, a new question is emerging: what should happen to the portraits?

Many remain cherished family possessions. Others have already passed into the care of younger generations, while some have been entrusted to a local museum.

Other families have made different choices.

Gaynor described the heartbreaking decision her family faced after their mother died.

"Taking them down, you're not taking a painting, you're taking them," she said.

The portraits were buried alongside their mother.

"We buried them with Mam in a white box, like a little coffin.

"We placed them facing each other.

"It felt like burying them again."

For Jeanette, the future of Edwina's portrait is a source of concern.

"I worry about what will happen to the painting," she said. "I want people to see them."

Denise feels the same pull between preservation and possession.

"It's a treasure," she said. "I could never part with it."

Nearly six decades after the disaster, the paintings remain extraordinary objects. They were created by a man who had never met the children, but his kindness ensured they were treasured by the families who received and loved them.

By painstakingly recreating the faces of children who had been lost, William Richardson gave something precious back to a community living with unimaginable grief.

For many families, the portraits did more than capture memories. They brought the children home.

Unseen: The Aberfan Portraits is available on BBC iPlayer and will be shown on BBC One Wales at 22:40 BST on Monday 19 October

Inside the shadowy world of anti-Putin sabotage from within Russia

BBC News Mon, 19 Oct 2026 00:06:25 GMT

Contains some strong language.

Two Russian men secretly working for Ukraine's intelligence services have given rare accounts of operations they claim to have been involved with, that have targeted military assets and personnel inside Russia.

One of the men, whom we are calling Ivan, claims to have played a role from Russia in Ukrainian drone attacks on strategic bombers and munitions factories on his home soil.

He features in a BBC World Service documentary about the shadowy world of Russian saboteurs.

The documentary, by independent Polish journalist Marcin Mamon, also features a man we are calling Foma, a Russian living in exile in Poland.

Foma runs a network of undercover volunteers in Russia, that surveils high-level officers that the GUR - Ukraine's military intelligence service - is considering targeting, he says. He stresses they are never involved in the attacks themselves.

He was also tight-lipped about who they were surveilling, but after Lt Gen Fanil Sarvarov was assassinated in December last year in Moscow, Foma admitted he had provided the Ukrainians with intelligence on him.

There have been previous media reports of Russian sabotage groups, but it is rare to get access to someone operating on the ground, like Ivan, explaining alleged activities.

The GUR has confirmed that Ivan and Foma are both working for the agency. But it also has acknowledged that it cannot know the full picture. When Ivan's handler was pressed on whether he could be trusted, the handler replied: "I'm not sure of anyone, except myself."

And both the GUR and the men are cautious about how much detail they share, making it impossible to verify the activities the men claim to have carried out.

The broad tactics Ivan and Foma describe, however, have been acknowledged by the Ukrainian authorities. Kyiv has spoken of its strategy of co-ordinated drone attacks on what it claims are legitimate targets inside Russia, and has acknowledged it uses secret agents for this.

There have also been several political assassinations in Russia since the start of the war. As a matter of policy, Ukraine never officially admits or claims responsibility for targeted attacks, though a Ukrainian intelligence officer has previously admitted to the BBC it was behind the killing of senior military figure Lt Gen Igor Kirillov in December 2024.

It is difficult to confirm how many Russians are doing this kind of work for Ukraine. According to Foma, they number about 300-500, though this is impossible to verify.

Ivan and Foma say they are both opposed not just to Russia's war in Ukraine, but to President Vladimir Putin's regime - and believe his political future depends on the war's outcome.

"At the moment... I think the [Putin] regime might fall if they lose the war… Through our actions... we are trying to speed this up," Ivan says.

His work, he told Mamon, involved surveilling military sites, and locating places to hide drone components, in preparation for potential attacks on Russian assets.

"When these [drone] components are combined… it turns out a formidable weapon, which with a single blow can destroy an object that costs many, many millions of dollars," Ivan said.

He sent Mamon a video which showed him apparently hiding explosives near a Russian military airfield.

If he had been caught, he would have been charged with terrorism, and jailed for decades.

Foma's work is different - he operates remotely, training his volunteers in Russia, online. Mamon watched him conducting one such tutorial - on how to trail a senior military official marked for surveillance.

"You will get a file... from me or a colleague… with the proposed target. The file will contain [the target's] photo, his data, his details, date of birth, age, and a description of him. There'll be information on his car, if he has one. When you go to the target, don't take a phone," he told his volunteers.

Foma was once part of the Russian elite, so he claims to have a unique set of contacts and constant flow of insider information.

He showed Mamon on his laptop how he mapped military targets.

"This shows a database... the location of storage warehouses, and military units. Where generals live… Where the pilots of strategic bombers who shell Ukraine live.

"In order to break the system, you need to understand how it works. Then you can aim for their weak points."

He said there were about "three dozen" people in his network split between Russia, Ukraine and elsewhere in Europe, with the contingent outside Russia providing logistical support, such as tracking targets' digital footprints.

Foma stressed that the GUR suggests the targets to be surveilled, but that he and his team check for themselves that these individuals should be considered military criminals.

"As a rule… we also check the data [on that person]… Only after that we say whether we work or not."

But he argued that his team's actions were justified.

"I want people who do terrible things on behalf of Putin and Russia in Ukraine… to understand that they'll have to pay for it. I want them to get scared."

Foma stressed that he only passed on intelligence to the Ukrainians, and his network did not carry out any assassinations themselves.

Of the assassination of Gen Sarvarov, killed in December 2025, he later texted Mamon to say: "Keeping track of him took quite an effort. He lived alternately with his mistress and his colleague. Covered his tracks and constantly changed his schedule."

But Foma did not share any plans with Mamon and the BBC in advance.

Ivan, however, was tight-lipped about the work he had been involved with, even after the event.

Foma did his own digging on Ivan.

After checking with his military intelligence contacts in both Ukraine and Russia, he thought it likely that Ivan had been involved in a plan to strike Russia's largest military drone factory at Yelabuga in June last year. One person was reported to have been killed in the incident.

Ivan stressed that the aim is always to try to avoid harming civilians.

Operations have clearly been risky for Ivan too.

"The most serious case was when my car was stopped for inspection and I had the handmade explosives on me. The risk was very high - however as you can see, I was not detected," he said.

To mitigate the risk of being compromised, "there is no clear structure" to the work, he said, adding he had never met and did not know the identity of others he had been working alongside.

Foma has the same rule for his operatives.

"As soon as you start gathering people in groups, in general chats… leaving a mark on the internet, with a high probability this whole group will be quickly detained or destroyed," he said.

Ivan stressed there were few people left in Russia suitable for this kind of work.

"Most of the ideological people have either left the country or are already behind bars," he said.

Many Russians involved in sabotage work on their native soil are therefore either oblivious - for example lorry drivers unaware that their cargoes have been compromised - or are individuals who have been paid, the BBC understands.

Ivan, on the other hand, says he is doing this work for ideological reasons - he used to be a member of the political opposition. As such, his movements would be expected to be monitored closely by the Russian authorities.

So it was a surprise that he managed to frequently leave Russia and return.

Mamon persuaded Ivan to drive him into the Georgian desert, where they could speak freely - and asked him how the Ukrainians could trust him.

"You go to a third country… where [Ukraine's] agents meet you… and conduct lie detector tests," Ivan told him.

Mamon asked Ivan to put him in touch with one of his GUR handlers in Ukraine. This man immediately rang Ivan on speaker phone - apparently demonstrating that Ivan worked for him. They spoke in code, referring to "repairs at the school".

But later, the handler admitted he could not rule out the possibility Ivan might work for the Russians too, either voluntarily or under duress.

Foma thinks the fact that Ivan can travel freely does not necessarily constitute a red flag.

"There are all sorts of holes in [the country's governance], and if you know them, or are just lucky, then you can jump through the holes… and live in the system. Like a mouse in a piece of cheese," he told Mamon.

Perhaps more compellingly, if Ivan had also been spying for FSB, it would seem likely that he would share what he knew of Ukraine's attack plans with the Russian agency. More than a year before a devastating strike by more than 100 Ukrainian drones, Ivan had been telling Marcin there would be a major attack on strategic bombers on military airfields across Russia, though he never said when or where.

Marcin asked Ivan how he coped with the work.

"Fear is always present," he said. "It follows me everywhere. Even if you don't do anything, you're still afraid. This is Russia."

But he was optimistic that eventually his life would change.

"Putin won't live forever," he said.

Noise-cancelling headphones prevent vomiting after surgery

New Scientist October 17, 2026

Nausea and vomiting are common after surgery, but wearing noise-cancelling headphones during the procedure helps prevent these unpleasant side effects. This simple intervention also supports the idea that our brain processes sounds even when we’re not consciously aware of our surroundings.

“That data is really encouraging and is actually in line with decades of research showing that anaesthesia is not simply an off switch,” says Vigi Katlowitz at the Baylor College of Medicine in Houston.

Powerful new book explores how noise has taken over the world

Nausea and vomiting are common side effects of anaesthetics. Patients are routinely given drugs to prevent them, but Huayue Liu at the First Affiliated Hospital of Soochow University in Suzhou, China, and his colleagues wanted to investigate a non-pharmacological approach and presented their results at the Anesthesiology conference in San Diego.

Advertisement

The team recruited 192 patients who had keyhole gynaecological surgery under general anaesthesic. Half were randomly assigned noise-blocking ear defenders, which they wore from the start of anaesthesia until the end of surgery. All the patients received standard anaesthesia and anti-nausea medication.

Free newsletter

Within 48 hours of the surgery, 35 per cent of those wearing ear defenders experienced nausea or vomiting, compared with 52 per cent of those without them. The researchers also found that symptoms were less severe among those whose hearing had been protected, defined as the patients vomiting less and it having less of an impact on their daily life.

Operating theatres aren’t generally quiet places, with Liu recording average noise levels of 66 decibels – around the level of a normal conversation – during the study.

The relationship between sound, nausea and vomiting, and anaesthesia is unclear. However, the latter affects the nervous system, and noise is thought to trigger a stress response that activates the autonomic nervous system. This helps regulate involuntary bodily functions, such as heart rate, and interacts with the brainstem pathways involved in nausea and vomiting.

From dementia to heart attacks, hearing loss has been linked to a wide range of effects across the body, and the condition is on the rise. Fortunately, we’re learning how best to safeguard this crucial sense and how we might be able to reverse the damage

However, Liu stresses that the researchers didn’t look into the mechanism behind how ear defenders prevent nausea and vomiting, so the idea of them dampening this response “remains a hypothesis”.

Nevertheless, the results tell us more about brain activity under anaesthesia. “The biological plausibility is that general anaesthesia produces unconsciousness without necessarily eliminating all neural processing of sound,” says Liu.

Liu hopes to one day conduct a larger trial at multiple locations that measures noise exposure relative to nervous system activity among patients under general anaesthetic.

Are we about to solve the greatest mystery of the neutrino?

New Scientist October 19, 2026

The funicular railway carries me downwards into the mountain, and the familiar, above-ground world vanishes. The tunnel is steep, bored through solid granite, and we gradually descend – down, down, down – for nearly a quarter of an hour. After a while, the pressure makes my ears pop.

When the passageway finally ends, we are 700 metres underground, and I can see a vast subterranean complex of caverns and pipes spread out beneath me. It is quite a sight. But then again, you would expect nothing less from an experiment that could change particle physics forever.

I have come to the Jiangmen Underground Neutrino Observatory, better known as JUNO, a machine in southern China designed to catch ghostly particles called neutrinos. These are the tiniest fragments of reality we know of, so fleeting that they barely exist at all. Studying them has already overturned some of our most basic assumptions about the universe – and there are good reasons to think they hold the key to some of its deepest remaining secrets. “Neutrino mass provides us with the only particle physics evidence that the standard model of particle physics is incomplete,” says physicist Silvia Pascoli at the University of Bologna, Italy.

Advertisement

Emergence: The mysterious concept that holds the key to consciousness

When it comes to the fundamental ingredients of reality, we know an awful lot about what is out there – but also know that we aren’t yet seeing the whole picture. The standard model of particle physics is a list of these ingredients, the fundamental particles and forces that make up the cosmos. There is an elegant symmetry to it, and it has been nothing short of a spectacular success. But it doesn’t include gravity or explain the nature of dark matter. Then there is antimatter. Every kind of matter particle has an antimatter counterpart, with the same mass but opposite properties, such as electric charge. When matter and antimatter meet, they annihilate each other in a burst of energy. That creates a puzzle because, as far as we understand, the early universe should have produced matter and antimatter in equal amounts – raising the question of why matter now dominates.

Because of these kinds of mysteries, physicists tend to believe that there must be something beyond the standard model – some piece of the puzzle that we are missing. And there is one lead that looks increasingly promising. Neutrinos barely interact with anything – trillions of them pass through your body every second. Yet we know they have a very, very small mass. This mass seems to manifest in strange ways, however, and we aren’t even sure how they get it. If we pull at this thread, might the mysteries of the standard model begin to unravel?

The first hint of neutrinos’ strangeness arose in another underground site: a gold mine in South Dakota. There, in the late 1960s, physicist Raymond Davis Jr. filled a huge tank with a chlorine-containing cleaning fluid to measure neutrinos streaming towards Earth from the sun. Like nearly all neutrino detectors, it was buried to screen out other particles, which would be blocked by the rock, while the neutrinos would pass through. Occasionally, a neutrino would strike a chlorine atom in the tank, transforming it into radioactive argon-37 that Davis could then count. But when he ran the numbers, there was a problem: around two-thirds of the neutrinos physicists had expected never showed up.

‘Dark photon’ theory of light aims to tear up a century of physics

Thanks to a gradual series of discoveries, we now know that, like the other matter particles in the standard model, neutrinos come in three types, called flavours. There is the electron neutrino, the muon neutrino and the tau neutrino. “Why nature is made like this, we have no idea, but that’s what we observe,” says Pascoli.

Then, around the year 2000, physicists at other neutrino experiments discovered that neutrinos have an additional peculiarity. As they travel, they can change from one flavour into another, a metamorphosis known as neutrino oscillation. An electron neutrino, the kind produced in the sun, might arrive at Earth as a muon or tau neutrino.

So, Davis’s detector in the gold mine – which had been designed to reveal the effects of electron neutrinos – wasn’t missing two-thirds of its quarry after all. Those neutrinos had simply changed flavour during their journey to Earth. “This was an absolutely gigantic discovery that had been building up for a long time,” says theoretical physicist André de Gouvêa at Northwestern University in Illinois.

The same experiments revealed another weird neutrino property. The oscillation is possible only because the three flavours don’t each correspond to a distinct mass. An electron neutrino isn’t simply lighter or heavier than a muon neutrino; none of the flavours has a single, well-defined mass. Instead, there are three neutrino “mass states”, and each is a strange quantum mixture of all three flavours at once. As they travel through space, the balance between these masses – and therefore the flavour we observe – changes. But what exact values make up that mixture still elude us.

Confused? If so, you’re in good company. “So, in the standard model, neutrinos don’t have mass – but now we know they do,” says physicist Anezka Klustova at Imperial College London. “But we don’t know what those masses are, and we don’t know how they get them.”

The fact that the masses are extraordinarily small adds to the intrigue. The disparity between the mass of an electron and a neutrino is roughly the difference between a fully loaded station wagon and a single playing card. For physicists, this vast gulf raises the question of whether neutrinos acquire their mass in a different way from other matter particles, whose masses arise through their interaction with the Higgs boson.

If so, that could fling open a new window on reality. Some proposed mechanisms for generating neutrino mass would violate rules about how reality functions that physicists currently assume to be true. That, in turn, could shed light on deeper puzzles, including the question of why matter won out over antimatter. “It is possible that whatever is giving the neutrinos a non-zero mass is also directly responsible for the origin of matter itself,” says de Gouvêa.

These questions about neutrino mass prompted the construction of JUNO. And one thing is for sure: we have come an awfully long way from Davis’s glorified tank of cleaning fluid. JUNO’s centrepiece is a vast acrylic sphere filled with 20,000 tonnes of a special fluid called a scintillator. About 53 kilometres away, the Yangjiang and Taishan nuclear power plants continuously produce a powerful and very clean stream of electron antineutrinos – the antimatter partners to electron neutrinos. A fraction of the antineutrinos are piped to JUNO, and when one interacts with the scintillator fluid, it produces a tiny flash. Thousands of spherical, golden orbs are positioned around the edges of the sphere to amplify these flashes.

The scale of the engineering takes my breath away. The cavern housing the detector could swallow a 14-storey building. Sadly, when I visit, the whole structure has been draped in black plastic – although perhaps it is fitting that this machine searching for the most elusive particles is itself hidden from view.

One of JUNO’s first goals is to resolve a tricky aspect of the puzzle around neutrino masses. Although we don’t know the exact masses of the three neutrino mass states, we do know that two of the states appear to be close together. This leaves open two possible configurations of the mass states: the normal and inverted hierarchies (see graphic below). These mass states are imprinted onto ordinary neutrinos and antineutrinos in the same way, so the fact that JUNO works mainly with the latter isn’t an issue.

Working out which hierarchy is the right one could help constrain what the individual masses actually are and narrow competing explanations of how neutrinos get them. One of the most intriguing possibilities is known as the “seesaw mechanism”, first proposed in the 1980s. It proposes that undiscovered neutrinos exist that are enormously heavy and therefore extremely difficult to observe. Their gargantuan mass would be linked to the tiny masses of the familiar neutrinos we see today – push one end of the seesaw up and the other drops. “This is an explanation which most of the neutrino theories consider plausible, and it also explains why neutrinos are much lighter than the [other matter particles],” says Pascoli.

Another possibility is that neutrinos get their masses indirectly, through interactions with other particles that have yet to be discovered. Their mass would emerge only through a more complicated quantum process, naturally making it much smaller. But intriguingly, in some versions of this idea, one of those undiscovered particles could be the mysterious dark matter that makes up most of the matter in the universe. It is important to say that both hypotheses are broad-brush and don’t offer exact predictions.

The daring idea that time is an illusion and how we could prove it

Still, JUNO should be able to help us. As the antineutrinos travel the 53 km odyssey from the power plants to the detectors, the different masses in the superposition leave behind a delicate interference pattern in the neutrinos’ energies: a succession of tiny peaks and dips whose precise positions depend on whether the third mass state lies above or below the other two. Measure that pattern accurately enough, and JUNO can begin to tease out the ordering. A smaller companion experiment, the Taishan Antineutrino Observatory, sits much closer to the Taishan reactor. There, it can measure the antineutrinos before they have had much of a chance to oscillate, giving JUNO a reference.

In June, the JUNO Collaboration published results that put it on track to produce a competitive measurement of the mass ordering in the next few years. These initial results lean towards the normal ordering, but more data will be needed before physicists can draw a firm conclusion.

Even then, we probably won’t have a bulletproof answer on how neutrinos get their mass. Instead, JUNO will act like a sieve, making some theories look more plausible while putting others under strain. If the normal ordering result does hold up, for instance, that would fit naturally with some of the simplest seesaw models. An inverted ordering, by contrast, could rule out those versions or force theorists to make them more elaborate. “By doing these neutrino experiments, I don’t think we’d learn all the answers, but we would get a lot of circumstantial evidence that points us in the right direction,” says de Gouvêa.

In a sense, JUNO is just the start of what could be a neutrino revolution in physics. Hot on its heels are two other epic detectors: Hyper-Kamiokande in Japan, which is set to start running next year, and DUNE in the US, due to open in the early 2030s. Both experiments will also be able to probe the neutrino mass ordering. But more importantly, they will search for whether neutrinos and antineutrinos behave differently.

Both Hyper-Kamiokande and DUNE will create beams of muon neutrinos by smashing high-energy protons into a solid target, like graphite. Unlike JUNO, though, the experiments have the luxury of controlling their neutrino source. They can switch their beams on and off and choose whether to produce neutrinos or their antimatter counterparts. The difficulty is that the results they detect will be affected by several tangled factors will affect the results, including the neutrino mass ordering. If JUNO can pin that down first, Hyper-Kamiokande and DUNE will have one fewer unknown to disentangle. With these three detectors working together, we could finally have answers to the neutrino riddles that have plagued us for so long.

The answers may hold sway far beyond the realms of particle physics. Neutrinos’ individual gravitational influence is negligible, but there are so many of them that, over cosmic time, they can affect how matter gathers into clusters, galaxies and stars. That makes them unusually interesting, given that our cosmological models are starting to show signs of strain.

Take dark energy, the unknown force that appears to be accelerating the expansion of the universe at an ever-increasing pace. The accepted understanding has long been that dark energy is a constant. But last year’s results from the Dark Energy Spectroscopic Instrument seemed to show that it may, in fact, be weakening. And there are other tensions, too. Matter in the universe appears, by some measures, to be slightly less clumped than expected. This suggests that something may have suppressed the growth of the universe’s structure over billions of years.

Could that something be neutrinos? Possibly. Because they move rapidly through the early universe, they resist being trapped inside growing clumps of matter and can smooth out structure. The heavier neutrinos are in total, the stronger that effect becomes. All of this means that the results from experiments like JUNO will help those studying the universe check whether their models make sense. “Neutrino properties can be very helpful in tensions like these,” says cosmologist William Giarè at the University of Hawaiʻi.

There could also be one final curtain call for JUNO. The hope is that it will run long enough to catch an extremely rare event: a star exploding somewhere in our galaxy. “The reason we want to have a 30-year lifetime is exactly for the supernova neutrinos,” says Yifang Wang, JUNO’s director. “We want to wait for one explosion.”

When a massive star collapses, neutrinos escape from its core before light can fight its way out. As such, a burst of supernova neutrinos detected on Earth would give us an extraordinary glimpse of the star’s final moments – and a fresh way to test our theories of how supernovae form. Plus, if the collapsing core is massive enough to form a black hole, the torrent of neutrinos could suddenly stop. Physicists would, in effect, watch the signal from the dying star switch off at the moment the black hole forms. “If a supernova goes off, that would be the physics result of the century,” says Pascoli.

If we admit that quantum numbers are the true essence of reality – not particles, space or time – then a surprising and beautiful new vision of reality opens up to us

Eventually, it is time for me to leave JUNO. I am led through a baffling series of tunnels to a cramped lift, where my guide pulls a chain-link curtain across the entrance. With a jolt, we shoot upwards, the lift screaming past an endless wall of rock. A few minutes later, I step back into daylight, almost 2 km from where I first stepped onto the funicular. It is a final reminder of JUNO’s improbable scale – complete with a detector weighing as much as three Eiffel Towers – all to study nature’s tiniest particles. Perhaps, in the next decade, a seismic shift in physics will come from its shyest, most diminutive character.

It’s about to get a lot harder to keep countries honest about climate change

New Scientist October 19, 2026

A delay in publishing a scientific report doesn’t usually have serious ramifications for the future of life on Earth. But an impasse between governments over when climate scientists should publish their next landmark assessment of climate change threatens to do just that.

A critical meeting of the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) in Addis Ababa, Ethiopia, was suspended on 16 October without an agreement on when the results of its seventh assessment cycle – called AR7 – should be made public.

Don’t be fooled by its less than catchy title. AR7 will consist of a series of high-profile scientific reports that will summarise the latest evidence on the threat posed by climate change, how countries should adapt and the emissions cuts needed to remain within safe climatic bounds. Its findings will make headlines around the world and create huge public and media pressure on countries to step up their efforts to fight climate change.

Advertisement

Why is this monster El Niño so strong?

The meeting in Addis Ababa was a last-chance opportunity to ensure the findings of AR7 are published in time for a crucial UN-led “global stocktake” in 2028, when countries are due to evaluate global progress towards cutting emissions.

This process takes place every five years and is meant to inform the next round of national climate goals that countries submit under the Paris Agreement. The regular stocktakes are designed to ratchet up pressure on countries to bolster their carbon-cutting ambition at regular intervals, closing the gap between projected global emissions and the goal of keeping global warming in relation to pre-industrial levels “well below” 2°C.

The last global stocktake took place in 2023, just months after the IPCC had finished reporting the results of its last assessment, AR6. The COP28 summit in Dubai – which marked the culmination of the stocktake – resulted in an international commitment for countries to transition away from fossil fuels, plus new global targets to triple renewable energy capacity and double energy efficiency improvement rates by 2030. Would these targets have been set without the public pressure generated by the IPCC findings?

Of course, countries can get information on the state of the climate, and the measures needed to mitigate and adapt to a warming world, from places other than the IPCC. The deluge of journal articles, summary reports and UN papers provides no shortage of data and analysis for those who want to find it, for the global stocktake or any other purpose. But an IPCC report has gravitas other missives can’t match, and generates the media interest that puts climate change at the forefront of public consciousness ahead of COP summits.

Free newsletter

Without a headline-grabbing IPCC report, countries will be under far less pressure to make fresh climate commitments. “It impedes global ambition,” says Richard Allan at the University of Reading, UK, and a lead author for AR7.

So why the delay? A small group of countries, including Russia and Saudi Arabia, are arguing that low-income countries need more time to properly review the IPCC findings before publication.

Their tactics mirror those used in climate summit negotiating rooms, where fossil fuel-dependent countries have, for years, sought to delay and obstruct proceedings to slow international action on cutting emissions. “It’s obviously a delaying tactic,” says Bob Watson, a former chair of the IPCC. “Those countries that want action fundamentally want these reports before this global stocktake. Those countries that don’t want action… they don’t want to see those reports because they know what they’ll say is we’re not on target for 1.5°C or even 2°C”.

It is now looking increasingly unlikely that the IPCC will be able to agree on a publication timetable that will align with the global stocktake. In a statement published on Monday, IPCC chair Jim Skea said he will reconvene the meeting “at the earliest opportunity” to push for a decision. A likely outcome now is that a report on the science of climate change – the least contentious of the three parts – may arrive in May 2028, with two further reports, which assess adaptation and mitigation, published the following year.

“It is an unhelpful fracturing of the process,” says Gareth Redmond-King at UK think tank the Energy and Climate Intelligence Unit. Without the IPCC underscoring the urgency of the crisis, there is a risk that “countries can behave as though the pressure is eased”, he warns.

Bottlenose whales may look after each other when they’re sick

New Scientist October 19, 2026

Northern bottlenose whales have stronger social bonds when they are starving or sick. This discovery was a surprise, because often in mammals, social connections are associated with better health. But during tough times, these whales may rally round and care for others in need.

That idea fits with early whalers’ descriptions of the animals’ behaviour. In a report from 1882, David Gray, commander of the whaling steamer Eclipse, said he had observed thousands of northern bottlenose whales, and noted they had a peculiar response to injured individuals. “The herd never leaves a wounded companion so long as it is alive,” he said. “They come from every point of the compass towards the struck one in the most mysterious manner.”

Killer whales and dolphins are ‘being friends’ to hunt salmon together

But such observations are hard to make. Northern bottlenose whales (Hyperoodon ampullatus), which belong to a relatively mysterious whale family known as beaked whales, live in isolated parts of the ocean and spend most of their time diving deep for food. “Seeing and studying this elusive species is not easy at all,” says Olaf Meynecke at Griffith University in Brisbane, who wasn’t involved in the research.

Advertisement

But Hal Whitehead at Dalhousie University in Halifax, Canada, and his colleagues have been studying a local group of northern bottlenose whales since the 1980s. This population is centred over a deep submarine canyon, a day and a half sail from Halifax.

The team has collected a database of photographs, taken as the animals come to the surface, stretching back 37 years. Different whales can be identified in the pictures from markings on their fins, providing a rare opportunity to track their lives over decades, says team member Sam Walmsley at Princeton University.

Free newsletter

The researchers recorded whether the whales looked plump or emaciated, as a marker for health. Around 11 per cent of the whales were classified as being in poor condition at any particular time. To map their social relationships, the researchers recorded which companions the whales appeared with in the photographs.

Walmsley expected to see a positive correlation between social bonds and health, as has been reported in many mammals, from mice to baboons. “If a whale is in poor condition, maybe it just needs to focus on getting enough squid [or] enough fish to survive,” he says, rather than investing energy in socialising. But, in fact, the sickly whales had more social partners than was normal for this species, and they hung out in larger groups.

Young mice seemingly attempt to revive an anaesthetised cage mate by grooming and biting it and will even pull aside the tongue to clear its airway

The reasons for this are unclear. Maybe sick whales are more likely to seek out others, says Walmsley, or maybe whales that are already in bigger groups have to compete more for food. But an interesting possibility, he says, is that “the whales are attracted to these whales in poor condition, maybe providing some additional support”.

Caregiving would fit with what is seen or suspected in other cetaceans, too, says Meynecke, even if it can be hard to prove. Humpback whales, which Meynecke studies, aren’t particularly sociable, but they share information about food abundance and hunt together if times are hard, he says. “We are seeing that when they are stressed, they do assist each other.”

For Walmsley, the finding also helps to put human relationships into context, as evidence mounts for how damaging social isolation can be for our health. “I think getting more specific about how health and sociality are related in a wide range of mammals is part of what helps us to think about the evolutionary side of that,” he says.

Discovery of T. rex’s cousin upends our understanding of tyrannosaur evolution

New Scientist October 19, 2026

A new species of tyrannosaur has been discovered by scientists in Canada. Fossils of the carnivorous dinosaur, a cousin of Tyrannosaurus rex, suggest it lived 77 million years and was 8 metres long with lengthy, lean legs. This is a rare addition to an unusual branch of the tyrannosaur family tree and complicates our understanding of how these dinosaurs evolved.

Tyrannosauridae, a family of dinosaurs, split into two subfamilies: tyrannosaurines, made up of T. rex and other stocky, heavy species with relatively long heads, and albertosaurines, which had relatively short skulls and lighter builds.

The shocking fossils that show T. rex wasn’t the king of the dinosaurs

When the first foot fossils of this new predator were uncovered by researchers in southern Alberta, Canada, in 2010 and 2011, it was unclear what subfamily of tyrannosaur they belonged to, says Mark Powers at the University of Alberta. As more of the skeleton has been unearthed and researchers have found additional specimens, it seems that the mysterious dinosaur had features of both.

Advertisement

Now, Powers and his colleagues have measured its bones and compared the dimensions to other tyrannosaur species. They found that the newly discovered dinosaur had a hole near the front of its upper jaw, like that in the robust Daspletosaurus, a tyrannosaurine – but it also had a small sinus system like Gorgosaurus libratus, an albertosaurine.

Free newsletter

“It was just so different and so unique that it was very clearly a new species,” says Powers. The researchers’ analysis classified the strange predator as an early member of the albertosaurine group and named it Tromerosaurus solumons.

Tromerosaurus means “frightful lizard”, a homage to similar translations of Daspletosaurus and Gorgosaurus. Solumons means “lonely mountain”, a reference to the isolated horn over its eye and to the lair of Smaug, the dragon in J. R. R. Tolkien’s The Hobbit. “Tyrannosaurs do have very similar iconography to dragons,” says Powers.

An exquisitely preserved fossil found in China shows that many anatomical features seen in birds also evolved independently in another group of dinosaurs

The mixture of features in Tromerosaurus may spur the need to re-examine whether other tyrannosaurs have been properly classified, says Powers. The criteria for defining the subfamilies might be less informative than scientists thought, he says.

The discovery also sheds new light on the evolution of tyrannosaur diversity. “Rather than the stepwise growth into T. rex as the culminating endpoint to tyrannosaurs, it might be a bit more complicated than that,” says Powers. “There might be multiple tyrannosaur lineages that continue on until the end-Cretaceous.”

Jared Voris at the University of Calgary in Canada says that examining fossils of even earlier albertosaurine species can help researchers iron out their evolutionary story. “We need to go deeper in the rock record,” says Voris. “What will the tyrannosaur species we find in 78- to 79-million-year-old rocks show us?”
