Error-correction record pushes quantum computers closer to usefulness

New Scientist October 19, 2026

Another milestone on the way to building useful and practical quantum computers has been passed. Researchers at the firm Quantinuum have used error-correction methods to make their Helios-1 quantum computer store information with an unprecedented degree of reliability, which is a key prerequisite for running complex calculations in the future.

Quantum computers hold immense potential for solving problems and making scientific discoveries that have, so far, been out of reach for even the best supercomputers. But they haven’t yet realised that potential, partly because all existing quantum computers make lots of errors. Consequently, researchers around the world are racing to perfect error-correction methods where a quantum computer’s physical building blocks, or qubits, are encoded into groups called “logical qubits”, which are a lot less likely to make errors when used to run calculations.

David Hayes at Quantinuum and his colleagues have now demonstrated the lowest error rate for logical qubits yet.

Advertisement

Google showcases way to fix quantum computer errors more efficiently

“This is definitely an impressive technical advance,” says Steven Flammia at Virginia Tech, who didn’t work on the project. “It’s super exciting,” says Hayes.

Helios-1 contains 98 qubits, each of which is based on an ion whose quantum state is controlled with lasers and electromagnetic fields. To turn these qubits logical, the team used a type of computer coding called “colour code”. When the qubits were then tested for their ability to store information, they made as few as five errors for every million uses of a qubit. This is an improvement on similar past experiments, where qubits would instead make hundreds of errors for every million uses.

The researchers also tested whether two of Helios-1’s logical qubits could be used for a simple, error-corrected mathematical operation. The error rate in this situation was roughly 10 times higher, or about seven errors for 100,000 qubit uses.

Hayes says Helios-1’s record-breaking performance partly follows from the Quantinuum team improving its control over the physical qubits. Specifically, whenever a qubit’s energy shifts in a deleterious way, which happens naturally but makes computations less accurate, it is now hit with a special laser pulse that corrects the shift. Then the colour code kicks in, leveraging the connections and correlations between the qubit and several others in the logical qubit to correct any remaining error.

We may finally have a way to rate a quantum computer’s usefulness

The researchers have also shown that each logical qubit’s error rate decreases as more physical qubits are added to it. Specifically, the error rate diminished twelve-fold when they increased a logical qubit’s size from seven to 19 physical qubits, with the same diminishing being seen when the physical qubit count rose from 19 to 37. This result is important because quantum computers gain computational power as their qubit number increases, so only error-correction methods that also improve with increasing qubit counts stand a chance of being truly useful.

Murphy Niu at the University of California, Santa Barbara, says the new experiment is a major step towards quantum computing that is error-proof.

Flammia says this work sets the course for building what John Preskill at the California Institute of Technology has dubbed the “megaquop” machine, a computer capable of 1 million reliable quantum operations. This could make meaningful scientific discoveries, for example in materials science, and is thought to be the next important stage in the evolution of quantum computers.

To succeed at scale, quantum computing must differentiate itself from AI, says columnist Karmela Padavic-Callaghan. But the two technologies are already mixed up in the eyes of the public

Helios-1’s low error rates fit the bill for a megaquop machine, but what remains to be seen is whether these will stay so low once the logical qubits are used to execute more complex mathematical operations, says Flammia. This is an important missing ingredient as far as achieving fault-tolerant quantum computing goes, says Thomas Wong at Creighton University in Nebraska.

The question of the total number of qubits also looms large. “They only have roughly 100 physical qubits, but on the order of 100 logical qubits would be needed for known useful applications of megaquop machines,” he says.

Hayes says Quantinuum’s next quantum computer, Sol, will be nearly twice as large as Helios-1. In his view, the new experiment establishes the foundation for Sol and for other computers the company plans to build in the future. “We are doing all of our homework up front,” he says.

But competition within the quantum computing industry is stiff. So far, several research teams have made quantum computer prototypes with more than a thousand qubits and the firm QuEra, whose devices are based on extremely cold atoms, has announced that it will build a megaquop machine by 2028.

El Niño is dramatically increasing sea levels – how bad could it get?

New Scientist October 19, 2026

Floods, droughts, famine – the record-smashing El Niño that is growing ever stronger is already starting to have massive impacts in many regions around the world. Dramatic sea-level rises too have already happened in the eastern Pacific and are set to continue in the coming months.

“Presently, the east Pacific is an astounding 40 centimetres above normal, and a strong westerly wind event will drive those sea levels even higher over the next few weeks,” says Paul Roundy at the University at Albany in New York state.

This could lead to coastal flooding and erosion in many places along the eastern Pacific, from Alaska to Chile, with especially high tides making things even worse. “Frequent coastal inundation will likely develop in many areas and may become severe or record breaking, causing significant disruption and possibly also some significant damage,” says Daniel Swain at the California Institute for Water Resources.

Advertisement

There are several factors combining to produce record-high sea levels in the eastern Pacific in the coming months. The most important is the seesaw-like shift in sea level across the equatorial Pacific caused by El Niño, with levels falling in the west and rising in the east. In simple terms, huge quantities of warm water are sloshing eastwards across the Pacific, driven by bursts of wind blowing in the opposite direction to the usual trade winds.

More technically, these winds trigger what are known as Kelvin waves, says Thomas Monahan at the University of Oxford. These are very different to normal waves, he says. “A Kelvin wave is more similar to raising the water level in a bathtub.”

The most ambitious ideas to save the world from El Niño

These waves take around 60 days to cross the Pacific and then travel along coasts. The end result is a sustained rise in sea level that will persist for months. “It’ll peak with the highest sea surface temperatures, which right now are projected for around late November or December,” says Monahan.

Because this El Niño is so exceptional, the changes in sea level will also be exceptional. In fact, a study by Monahan and his colleagues has found that changes in sea level are amplified by strong El Niño events, rather than being linearly related. “So, if you were to just extrapolate from smaller events, you would miss what is happening in the stronger events,” he says.

The changes will be greatest nearest the equator. Based on analysis of past events, Monahan’s team calculates that sea level could rise between 24 and 40 cm in the Galapagos islands, depending on how strong this El Niño becomes. On the mainland, the effects are set to be a bit smaller. Peru and Ecuador could see rises of between 19 and 33 cm.

These rises are occurring on top of the 20-cm rise in global mean sea level since 1900 due to global warming. In other words, even if this El Niño isn’t as strong as the 1877/78 one, the sea-level rises will still be bigger than they were then.

In places such as California, further from the equator, the team estimates that sea level will rise between 9 and 13 cm. However, unlike in South America, several extra factors are at play along the west coast of the US and Canada.

Free newsletter

One is extra high tides because of long-term lunar cycles. There is the 18.6-year lunar nodal cycle, due to the moon’s orbit being inclined relative to Earth’s equator, and the 8.85-year perigean cycle, due to the rotation of the moon’s elliptical orbit. The highest tides due to these cycles will coincide with this El Niño, effectively adding around 5 cm to sea level along California on top of the El Niño effect.

“We’re already seeing this start to play out in California, where we’ve seen some major flooding occurring in the aftermath of tropical storm Rachel,” says Monahan. “Rather problematically, the biggest peaks in the tides are expected to occur during Thanksgiving week and Christmas week, among the highest in terms of travel and people being around.”

What’s more, El Niños deepen an area of low pressure near the Aleutian islands off Alaska, increasing storm activity, he says. That means storm surges can get bigger during El Niños.

The final factor is that these storms whip up bigger waves. During the 2015/16 El Niño, waves over 15 metres hit Oregon – the largest ever recorded on a US coastline. So, the danger for the west coast is that massive waves and big storm surges could coincide with extra high tides at a time when sea level is much higher than normal, massively increasing the risk of coastal flooding and erosion.

“We may see coastal flooding and erosion in some areas that rivals or exceeds historical records – perhaps by a significant margin,” says Swain.

This is part of the reason why California declared a state of emergency in September. Another major concern is extreme rainfall due to El Niño.

“Rainfall with this El Niño event is the biggest concern for California. In the comparable event of 1877, the Central valley profoundly flooded,” says Roundy. “There is risk of something similar this year, and coastal flooding at the same time is a genuine risk.”

Why the Drake equation is still important 65 years after its creation

New Scientist October 19, 2026

It is the refrain of teachers everywhere preparing their students for standardised tests: “Make an educated guess.” An answer is always better than no answer, they say, and if you can apply what you know to the question to rule out some of the choices, even better. Of course, scientific research isn’t a multiple-choice exam, and its bedrock is the idea that an educated guess without solid evidence just isn’t good enough. But the concept is still a useful one, particularly when our questions outpace the technology we currently have to answer them.

The key part of the phrase “educated guess” is the first word. Put another way, a guess based on nothing may be worse than no guess at all. “But Leah,” I hear you asking, “Do you have a framework, or a favourite example, for educated guesses?” And just because you are clamouring for it, and I’m the kind of person who has favourite equations, I will tell you about it. The Drake equation, which turns 65 years old this month, is an incredibly useful tool for framing our thinking about life in the cosmos – even though, at its core, it is simply a method for making an educated guess.

Why the most central law in cosmology may need to be broken

Astrobiologist Frank Drake came up with his eponymous equation in 1961, before convening the first scientific conference on the search for extraterrestrial intelligence (SETI). According to an account written by his daughter, science journalist Nadia Drake, he sketched out the equation on a bit of a whim to get the few attendees of the meeting talking and is, to this day, astonished by how important it is now considered.

Advertisement

The equation has seven key terms, and when multiplied together, they provide an estimate of N: the number of intelligent civilisations in the Milky Way galaxy with whom we might someday be able to communicate. It looks like this:

N = R* × fp × ne × fl × fi × fc × L

The first few terms are relatively simple. R* is the rate of star formation in our galaxy, which has been measured at about 1 to 3 stars per year. The fraction of those stars with planetary systems is fp, and we now think that number is about 1 as well – most stars seem to have planets. The number of planets per star with an environment suitable for life is ne, and that is where things start to get more complicated. “Suitable for life” is a broad idea, and one that’s difficult to define. Even the most basic requirement – that the planet be in its star’s habitable zone, where temperatures allow liquid water on the surface – is required for Earth-like life, as far as we know, but it’s certainly possible that other lifeforms have different needs. In our own solar system, there are either 2 or 3 planets in the habitable zone, depending how you slice it – but Venus and Mars don’t seem particularly suitable for life, and there are several moons in the outer solar system that may well be.

That is the first time the equation forces us to make an educated guess. The second comes hot on its heels with fl, the fraction of the habitable planets that go on to develop life. On this, we have an even smaller sample size. We haven’t found life anywhere but Earth, so this number could be very small, or it could be 1 – remember, this includes life that arises at any point in the history of the cosmos. But until we do find life elsewhere, it will be more of a philosophical argument than anything else. The same is true of the next two terms of the Drake equation: fi, which denotes the fraction of life that is intelligent – the definition of which is also wily – and fc, the fraction of intelligent lifeforms that eventually broadcast their existence into space and are thus capable of communicating with us. The final term is L, the length of time in which a civilisation of intelligent lifeforms sends detectable signals out into space. As the astronomer Carl Sagan pointed out, this depends heavily on whether such civilisations can avoid self-destruction, which isn’t something we can know for sure – but we make our best guess based on the only evidence we have: human history.

We may have finally solved cosmology’s chicken-or-the-egg problem

If you combine all the lowest estimates, N could be one-trillionth or even lower, implying that we are totally alone in our galaxy. If you combine the highest estimates, there could be tens of millions of civilisations in the Milky Way that we could communicate with, which to me would say it’s only a matter of time before we find them. At Drake’s original SETI meeting, the researchers set N between 1000 and 100,000,000, and the lower end of that sounds about right to me – an estimate that, like those at the meeting, is based largely on my not-particularly-scientific opinions about how long our civilisation might last.

But when it comes down to it, the number itself isn’t the important part of the equation; the important part is the process of estimating each of its terms. In doing so, we force ourselves to consider some of the biggest questions in science: How similar are other places in the universe to our own cosmic neighbourhood? How likely are those most-similar places to develop life? What is life, anyway? What does life truly need? What is intelligence? How can we search for it? And how long will we be capable of searching for it? None of those questions are answered definitively, but pondering them can help us direct our scientific research – and more than that, it gives us an idea of our place in the grand scheme of the universe. That’s why teachers tell their students to make an educated guess, and it’s why the Drake equation is still considered so important. The value in an educated guess is in taking account of what you know and what is still out there, waiting to be known.

Archaeologists are uncovering the meaning of a unique rock art site

New Scientist October 19, 2026

It’s 6am at the Penascosa rock art site in Portugal’s Côa valley, and under the raking glow of torchlight, a faded carving of an aurochs – a wild ox that lived during the last glacial period – suddenly comes into focus against the pre-dawn gloom. For three weeks, archaeologist Thierry Aubry from the Côa Park Foundation and his team have been digging beside the engravings in search of ancient tools that might help them understand the function of the valley’s oldest rock art. As we enter the final day of excavations, they have finally found what they are looking for: thumbnail-sized slivers of razor-sharp stone that were used as hunting weapons by prehistoric hunter-gatherers.

“This technology is typical from 26,000 years ago”, says Aubry in a voice tinged with excitement and relief. “It’s the first time we’ve found material this old next to the art.”

Finding these artefacts just a few metres from one of the most significant rock art panels in the entire Côa valley helps to demonstrate that art wasn’t just something our ancestors placed at remote sacred sites, but was “part of daily life”, says Luís Luís from the Côa Park Foundation.

Advertisement

A cave in France is revealing how the Neanderthals died out

Within the archaeological layers containing the stone bladelets, researchers also found the remains of other flaked tools as well as hearths, indicating that people made fire and used a range of utensils within touching distance of the engraved panel. Or, as Aubry puts it, “they were living inside the art”.

The stone tools at Penascosa provide vital clues about the social context in which the rock art was created and viewed, revealing how it shaped the encounters between groups of people who migrated to Côa to hunt and interact. “The most logical function is to transmit some mythology, but also to transmit some practical information for hunters,” says Aubry.

The Côa valley is the largest open-air collection of Palaeolithic rock art in the world. The engravings, which were first discovered in 1991, are spread over some 17 kilometres of river valley. “Art preserves well in caves, but not in the open air,” says Luís. “But here in Côa, we have conditions that allowed open-air art to be preserved, because it’s a dry region and the local schist is very resistant to erosion.”

The discovery of these exposed motifs triggered what Luís calls a “Copernican revolution” in archaeology by proving that rock art wasn’t restricted to the dark underground settings associated with religion and ritual, but was often a very public phenomenon.

“The Côa valley discovery prompted people to search for similar stuff elsewhere, and now we know from the last 30 years of discoveries that, in fact, it must have been all over the place,” says João Zilhão at the University of Lisbon in Portugal, who set up the Côa Valley Archaeological Park in 1996. Since then, further open-air sites of Palaeolithic rock art have been identified across the Iberian peninsula and beyond, with stylistically similar engravings found as far away as the Nile valley.

At Côa, the earliest phase of rock art production corresponds to the transition between the Gravettian and Solutrean periods of the Upper Palaeolithic, some 26,000 to 27,000 years ago at the onset of the last glacial maximum. To understand why hunter-gatherers chose to fill this valley with engravings 10,000 years before the Lascaux cave paintings in France were made, researchers have spent the past three decades searching for signs of occupation during the late Gravettian at Penascosa.

Subscriber-only newsletter

“In 1995, everybody said it would be impossible to find this because it’s an open-air site and it’s right by a river, so everything will have been washed away [during flooding events],” says Aubry. “But if you don’t look, you don’t find.”

The first attempt to find evidence of an ancient campsite was overseen by Zilhão. Yet by the end of the last major round of excavations, which Aubry led in 2018, layers showing signs of human occupation still hadn’t been found. In 2025, however, a test pit dug right in front of Penascosa’s Rock 3 – which is engraved with a series of overlapping animal motifs – revealed a number of fire-damaged rocks and flaked stone tools that match the style of the late Gravettian and early Solutrean.

For the first time, the team had direct evidence of people sitting around fires and manufacturing survival technologies at Penascosa, just as the landscape was being monumentalised through rock art. “What this shows is that the hunter-gatherers of the Palaeolithic were just like the hunter-gatherers of today,” says Zilhão, referring to certain Aboriginal Australian communities who continue to use rock art in a similar way. “They decorated the territory they lived in.”

Returning to Penascosa last month to excavate this prehistoric living room, the team uncovered buried slabs of schist that had once formed a natural overhang, beneath which ancient hunter-gatherers had taken shelter until the heat from their campfires caused it to collapse. Digging through the layers of time, the archaeologists unearthed a sequence of artefacts that traced the course of human history from the Palaeolithic all the way up to Roman times. Unlike western Europe’s famous painted caves, then, the Côa valley and its rock art didn’t remain sealed off from the ever-changing outside world, but provided a stage for the social dramas that shaped the lives of ancient Iberians for millennia.

Eventually reaching the 27,000-year-old Gravettian occupation layer just as time was running out on the dig, the archaeologists uncovered the evidence they needed to orient Penascosa – and its earliest engravings – within the social landscape of ancient Iberia.

“This flint comes from central Spain, at least 150 kilometres away,” says Aubry, holding a tiny bladelet from Penascosa. “But this flint is from central Portugal, 200 kilometres the other way,” he says of another bladelet that was found in the same deposit. The convergence of these far-flung materials at this one spot suggests that, 27,000 years ago, the Côa valley sat at the heart of a vast network of exchange that spanned half of Iberia.

Before the Stone Age: Were the first tools made from plants not rocks?

“This also explains why the art here is so similar in style to what you see in northern Spain, or even as far as the Rhône valley in France,” says Zilhão. These similarities, he suggests, indicate that rock art functioned as “a shared code of representation” belonging to “a network of people that exchanged information, personnel and objects, forming a very widespread area of cultural homogeneity”.

Yet the Côa valley may have been more than just another node in this network. “This region is a natural border between the [Atlantic] coast and the Iberian interior, so we think it was an important meeting place for populations from these different areas,” says Luís. For decades, archaeologists at Côa have argued that the valley was a social aggregation site, where bands of hunter-gatherers from across the Iberian hinterland periodically came together to meet and hunt. “The lithic materials give us that information,” says Luís. “We no longer see these populations as isolated.”

The valley’s rock art can therefore be understood as a key component of the social world that gave rise to it, in which highly mobile bands of hunter-gatherers repeatedly came face to face at Côa. In other words, as Luís says, “the art was used in moments when distant groups came together”.

To highlight the role that rock art may have played in these encounters, Aubry takes me to Fariseu, another of the valley’s decorated sites. Here, archaeologists have found evidence that hunter-gatherers repeatedly lived among the artworks – although, unlike at Penascosa, they are yet to discover occupation layers dating to the late Gravettian, when the site’s earliest engravings were made.

“It’s a story, with a beginning, a middle and an end – like 16th-century art,” says Aubry as we stand before one of Fariseu’s engraved panels. “But I don’t think it was meant for the people from here. It was for people coming from other regions.”

On the rock face is a repeating series of motifs consisting of four female aurochs, each accompanied by a calf and apparently moving towards the nearby river. “One function was probably to establish a relationship with these animals, to show to people from other places that you are from a particular group,” says Aubry. This notion chimes with one presented by other scholars, who suggest that the Côa valley artists may have used animal motifs to represent humans.

Yet these engraved narratives may also have conveyed information about large herbivores and how to hunt them. The aurochs calves, for example, all appear to be around 6 months old, leading Aubry to speculate that the composition may depict the animals’ behaviour “at a specific moment in the year”.

“I think the aggregation moment was probably a hunting moment,” he says. “So the transmission of mythology was the social function [of the rock art], but the hunting function was also essential.” Rather than separating the symbolic from the practical, then, the same images could have performed both functions at once.

The untold story of our remarkable hands and how they made us human

“Obviously it’s very difficult to understand the meaning of the art, but it may have been part of a survival strategy,” says Luís. As travellers and locals met at Côa’s engraved sites, the images they created may have facilitated vital exchanges between bands of strangers while also enabling them to hunt together.

“Côa revolutionised everything, because it made many of us realise that this is normal Ice Age art,” says freelance archaeologist Paul Bahn, who isn’t involved in the excavation. “I always assumed that they were living very close to the art, if not in the art sites themselves, so I’m delighted that they’ve finally got evidence of that.”

For more than three decades, discoveries in the Côa valley have helped to reshape the perception of Palaeolithic rock art from something produced exclusively in caves for ritual purposes to something that was often outdoor and multifunctional. “The vast majority of it was in the open air, and the stuff in caves was almost a marginal phenomenon,” says Bahn. “It just happens to have survived much better.”

To truly understand such art, though, Aubry says we must stop studying it as a distinct phenomenon and view it instead as an integrated component of the everyday world of ancient hunter-gatherers. “Archaeologists need to realise that we are not studying a monument,” he says. “We are studying people living in a space.”

Japan is launching a mission to Mars’s largest moon Phobos

New Scientist October 16, 2026

We may be on the verge of solving the mystery of the Martian moons. On 20 October, the Martian Moons eXploration (MMX) spacecraft launches towards the larger of the two moons, Phobos, with the goal of bringing back a sample that may finally explain how Phobos and its sibling, Deimos, formed.

MMX will launch from Tanegashima Space Center in Japan. If all goes to plan, it should arrive at Mars in August 2027, entering an orbit that keeps it alongside Phobos so it can build a detailed map of the surface. Along the way, it will also observe the surface of Deimos.

Once the map is complete enough, the spacecraft’s operators at the Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency (JAXA) will use it to pick out a spot on Phobos for MMX to land. During one or two brief landings, it will take on two tasks: to drop off a small rover called IDEFIX and to pick up samples. The rover is the first anyone has ever placed on such a small cosmic body, so part of its purpose aside from scientific observations is to confirm that a wheeled rover even works on an object with such low gravity.

Advertisement

Possible signs of ancient life on Mars are rich in complex carbon

The samples, though, are the most important part of the mission. MMX has two different sampling devices: one that shoots a puff of gas onto the surface, blowing dust and pebbles back up into a sampling container, and another that blasts a hollow cylinder into the ground to take a sample a several centimetres deep. After the samples are taken, they will be stowed away inside the spacecraft, which will then head back towards Earth. It is expected to arrive home in 2031.

Once these samples get back to Earth and are analysed by scientists on the ground, they should finally solve the mystery of how Phobos and Deimos formed. For more than a century, researchers have debated whether the two are captured asteroids or formed from an impact on Mars, similar to how Earth’s moon formed. On first look, their shapes and surfaces resemble asteroids, but their circular orbits around Mars’s equator are more consistent with the impact hypothesis. Figuring out what they are made of should settle it once and for all.

Free newsletter

This will also help illuminate what the solar system was like billions of years ago when these strange moons formed. “Having the answer will help illuminate that early era when Earth and the other inner planets may have been acquiring much of their water and organic compounds,” said Tom Statler, part of the NASA team that is collaborating on the MMX mission, in a statement.

If we are very lucky, the samples from Phobos may even contain bonus bits of dust and debris from Mars itself. Impacts on the planet could have launched material into space, which would have collected on the moon’s surface and been preserved there for billions of years. That means that these samples could illuminate not just the history of Phobos and Deimos, but also of Mars.

The supermarket chain confirmed it no longer had butchers in its South Island stores, following a gradual move away from in-store butchery.

“In the past few years, recruiting butchers in the South Island has been an ongoing challenge. To address this, we decided to migrate our meat offering to a centralised model,” a Woolworths NZ spokesperson said.

“We have been centralising our South Island meat offering for some time, and as of today we no longer have butchers in our South Island stores.”

The spokesperson said the centralised model enabled Woolworths to deliver consistent quality, longer shelf life and enhanced freshness.

“Our in-store butchery teams have served our customers with incredible skill and dedication for many years, and we thank them for their contribution.

“We remain committed to supporting South Island farmers and delivering great value and quality for our customers every day.”

The company’s response did not specify how many workers were affected, whether they had been redeployed or made redundant, or where the South Island’s meat would be processed.

The move follows a trial reported in April, when Woolworths was considering replacing its remaining South Island butcheries with pre-packaged meat.

He said workers feared the trial would lead to restructuring and were getting out ahead of it.

Centralised processing is already established in Woolworths’ North Island business.

National has pledged, if re-elected, to pursue splitting Foodstuffs into two competing nationwide grocery chains, subject to a Commerce Commission assessment finding the change would benefit shoppers.

NZ Super Fund may have helped Australia drop retrospective capital gains tax proposal

New Zealand Herald October 19, 2026

The Australian Government was told broadening the tax base would “establish a concerning precedent". Photo / Getty Images

Contentious tax changes in Australia were watered down after pushback, including from the New Zealand Superannuation Fund.

The Australian Government already taxes foreign residents on capital gains from certain Australian assets, including property and certain interests connected to Australian land.

However, it proposed broadening the assets captured by the tax to include the likes of wind turbines and transmission lines. It also proposed backdating the changes to 2006, when the capital gains tax was first introduced.

Even if the now chucked-out retrospective proposals were agreed to, Inland Revenue officials said ordinary Kiwi investors were not expected to be directly impacted by the changes, as rules around investment property were unchanged.

Documents Inland Revenue released to Newstalk ZB, after the Ombudsman forced its hand, show the tax department detailed its concerns over the proposals to Finance Minister Nicola Willis and Revenue Minister Simon Watts.

The NZ Super Fund teamed up with its Canadian counterpart, the Public Sector Pension Investment Board, to raise concerns directly with the Australian Government over how the proposals risked “weakening Australia’s reputation as a stable and predictable investment jurisdiction”.

The Australian Government ended up forging ahead with its proposal to broaden the assets captured by the capital gains tax but decided to only apply changes going forward. It shut down the contentious proposal to backdate the tax reform to 2006, two decades on.

Changes took effect on October 1.

In an April submission, the NZ Super Fund and its Canadian counterpart raised concerns over the retrospective element of the proposal.

“As currently drafted, the Government would be taxing long-term foreign investors on gains that accrued when such assets were not subject to CGT in Australia,” the pension funds said.

“They also point to competitiveness issues, noting a widening tax differential between foreign investors and Australian superannuation funds.”

The NZ Super Fund and the Canadian scheme said broadening the tax base as proposed by the Australian Government would “establish a concerning precedent as the Australian Government would be taxing assets and gains that were previously subject to deliberate policy concessions or exemptions under Australia’s tax framework”.

The submission said the New Zealand Super Fund had “NZ$89.9 billion of assets under management as at 31 October 2025 and invests in diversified assets throughout the world, including Australia”.

As for Inland Revenue, it initially declined to release its briefing to Finance Minister Nicola Willis and Revenue Minister Simon Watts on the impact of the proposals, citing concern this could damage New Zealand’s standing with Australia.

Inland Revenue argued that “making available ... that information would be likely to prejudice the security or defence of New Zealand or the international relations of the Government of New Zealand”.

However, the Ombudsman intervened after Newstalk ZB complained the document was withheld, as Willis herself had issued a press release criticising aspects of Australia’s CGT.

In its briefing, Inland Revenue noted the Australian Government’s original proposals “provoked a significant negative reaction in Australia” and created “sovereign risk”.

Inland Revenue officials said “commentators warn that the changes, particularly if made without transitional relief, may lead to decreased confidence in Australia as a location for long-term investment. The proposed changes follow several other recent measures tightening Australia’s investment settings for non-residents.”

Inland Revenue warned reduced investment in Australia could impact New Zealand, as investors often looked to New Zealand once they had invested in Australia.

Inland Revenue officials said “direct investment in New Zealand often follows as a second step from direct investment into Australia”.

Officials suggested investors were “likely to be dissatisfied” with aspects of the then-proposed tax changes, such as the fact the only concession was for renewable energy assets.

Inland Revenue met with Deloitte and the New Zealand Superannuation Fund to further discuss “stakeholder concerns”. Details of these concerns were not made public under the OIA.

It comes as political discussions around a proposed capital gains tax take shape on the campaign trail.

National Party finance spokeswoman Nicola Willis said it was “another example of extra tax backfiring and damaging prospects for investment and growth”.

“The New Zealand Labour Party’s capital gains tax and all the other taxes proposed by its political mates would have exactly the same impact here,” Willis said, adding New Zealand needed to attract investment, and not discourage it.

Labour has been campaigning on a “simple, targeted” CGT it promises nine out of 10 Kiwis will not pay.

Willis previously used Australia as an example to claim “a capital gains tax always grows”.

Tauranga landslides inquiry delayed by agencies too slow to provide information

New Zealand Herald October 19, 2026

People reflect at a memorial site for the six people who died in a landslide in Mount Maunganui. Photo / RNZ, Kim Baker Wilson

By RNZ

The government inquiry into the fatal landslides in Tauranga had to be extended because agencies were too slow to provide information, official documents show.

It was announced in September that the Government inquiry would now report back in February, two months after originally planned.

The inquiry was established following the January slips at Mt Maunganui and Welcome Bay Rd in Pāpāmoa, which killed eight people.

Brooke van Velden, the minister responsible for the government inquiry, said chairman Sir Mark O’Regan had asked for an extension because the review commissioned separately by the Tauranga City Council was completed about two months behind schedule.

A proactively released Cabinet paper from September 2 shows the primary factor at the time of the request for an extension was “uncertainty about the timing of the Davison review”, referring to the separate inquiry.

However, the documents state that two other key factors also “put pressure on the reporting deadline”.

Firstly, “delays in evidence gathering and analysis because of delays in participant agencies providing information requested”. The document did not state which agencies those were.

But it noted that participant agencies had “a number of competing priorities”, including multiple landslide-related inquiries as well as responding to Coronial Inquiries into the Auckland Anniversary floods, Cyclone Gabrielle and Whakaari White Island.

As well as the delays getting information from unnamed agencies, the paper also noted the “volume of material received by the inquiry, with over 20,000 documents having been provided to date”.

The paper also noted the inquiry had a budget of $5 million, and the inquiry had advised it expected to meet the costs of an extension within its budget.

However, if additional funding was required, the minister proposed reprioritising forecast underspend from the Royal Commission of Inquiry into Covid-19 Lessons up to a maximum of $100,000.

In a statement on the Department of Internal Affairs website, O’Regan said he recognise that extending the reporting date may be disappointing for some.

“We are grateful for the continued patience, trust and engagement we have received as we complete this important work.”

The Inquiry continued to make steady progress but is considering a substantial volume of evidence, comprising about 20,000 documents, he said.

“Taking the time to properly examine and assess this material is essential if we are to produce a thorough, independent and evidence-based report that New Zealanders can have confidence in,” says Sir Mark.

Following an assessment of progress and the work still required, the Inquiry advised that additional time was needed to fully consider all available evidence and fulfil its responsibilities under the Terms of Reference.

The Inquiry’s work is separate from the Davison Review recently released by Tauranga City Council.

While the Inquiry is required to have regard to the review’s findings, it is not bound by them.

“The Inquiry has its own Terms of Reference, evidence base and reporting responsibilities. Our role is broader in scope, and we must reach our own independent findings based on all of the evidence before us.”

The Inquiry is now moving from evidence gathering into detailed analysis, deliberations and preparation of its final report.

“Our objective remains unchanged: to establish how the fatal landslides occurred, examine how risks were managed, and identify lessons that may help prevent similar tragedies in the future.

“We remain committed to delivering a robust and independent report that honours the significance of this event and the people affected by it.”

-Additional reporting by NZME

One of the world’s few surviving moa eggs is being returned to New Zealand after 60 years in a private American collection.

The “exceptionally rare” giant moa egg was snapped up for an undisclosed sum by US de-extinction company Colossal Biosciences, which is behind an ambitious genetic bid to bring the bird back from the dead, and will be gifted to local iwi Ngāi Tahu.

Contact our South Island newsroom

Hollywood movie producer Sir Peter Jackson says he is “delighted” that the egg – one of less than 40 known whole moa eggs – is returning to Aotearoa.

It comes as a Jurassic Park-style de-extinction project, backed by Ngāi Tahu and Canterbury Museum, has made “significant progress” in the past six months.

Scientists and archaeologists have been collecting samples from cave and subfossil sites across the South Island, which will be needed to sequence the genomes of multiple moa species.

And in May, Colossal, which has already revived a modern version of the dire wolf, and has designs on the woolly mammoth and dodo, also hatched healthy chicks using a shell-less artificial incubation system designed to eventually support eggs approaching the size of a moa’s.

“In fieldwork and research undertaken across Te Waipounamu [South Island], we’ve often worked with fragments of bone and eggshell that help us reconstruct the story of moa and the people who lived alongside them,” said Kyle Davis, a Ngāi Tahu archaeologist and expert in cultural heritage.

“To see an egg of this rarity return to Te Waipounamu is extraordinary. It carries information about the moa species that birthed it, the landscape it came from and potentially the people connected to it.

“Most importantly, it will now be cared for and further researched in collaboration with Ngāi Tahu researchers, where decisions about its future can be guided by tikanga and grounded in the place to which it belongs.”

Moa eggshell has long been an important source of information for scientists. Published research has recovered ancient DNA from moa eggshell fragments; for example, an eggshell structure and thickness have helped researchers understand how moa nested and incubated their eggs.

Future scientific study in New Zealand of the returned egg could include non-destructive imaging or sampling for DNA and/or isotopes to confirm the species and geographic origin of the egg. Whether and when to take on this work will be decided by the Ngāi Tahu Research Centre in accordance with tikanga.

“Fewer than 40 whole moa eggs are known, and each one holds information we can get nowhere else – sometimes even their DNA,” said Beth Shapiro, PhD, Colossal’s Chief Science Officer.

“An egg like this belongs in Aotearoa, in the hands of the people and institutions who study and care for moa, and not in a private collection.”

According to auction records, the egg was discovered in New Zealand on January 14, 1966, and has remained in a private American collection for approximately six decades before Colossal purchased it from Artemis Gallery in Colorado in June, when it resurfaced in the public auction.

Auction records indicate that the egg may have originated from a human burial site dating to the Moa Hunter period, around AD 1300, although further research will be required to confirm its provenance.

While thousands of moa bones have been recovered from swamps, caves, and dune sites across New Zealand, whole eggs are scarce.

The repatriation was announced yesterday at a meeting of the world’s top fossil birds experts in Christchurch.

Dr Paul Scofield, senior curator of natural history at Canterbury Museum, and a collaborating scientist on the moa programme, together with colleagues from the University of Canterbury and Flinders University, said he had never seen a moa egg surface for auction.

“Its homecoming will create new opportunities for research while ensuring that this extraordinary taonga is cared for in the land – and by the people – to which it belongs,” he said.

“It’s really fantastic that it is coming back to New Zealand because the international dinosaur market collectors value these things and it could well have been that it was outside the price of the cost of any New Zealand institute to purchase. So it’s a remarkably philanthropic act that Colossal have purchased this egg and actually are repatriating it to New Zealand.”

Under New Zealand’s Protected Objects Act 1975, intact moa remains are protected objects that cannot be exported without permission from the Ministry for Culture and Heritage. This egg left the country before that law was in force.

After discovering the egg listed for auction, Colossal says it “immediately acted to procure it so as to ensure its safe return home” to be cared for under the direction of the Ngāi Tahu.

Colossal plans to present the egg to Professor Te Maire Tau (Ūpoko of Ngāi Tūāhuriri, a hapu of Ngāi Tahu), a distinguished Māori historian, academic leader, and tribal leader in New Zealand based in the Tuahiwi region of Canterbury.

Jackson, the star director behind The Lord of the Rings trilogy, and who was also an early investor in Colossal Biosciences, reportedly putting in more than $10 million of his own money, said every Kiwi grew up knowing the story of the moa.

“Whenever I’ve been walking deep in the New Zealand bush, I can’t help but keep looking into the thick forest, hoping for a glimpse of the mythic ‘last moa’ - an amazing bird that sadly no longer exists, no matter how hard you look … and hope," he said.

“When we learned that this exceptionally rare moa egg was being sold outside of New Zealand, we spoke to Colossal, who not only offered to rescue it at their own considerable expense, but to also fly it privately to New Zealand, so it returns home safely. I’m delighted this treasure will now be in the care of Ngāi Tahu.”

When the moa programme was launched by Colossal last year, CEO and co-founder Ben Lamm said it made a clear commitment that indigenous leadership would “guide the science and every decision surrounding the project”.

“Securing and transporting this egg back to its rightful home is just part of that commitment,” he said.

“Regardless of when and how it left the country, we strongly feel all recognisable moa bones and remains as well as any other New Zealand artefacts should be returned to the country and its people.

“To quote Indiana Jones, ‘It belongs in a museum’ – a museum in Aotearoa, under the care of the people whose ancestors lived alongside these extraordinary birds.”

Kurt Bayer is NZ Herald South Island Head of News based in Christchurch. He is a senior journalist who joined the Herald in 2011.

The Mt Dixon avalanche victim has been described as a highly experienced mountaineer and “deeply talented” in his field.

Troy Forsyth was today named as the man who died in an avalanche on the east face of Mt Dixon in Aoraki Mt Cook National Park on Sunday.

He was skiing down the peak when he was buried by snow.

The New Zealand Mountain Safety Council (MSC) said Forsyth was an avalanche snow safety officer and ski patroller at The Remarkables Ski Area in Queenstown.

He was also an assistant ski guide with the New Zealand Mountain Guides Association (NZMGA).

He was with three other experienced ski mountaineers when the avalanche occurred near the summit of Mt Dixon while the party was skiing down the east face.

NZMGA spokesman, friend and fellow Remarkables ski patroller Will Rowntree said Forsyth was skiing with experienced friends and was not working in a professional capacity on this occasion.

“Troy was a deeply talented and respected practitioner within his field. He will be dearly missed by his family, friends and colleagues.”

Contact the NZ Herald newsroom

MSC chief executive Mike Daisley says the tragedy is a sobering reminder of the inherent risks associated with skiing and mountaineering in New Zealand’s high alpine environment.

“Troy was also an MSC-endorsed avalanche educator. The alpine community is a close-knit one, and Troy’s passing will be deeply felt by all those who knew him and shared his passion for the mountains.

“Ski mountaineering takes place in a complex and constantly changing environment.

“Avalanches are one of the hazards that can have devastating consequences, even for those with extensive experience and specialist knowledge.

“Experience, training and careful decision-making are fundamental to managing alpine risk, but they cannot eliminate it entirely.”

MSC and NZMGA extended their “sincere condolences” to Forsyth’s family, friends, colleagues and the wider mountain, guiding and snow safety communities.

Police said emergency services were alerted about 10am on Sunday and a search and rescue operation was launched.

Senior Sergeant Craig Ellison said the man was found unresponsive and died a short time later.

Experts warned good weather and mountain conditions could mask avalanche dangers.

Nathan Watson, operations manager at MSC, said a recent storm brought new snow.

He said it was a reminder that “good weather conditions don’t necessarily mean no avalanche danger”.

“Different storms come through, and they bring new snow.

“There’s wind, there’s rain, there’s varying freezing levels and what happens is the snowpack builds up and changes over time.

“Within the snowpack, there can be different layers of weakness.”

Watson said even in good weather, there can be weaknesses or instabilities beneath a snowpack.

“Then if that’s triggered in a certain way, such as with a human on it, that stability can break and release and still trigger an avalanche.

“So the good weather at a particular time is not necessarily an indicator that there isn’t a risk within the snowpack.”

The death will be referred to the coroner.

Is the Aussie dream fading?

New Zealand Herald October 19, 2026

Annual growth was 2.6% in NZ in the second quarter, above Australia's 2.1%. Photo / 123rf

By Susan Edmunds of RNZ

With Australian unemployment numbers increasing sharply, economists say the transtasman pull may lessen for New Zealanders.

Data last week showed the Australian unemployment rate reaching 4.7%, the highest in a decade. That is still below New Zealand’s rate, currently 5.6%, but the International Monetary Fund says Australia is on track to have the largest increase in unemployment in the developed world over the next year.

BNZ chief economist Mike Jones said the gap between the Australian and New Zealand economies was narrowing.

“Australian economic growth is slowing, the labour market is losing steam and house prices are falling, so there’s an element of catch-down happening,” he said. “At the same time, the NZ economy is managing to maintain momentum, with forward indicators still consistent with reasonable growth ahead.

“It’s notable that NZ’s economic recovery, underwhelming though it’s been, has closed the growth gap to Australia. Annual growth in the second quarter was 2.6%, above Australia’s 2.1%.

“It’s nonetheless important to emphasise that the bar for some NZ growth catch-up has been low, given the weak economy of the past few years, and a faster rate of NZ growth over the next 12 months or so will not close the gap in the level of activity that opened up as the NZ economy struggled through 2024 and 2025.

“Job opportunities tend to be the swing factor in transtasman migration trends. Rising unemployment in Australia might put some off, although the labour markets in both countries are relatively weak.

“We noted recently that it looked like annual migration outflows to Oz could ease off to about 20,000 over the coming 12 months, so a reduction in net outflows, but a long way from Kiwis beating a path back to our shores en masse.”

At ANZ, Miles Workman said New Zealand and Australia were at different points in the economic cycle.

“New Zealand is recovering from a cyclical downturn, while Australia’s economy appears set to soften from a stronger starting point,” he said. “That divergence is likely to be reflected in labour market conditions and, in turn, transtasman migration flows.”

He said flows between the countries would likely be affected, because when Australia’s labour market was stronger than New Zealand, more people tended to move there.

Westpac chief economist Kelly Eckhold agreed.

“I think that will certainly be a factor in continuing the trend that we’ve seen probably for maybe for 6-7 months, 6-8 months now that there have been fewer people departing New Zealand to go overseas.”

He said consumer sentiment in Australia had turned sharply, whereas New Zealand’s had generally improved for the past six months.

“In Australia, consumers are really having to deal with a much more aggressive central bank. They’ve had three tightenings this year.

“Expectations will be, you know, one more at least coming down the pipe and the housing market over there has really changed around a bit in terms of trends and sentiment.”

New Zealand faced higher interest rates too, but he said the turnaround was bigger for Australia.

Data from Stats NZ shows that, in the year to August 2026, there was a net loss of 38,200 migrants compared to 39,900 a year earlier.

In the year to March, 27,900 New Zealand citizens went to Australia, compared to 31,100 in the March 2025 year.

The British drum and bass duo will bring their full live production to Forsyth Barr Stadium on March 5, 2027, while Adams will perform his acoustic Bare Bones show at Dunedin Town Hall on Saturday, March 13.

Contact our South Island newsroom

The announcements offer a welcome lift for the city’s concert calendar.

Pink’s March 2024 performance was the stadium’s last major international concert, meaning the bookings for next year come after a three-year gap.

Chase & Status are the first major headline act announced under new Dunedin Venues chief executive Phil King, who said the booking was an indication of what was to come.

“When I said I believed a golden age of events was coming to Forsyth Barr Stadium, this is exactly what I meant.”

Announcing the act in Dunedin this morning, King said: “I think there’s no better town to host an event like this, with the university students right on the doorstep.”

The Brit Award-winning duo, whose songs include the Stormzy collaboration Backbone, will play their first New Zealand stadium show.

Dunedin Venues is billing it as their biggest concert in the country.

On the other hand, Adams’ appearance will be decidedly more low-key.

His Bare Bones show draws on more than four decades of songs, including Summer of ’69, Run to You, Heaven and (Everything I Do) I Do It for You.

“Two very different shows, two world-class artists, one month,” King said.

“Whether you’re in the stadium for Chase & Status or in the Town Hall for an unforgettable night with Bryan Adams, March 2027 is shaping up as a massive month for live music in Dunedin, and for our local economy, which greatly benefits when fans come to town.”

The stadium’s sparse concert calendar has prompted efforts to broaden the range of acts it can accommodate.

The Herald reported in March on plans for retractable curtains to accommodate smaller audiences at Forsyth Barr Stadium.

The proposed capacity-reduction system would allow configurations ranging from a 3000- to 5000-person mini-arena through to larger events.

Ticketek Entertainment Group chief executive Cameron Hoy said the show reflected the intent of that agreement.

“When TEG and Ticketek locked in our 10-year partnership with Dunedin Venues in March, this is exactly what we had in mind: bringing major international acts to Forsyth Barr Stadium for fans across the South.”

Handsome Tours had secured the act, while King and Dunedin Venues had provided the venue, Hoy said.

“There’s plenty more to come for Dunedin.”

King said about 60% of stadium crowds travelled from outside Dunedin, and he expected the show to draw fans from across the South Island and farther afield.

Mayor Sophie Barker said visiting concertgoers would benefit accommodation providers, hospitality businesses and retailers.

Frontier Touring chief executive Dion Brant said the Town Hall suited Adams’ stripped-back performance.

Christchurch will be New Zealand’s sporting mecca for the next month, with all roads leading to the Garden City.

No fewer than eight major international sporting events are scheduled for spring in the city, starting with the best netball teams in the world taking the court on Wednesday.

Before that, the best domestic competition in the country draws to a climax.

Contact our South Island newsroom

NPC – Canterbury hosts Northland in the final of the NPC at One NZ Stadium on Monday afternoon. Much was made of the heat inside the stadium in their quarter-final against Waikato a fortnight ago, with temperatures reportedly rising above 30C inside the enclosed arena. The forecast for the week ahead sees temperatures in the mid-20s. Venues Ōtautahi are confident that they can make conditions more comfortable for spectators in future events.

Netball – The Silver Ferns take a 1-0 lead into game two of the Constellation Cup against their arch-rivals the Australian Diamonds, with the second match of the series to be played at Wolfbrook Arena on Wednesday night. Last time the two met at this venue, it ended in an overtime series victory to the Diamonds in a pulsating finish to the 2025 series. This time the Ferns take the court as reigning Commonwealth Games champions.

Cricket – The overlap between winter sports and our summer game begins this week, with India arriving for a much-anticipated series against the Black Caps. The first match is at Hagley Oval on Thursday evening, followed by the second at the same venue on Saturday night. The long-range weather forecast looks like it’ll play ball. The two teams return at the end of November for the second test match – and final game of the tour.

League – The Rugby League World Cup rolls into town this Sunday, with a double header at One NZ Stadium. First, the Kiwi Ferns take on France at 4pm and then the Kiwis face Cook Islands at 6pm. The matches are virtually sold out, with only Field Club tickets still available.

Rugby – The Black Ferns get their first taste of One NZ Stadium on October 31 when they host France. Fans are being encouraged to enter into the “Halloween spirit” for the match, which kicks off just after 7pm. Both teams play freely and will have enough tricks to ensure the spectacle is a treat.

Racing – From November 7-14 it’s Canterbury’s famous Cup Week, with the premier races being the New Zealand Trotting Cup at Addington on the 10th, the TAB Mile on the 11th and the New Zealand Cup at Riccarton on the 14th.

Football – The All Whites round out an action-packed month for Christchurch when they host India at One NZ Stadium on November 15. The second of a two-match series to recognise “100 years of unity through sport” between the two nations.

Traveller’s guide to Sydney’s new 24-hour international airport

Sydney Morning Herald October 20, 2026

The opening to passengers of Sydney’s new international airport on the western fringe marks the culmination of 80 years of struggle to realise a second aviation hub.

For passengers long accustomed to trekking through the city’s long-established airport at Mascot, the first flights out of Western Sydney International Airport give them greater choice.

The new curfew-free airport ends the privately owned Kingsford Smith Airport’s monopoly in the Sydney basin.

The era of airport competition in Sydney – often dubbed the gateway to Australia – raises the likelihood of a better deal for passengers on everything from car parking fees to airfares. In the case of the latter, it will hinge on airlines passing on the prospect of lower airport fees and the extent to which they have to discount fares to put bums on seats.

Flight Centre founder and managing director Graham Turner expects airlines flying to both of Sydney’s airports to offer special fares when they have disparities in passenger loads on flights from either.

“Overall we think they will be cheaper. If they’re having trouble filling [seats on flights from one of the airports], almost certainly they’ll bring out specials,” he says of airlines such as Singapore Airlines and Air New Zealand, which will be flying to both airports.

So far, Jetstar and Qantas have committed to domestic flights, while Fiji Airways and Vietnamese budget carrier Vietjet join Singapore Airlines and Air New Zealand in flying international routes to the new airport, named for Nancy-Bird Walton.

Turner expects Middle Eastern airlines will adopt a “wait-and-see” approach on the new airport, and Virgin Australia to watch Jetstar’s performance in the first six months before it considers whether to “stick their necks out”.

Retailers have spent recent weeks fitting out shops and other outlets on the terminal’s first floor, where passengers will arrive after passing through security.

From the opening this Sunday, 12 outlets will be operating, including duty-free shops, currency exchange and retailers for high-end sunglasses and tech accessories, as well as several convenience stores.

More shops and eateries will open over coming months: two Mountain Culture restaurants, cafes and specialty shopping including a toy retailer. Those hoping for the Golden Arches and its rivals will have to wait, although fast-food outlets are expected to open as passenger services increase before the end of the year.

For high-end travellers, an international passenger lounge will open on the terminal’s mezzanine level next month for the launch of Singapore Airlines flights on November 23. Named the Rayleigh Lounge, it will have about 80 seats with room to grow to about 130.

Two play areas for children in domestic, and one in international, can be found on the departure concourse. The terminal has other features travellers have long become accustomed to in airports ranging from free Wi-Fi and drinking water stations to prayer rooms, quiet spaces and outside areas for smoking.

The terminal also has “pet relief” rooms for those travelling with assistance dogs and other animals, complete with toileting areas and water bowls.

The cost of car parking at airports is one of travellers’ chief gripes.

With more than 6000 car spaces, the new airport’s launch prices range from $15 a day for long-stay parking to $29 a day for saver parking, and from $49 a day for premium covered spots.

The launch prices for parking from opening day to the end of next April have been available to book online since October 12.

Three hours of free parking for visits from October 26 have also been offered for a “limited time”, which has been unspecified.

Importantly, travellers and those dropping them off or picking them up by car can use a free 15-minute express zone.

Dozens of electric vehicle charging bays are available, alongside covered parking spots and accessible options, while long-stay parking at the airport business park is about a five-minute free shuttle ride to the terminal.

The P1 premium and P2 saver parking areas are within a two- to-three-minute walk from the terminal.

A multibillion-dollar metro train line was meant to start whisking passengers to and from an underground station, a short walk from the terminal when the airport opened.

Instead, the 23-kilometre rail line linking the airport by driverless train to Sydney’s heavy rail network at St Marys, and the new city of Bradfield in the south, has been delayed until at least December next year.

Passengers opting for public transport will have to rely on free shuttle buses running every 30 minutes between St Marys and the airport from October 25 until the metro line opens. A one-way bus will take about half an hour, twice the journey time of metro trains when they eventually start.

New bus routes are already operating every 30 minutes from 5am to 10pm each day between the airport and Penrith, Liverpool via Bonnyrigg or Leppington, Campbelltown and Mount Druitt. Journey times range from 50 minutes to 66 minutes for a one-way trip end to end.

A direct bus shuttle by a private operator will link the airport with Parramatta, the Sydney CBD and Kingsford Smith Airport, and be timed to meet arriving and departing planes at the new airport from the start of passenger flights.

Super Shuttle’s launch fares for adults are $55 for a one-way trip to central Sydney, $65 for a connection to Kingsford Smith Airport and $25 for a trip to Parramatta. A trip from the airport to the Sydney CBD by shuttle bus is forecast to take between 45 minutes and an hour.

Once metro trains start, fares to catch them to the new airport will be priced the same as elsewhere on the rail network, unlike those for the two stations at Sydney Airport where an “access fee” is levied on top of the ticket price for double-deck train services.

The $18.61 fee for an adult passenger pushes the total cost of a train from the Sydney CBD to Kingsford Smith Airport to almost $23 during peaks.

While the metro line’s opening has been delayed, it is important to remember that Sydney will have two international airports, both linked by train lines by 2028. In contrast, Melbourne has one main international airport which is years away from having a train line built to it.

With the vast majority of passengers set to travel to and from the airport by car, the new toll-free M12 motorway will be their gateway to the aviation hub.

Unlike the metro train line, the final piece of the 16-kilometre motorway was opened on time in June. A major interchange at Cecil Hills, near Bonnyrigg, links the M12 to the M7 toll road. The western end of the M12 connects to the Northern Road at Luddenham.

The airport is about 39 kilometres by road from Parramatta and more than 60 kilometres from the Sydney CBD.

It is a frequently asked question: does the new Commonwealth-owned airport’s opening signal the end of Kingsford Smith Airport, which is about nine kilometres from the Sydney CBD?

Absolutely not. In fact, the arrival of a competitor coincides with Sydney Airport embarking on its largest terminal expansion since the city hosted the Olympics 26 years ago.

Let the competition begin.

Pilots who are flying cargo aircraft to the new hub find it smoother than Kingsford Smith Airport where space is at a premium on the ground and in the air.

Over three dozen Congress members’ offices targeted with white powder envelopes

The Guardian Mon, 19 Oct 2026 19:44:47 GMT

Envelopes containing powder come weeks before midterms as federal agents try to identify who is behind campaign

More than three dozen members of US Congress have had their offices targeted with envelopes containing white powder, less than three weeks before the 3 November midterms, as federal agents try to identify who is behind the campaign.

The latest is the Virginia Democrat Suhas Subramanyam, whose Leesburg district office was evacuated on Monday after an envelope containing a suspicious substance arrived. He said the office was cleared quickly, adding that “acts of political intimidation have no place in our country”.

Subramanyam’s office said preliminary tests showed the powder was not hazardous.

Law enforcement sources told ABC News that more than 100 letters thought to contain white powder are circulating in the US mail system. The FBI, Capitol police and US Postal Inspection Service are investigating, according to a notice sent to Senate staff on Thursday.

Election offices in at least 15 states had reported receiving or being targeted by suspicious mail by Thursday evening, according to the Tampa Free Press, which cited federal authorities. No suspect has been named, and federal authorities have not released a confirmed figure.

The FBI declined to confirm “specific instances or letters”, but said in a statement: “The FBI and US Postal Inspection Service are investigating a series of suspicious mailings sent to various addresses nationwide, including secretary of state offices and their related election offices, and congressional offices.

“Some of the letters contained an unknown substance and we are working closely with our law enforcement partners to respond to each incident. We are also working with our partners to identify the individual or individuals responsible for the letters. This FBI and the US Postal Inspection Service will continue to safeguard the public and secure elections for American citizens.”

Senators have been targeted across the political spectrum, and country. Letters addressed to the Democratic Senate minority leader, Chuck Schumer, and California senator Alex Padilla were intercepted by authorities, while Chris Murphy of Connecticut said the FBI, the Senate sergeant at arms and Capitol police alerted his team of a letter as well. Republicans in South Dakota, Texas and Nebraska were also targeted, with Mike Rounds saying his Sioux Falls office was evacuated, along with Pete Ricketts and Ted Cruz also reporting a suspicious letter.

In the House, at least 10 people were exposed after white powder was sent to the offices of the New York Democrats Hakeem Jeffries, Ritchie Torres and Tom Suozzi. In California, Jimmy Panetta said a staffer opened an envelope at his Santa Cruz office, then cleared the room and called 911. He said such attempts to intimidate “will not deter us from doing our job”. In Massachusetts, five staffers left Seth Moulton’s Salem office while police investigated, and testing found no substances of concern.

Investigators have described several common features connecting the suspicious letters sent to public officials and election centers.

The FBI has stated that the recovered envelopes were processed through a north Texas mail processing center and carry a postmark or stamp reading “Thinking of You”. Senate staff and House offices were warned to watch for plain white envelopes featuring these distinct markings.

The vast majority of these envelopes were intercepted by the US Postal Inspection Service and screening facilities before being delivered.

In 2024, election officials were targeted in 17 states before the 2024 presidential election, and no suspect has been named in this case.

Uefa demands Fifa releases documents relating to World Cup sell-off scheme

The Guardian Mon, 19 Oct 2026 18:52:05 GMT

European governing body gives two-week deadline

Letter addresses other issues including Balogun affair

Uefa has given Fifa a two-week deadline to release key documents relating to Gianni Infantino’s World Cup sell-off plan and other governance issues in its latest critique of football’s world governing body.

A letter sent to Fifa’s general secretary, Mattias Grafström, by his counterpart at Uefa, Theodore Theodoridis, is accompanied by an eight-page document that has more than 50 questions about Fifa’s handling of dozens of issues over the past 12 months. These include the proposed sale of 20% of its commercial rights, the Folarin Balogun affair, the peace prize and relations with Donald Trump and the arrangements for next year’s Fifa presidential election. Uefa’s document also makes a number of allegations about potential conflicts of interests at Fifa, as well as repeating calls for a “genuinely independent” governance review.

Uefa’s latest intervention follows last week’s meeting of the Fifa council in Zurich, the first time it had gathered since the emergence of the Fifa Forward Enterprise (FFE) controversy in July. Infantino listened to questions on FFE and other matters, but declined to provide substantive answers, instead asking council members to submit them in writing before their next meeting in Doha on 16 December.

In a letter sent on Monday, Theodoridis wrote: “These explanations have not begun satisfactorily to address a number of fundamental questions raised by Council members.

“Others remain unanswered, and the information and documentation requested have not been provided.

“Following the invitation made during the meeting to submit our questions in writing, we therefore enclose a consolidated set of questions and requests for information.

“We formally request a substantive written response to each question, together with all supporting documentation by Monday 2nd November. Any refusal to disclose information or documents should be justified individually, with a clear explanation of the specific grounds relied upon.

“These questions require answers now. They cannot be deferred until the next meeting of the Fifa Council – nor can future governance reforms substitute for scrutiny of decisions already taken and accountability for them.”

The accompanying document and list of supplementary questions constitutes a damning takedown of Fifa’s leadership under Infantino, who, as it stands, is on course to be re-elected unopposed as president next year, although Uefa is increasingly hopeful of identifying a candidate to take him on before nominations close on 18 November.

Uefa also wants answers on the processes behind other major decisions taken by Fifa over the past 12 months including moving the men’s World Cup draw to Washington DC from Las Vegas, the introduction of hydration breaks and the 27-minute half-time at the World Cup final.

“A series of decisions, transactions and interventions involving the Fifa President, the President of the United States and individuals associated with him raise serious questions concerning potential conflicts of interest, transparency and institutional accountability,” Uefa states.

The amount Fifa is paying to rent office space in Trump Tower is also queried, as is a report in the Times last week that Infantino in 2024 “received substantial additional remuneration which was not disclosed in Fifa’s annual report”. Fifa has said it “does not pay a second salary to the Fifa president and complies with all reporting requirements in relation to compensation”.

Uefa also raises concerns about March’s presidential election, specifically regarding the involvement of Bruno Chiomento, the chair of Fifa’s electoral committee. “We understand that Mr Chiomento has known the Fifa President for approximately 20 years and is regularly invited to Fifa events and competitions at Fifa’s expense,” Uefa’s document states. “We further understand that he attended the entire 2026 World Cup as an accredited individual, with his expenses covered by Fifa for more than five weeks.”

Uefa has also requested a complete list of Fifa guests in VIP and VVIP areas at the World Cup final, on the grounds that “numerous guests were apparently given priority over Presidents of Member Associations and Secretaries General of Confederations”.

Fifa has been contacted for comment.

Hurts’s condition is considered stable and ⁠he “has no significant ⁠functional limitations,” ​the team said. His treatment for a new diagnosis of deep vein thrombosis and bilateral pulmonary ⁠emboli will involve blood thinners, during which time he is unable to participate in contact activities.

The 28-year-old’s prognosis is good and the Eagles said they expect ​a full recovery with no long-term ‌effects.

Specialists in England ‌initially diagnosed superficial clots in Hurts’s left calf before Philadelphia’s loss to the Jacksonville Jaguars in London on 11 October.
