Burnham urges officials to come up with more radical options for Thames Water

The Guardian Mon, 19 Oct 2026 18:37:14 GMT

Exclusive: Utility seen as ‘litmus test’ of PM’s promise to bring ‘essentials of life’ under public control

Andy Burnham has told officials to rip up their plans for how to fix Thames Water and present him with more radical options for what to do with the stricken company.

In an early test of his promise to bring “the essentials of life” under public control, the prime minister is urging his advisers to go back to the drawing board and create a new list of policies for the utility.

One option being looked at is to convert about £100m of outstanding fines into a government stake in the company, saving its creditors money but giving ministers some say in how it is run.

Burnham previously said he would nationalise Thames, which is running out of cash and recently asked its creditors for an additional £2.4bn, but is struggling to find a way to do so without spending billions of pounds, getting tied up in a lengthy court battle, or both.

Sources familiar with the prime minister’s thinking say he has now told policy officials across Whitehall to contemplate options that were not previously considered feasible, even if that means spending taxpayer money and going to court.

One government source described the fate of the company as a “litmus test” on whether the government could deal with challenges in the medium term, rather than just immediate cost of living support and longer-term structural changes.

“There are more options than people have assumed to date including ones that have never been properly considered,” the source said.

Another said the prime minister had told his officials to “look at all the options and not feel constrained”, in a departure from the advice under Burnham’s predecessor, Keir Starmer.

Burnham has promised to end what he calls “40 years of neoliberalism” and has instructed his ministers to draw up a 10-year plan for government later this year, including detailed proposals for bringing utilities under public control.

Meanwhile, Angela Eagle, the environment secretary, is working on a water bill that will lift a Thatcher-era cap on government ownership of water companies and could rewrite how the bankruptcy regime works for the industry.

Government advisers believe changes to the “special administration regime” (SAR) would make it easier to take companies such as Thames into state control in the future.

But Burnham is also looking for a more immediate solution to Thames’s problems.

When the prime minister came to office, government insiders say he was presented with two main options for Thames: strike a bailout deal with the American hedge funds that own its debt, or pursue an SAR.

Thames’s creditors had proposed a £10bn rescue plan for the company, but Emma Reynolds, the previous environment secretary, made clear her opposition to such a plan before Burnham became prime minister.

Government lawyers also believe it will be difficult to have the company placed into SAR given that it is being kept afloat financially by its creditors and has managed to keep services running.

Among the other options being discussed is the waiving of the approximately £100m in environmental fines the company still owes and taking a stake in it instead. Then, if and when the company is fined again, the government would automatically increase its share rather than collecting the cash.

While some believe this would be a relatively straightforward way to give the government a say in how the company is run, many also believe it would fall short of Burnham’s promise to nationalise the company outright.

The prime minister is under pressure to go further, for example by stripping Thames of its licence, pushing for it to go into SAR immediately and then taking it out of administration without offering anything to the existing creditors.

Such a plan will inevitably be challenged in court, but Burnham is understood to be more willing to take on legal action than Starmer was. One adviser said: “Litigation was always a 100% certainty.”

The prime minister’s advisers also believe they can go further with Thames than with other companies because international investors see the company as a unique case, and not an indication of how the government intends to treat every water company.

Officials say other water companies are likely to be dealt with in different ways, through a mixture of stricter regulation and increased oversight by elected officials such as mayors.

Ewan McGaughey, a professor in law at King’s College, London, said: “The government’s best option is to start a special administration process for Thames Water before it runs up more debts, and sends billions more overseas.

“An orderly transition to public ownership does not require that banks in control are bailed out – on the contrary, the law says polluters should pay.”

Lena Swedlow, deputy director of the Compass campaign group, said: “The obvious solution is to put Thames Water into SAR, and then brought into public ownership so it truly works for everyone.

“While reform of the failing regulatory mechanisms is welcome, any recapitalisation and debt-to-equity schemes that do not seek to permanently wrestle the company from private hands will fail to be in the interests of the workers, stakeholders, and the 16 million people Thames serves. Everything else is noise in the wind.”

France imposes partial curfews in several cities, including parts of Paris

The Guardian Mon, 19 Oct 2026 18:16:45 GMT

Interior minister concedes police ‘lost control’ of weekend protests as PM vows to restore public order

Partial curfews have been issued for a number of French cities, including parts of Paris, after the government admitted police had “lost control” during violent weekend protests around the country.

Sébastien Lecornu, the French prime minister, said after an emergency cabinet meeting on Monday he was “fully resolved to restore public order” and had called for “local and partial” curfews if needed. There was “no question” of imposing a full curfew on entire cities, he said.

His office later announced partial curfews from 8pm to 6am on Monday and Tuesday nights in four northern cities, including Lille.

Police also imposed a curfew from 11pm Monday until 6am on Tuesday on two locations in Paris: Place de la République, where rioting took place on Saturday; and the shopping neighbourhood of Les Halles, which has been subject to looting.

A statement from police said the orders banned gatherings and demonstrations and prohibited anyone from entering or remaining in the two designated areas.

France’s second city, Marseille, earlier announced independently that it had banned all gatherings and demonstrations on Monday. French unions, meanwhile, called for a new ⁠round of strikes and rallies on 5 November.

Lecornu told reporters that if declaring a state of emergency was deemed necessary “we could do so”, but ⁠added that at this stage partial curfews seemed “more appropriate”.

Lecornu’s comments came after France’s interior minister conceded that police had “lost control” in some cities during Saturday’s protests and the president, Emmanuel Macron, demanded a full security review and “new operational methods” to end the rioting.

Laurent Nuñez said on Monday there had been a “lack of anticipation” in preparations for the protests and acknowledged that police numbers had sometimes been inadequate to deal with rioters and looters on the fringes of the demonstrations.

Nuñez said intelligence had suggested there would be 200,000 demonstrators around the country. In the event, there were more than 500,000 and peaceful protests were hijacked, morphing into one of France’s most violent days of unrest in recent years.

He said he had tendered his resignation to Macron because he felt “responsible for everything that happened”. Macron refused it, demanding instead that Nuñez “take all necessary steps to ensure transparency over planning and intelligence failures”.

The protests follow weeks of demonstrations by high school students that have been marred by sometimes violent clashes with police, rocking the country six months before a crunch presidential ⁠election and amid mounting economic pressures.

Public buildings including a town hall were attacked and set ablaze and an estimated 2,000 shops were ransacked and looted, authorities have said.

France’s digital minister, Anne Le Henanff, urged online resale platforms to remove listings for “stolen items” and summoned representatives of companies including Vinted and eBay. According to the commerce ministry, representatives of Amazon, Leboncoin, Meta and TikTok were also invited.

Nuñez said 60,000 police and other security forces had been deployed around the country, but acknowledged it had not been enough to control determined, organised groups of violent rioters in major cities including Paris, Marseille and Lyon.

“You couldn’t look shopkeepers in the eye after hundreds of shops had been looted and say we hadn’t lost control,” the minister told French radio, but added that the responsibility of “rioters, looters and ultra-left militants” should not be glossed over.

The justice minister, Gérald Darmanin, also said intelligence failings had left the state vulnerable. “There’s no good policing without good intelligence,” he said, adding that many of those arrested had police records and “about 80%” were being prosecuted.

Darmanin said 2,513 people had been arrested and 67 people had been imprisoned since the violence that marred the demonstrations this weekend broke out, Liberation reported.

Some 70% of those arrested were adults and almost 1,000 police and gendarmes have been injured.

Macron’s office said in a statement on Monday that besides reviewing the security shortcomings, Nuñez had been tasked with “promptly implementing new operational methods for security forces to use on the ground in combating rioters”.

Rioting and looting continued on Sunday. The mayor of Paris, Emmanuel Grégoire, said on Monday that about 30 shops had been targeted in the capital the previous day, with a further 350 people arrested overnight.

“Maintaining public order is the responsibility of the state. It is the state that was at fault this weekend,” Grégoire said. “We have a social movement that is spreading, and no political prospect for a constructive way out. So the protests will continue.”

Marseille’s mayor, Benoît Payan, said not just democracy but “the very foundations of the Republic” had been undermined. Describing the situation as “almost insurrectional”, he said the government’s stance amounted to “petty political manoeuvring”.

On Monday, protesters blocked entrances to the Louvre Museum in support of the nationwide high school student protest movement and to denounce “police repression”. The museum could not open as scheduled because of the protest.

A leaflet displayed outside the museum read: “We are proud to announce that we are blocking the world’s largest museum.”

In a televised address on Sunday, Macron criticised the “unbridled” violence and said local authorities would be able to ban some demonstrations in the coming days, but stopped short of drastic measures such as declaring a state of emergency or curfew.

Saturday’s protests, by students, teachers, parents, unions and workers, focused on the high cost of living, an issue that also prompted demonstrations in several other European countries including Italy, Belgium and Albania over the weekend.

Israeli police detain 10 people in rare raid against West Bank settlers

The Guardian Mon, 19 Oct 2026 18:05:14 GMT

Move comes after US photojournalist and group of European diplomats and Palestinians were assaulted in separate attacks

Israeli police have detained 10 people in a rare raid against settlers, after a weekend of extreme violence in the occupied West Bank including an attack on US photojournalist Heidi Levine, which she described as an “attempted lynching”.

She was knocked down, kicked and beaten by a group of masked Israeli men as she covered the olive harvest in a Palestinian village on Friday. The militants broke four vertebrae and a rip, ripped open her finger so it required surgery and left her with lacerations across her body.

“I was practically, basically lynched by a gang of Jewish settlers in the area of Ramallah,” Levine said, in an interview with the BBC from her hospital bed on Monday.

The day after that assault, Israeli militants armed with sticks and iron bars attacked a group of European diplomats and Palestinians harvesting olives outside the town of Taybeh, assaulting a visiting French mayor, smashing the window of an official car, and causing severe injuries to a young Palestinian man.

The Israeli prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, questioned the accounts of Israeli militant violence, ignoring extensive video and witness evidence.

He referenced an “alleged attack” on Levine, whose severe injuries were visible in interviews from her hospital bed, and “unproven allegations” the diplomats had been targeted by militants.

The attacks and his response drew a furious international reaction, including from the US secretary of state, Marco Rubio, the US ambassador to Israel, Mike Huckabee – generally considered a staunch ally of the current Israeli government – European nations and the editor of the Washington Post, Matt Murray.

On Monday morning Israeli police released footage of a rare raid on settlers, and said they had detained 10 people connected with the attacks on foreigners and construction of an illegal outpost.

Hours later a court extended the detention of six men connected with the attacks on foreigners, to between three and four days.

There has been little response to extreme violence against Palestinians across the West Bank, and Levine said the global focus on her attack highlighted extreme double standards.

“People are dealing with this, undergoing attacks, losing property, losing family members, being injured all across the West Bank and nothing is being done,” she said.

Israelis target Palestinians with near total impunity in the occupied West Bank, where arrests are unusual, indictments rare and convictions even more unusual.

Israeli human rights group Yesh Din has documented 561 incidents of settler and soldier violence against Palestinians in the occupied West Bank over three weeks since 27 September. That is an average of more than 26 each day.

“It is telling that it took attacks on foreign nationals to prompt a significant response from Israeli authorities,” said the group’s executive director, Ziv Stahl. “Palestinians have endured years of systematic settler violence, with 94% of investigations into cases of settler violence against Palestinians closed without indictments.

Levine said her body armour and helmet had prevented even more serious injuries, and she considered herself “lucky” given the ferocity of the attack. Netanyahu’s attempt to cast doubt on the attack felt like a “a big slap on my face”, she added.

Netanyahu’s statements, apparently undermined by security forces arrests days later, were widely seen as an attempt to court far-right voters inside Israel, as the country heads into the final days of an election campaign.

His coalition partners include extremist settlers, who support the campaign of violence that has driven thousands of Palestinians from their homes and land in the occupied West Bank over the last three years.

Haaretz reported on Monday that political pressure was preventing the army from confronting “Jewish terrorism” in the West Bank, even when the targets were foreigners including diplomats and journalists.

Commanders are reluctant to challenge settler leaders, or take action against Israeli civilians and soldiers who attack Palestinians, Israeli defence officials told the paper.

Formal investigations and disciplinary procedures are limited and undermined by unofficial but clear messages of support from top commanders, the report said.

It cited the response to an attack on a CNN crew in March. Central Command chief Maj Gen Avi Bluth suspended the battalion responsible from operational duty and announced disciplinary action against soldiers involved.

Later that night, the brigade commander came to a base where the soldiers were staying to express his support and join them in prayer, Haaretz said.

ITV’s exposé of racism and misogyny in Reform? Just a few (more) bad apples

The Guardian Mon, 19 Oct 2026 17:42:46 GMT

While the party’s MPs went into hiding, it was left to its failed byelection candidate Matt Goodwin to defend it

It was the dog that didn’t bark in the night. After Sunday night’s ITV exposé of widespread racism and misogyny within Reform, you might have expected one of its MPs to have taken to the airwaves on Monday morning to defend the party’s honour. To try to persuade viewers that the real problem lay with the journalists who couldn’t stop themselves from investigating Reform rather than the fact that the party’s bigotry was endemic.

Instead, we got nothing. Every Reform MP was otherwise engaged. Were too busy having breakfast. Nothing from Nigel Farage. Nothing even from Robert Jenrick. Maybe he realised he had crashed and burned a few days earlier by suggesting it was just one of those things. One of life’s little mysteries. The BBC was riddled with paedophiles and Reform was awash with racists, said Honest Bob. No big deal. Every organisation had its crosses to bear.

The only MP to post on X in the morning was Richard Tice, who was feeling decidedly grumpy, having only just got married to Isabel Oakeshott. Perhaps he had a hangover. Though his main gripe was that British Airways was yet another failing British institution because it had mislaid at least one of his bags.

Dicky’s social media post had more than a touch of the “don’t you know who I am” to it. You can only imagine the baggage handler may have known exactly who Dicky was and had taken great pleasure in diverting one of the fake Louis Vuitton suitcases from Dubai to Manila. Via Buenos Aires.

The one person out and about for Reform was the one person you would have thought the party would want to keep hidden. Step forward Matt Goodwin, the party’s failed candidate for the Gorton and Denton byelection whose own views could easily pass off as borderline racist in polite circles. Matt is going through his own personal anti-growth agenda. Working hard to deconstruct himself from low-level academic to incredibly dim primate with low social skills. Almost every day, voters in Gorton and Denton thank their lucky stars for having dodged that bullet.

Matt’s defence of Reform was … unorthodox, to put it kindly. So much so that you began to wonder whether he was even conscious. Luckily for him, he was only allowed out on Times Radio. Though that was more than enough. To try to understand Matt is to make a category error. The whole point is to not understand him. That’s the way you stay sane. Because what he wanted listeners to believe was that Nige was a buffer zone against racism. That hordes of would-be racists begged to be allowed to join Reform, only to find out that Nige was a man of peace and love. The one politician who wanted nothing but good things for all immigrants.

It got better. Because Batshit Matt also wanted us to believe that the ITV documentary had just uncovered a few bad apples in the party. So in a way it had done Reform a favour. What were the chances? The ITV journalists had managed to uncover the only seven racists in the Reform ranks. Everyone else was Team Nigel. Never had a bad word for anyone. Except, there was another way of looking at this. That ITV had filmed about 10 Reform councillors and found that seven of them had views that included beheading King Charles for being a Muslim. Some statisticians might put that down as a 70% hit rate. Not so much a few wrong ’uns but a whole army of them. Poor Nige. Always the victim.

Over in the Commons, Wes Streeting was preparing for other threats during departmental defence questions. Though John Healey was not one of them. Instead, Wes seemed more interested in persuading himself that there was absolutely nothing unusual in Donald Trump switching the Starlink satellite system on and off at random moments, thereby allowing Russian drones to do untold damage on Ukraine. This was just standard procedure. The only way you could tell the system was working properly was if you turned it off from time to time. Obvious when you think about. Wes was also totally chilled about Trump trying to lower US pump prices by allowing Russian imports of diesel. Fuel that the Russians had also imported from Iran and with whom, coincidentally, the US was at war.

All of this apparently made perfect sense not just to Streeting, but also to Labour and opposition backbenchers. Wes could reassure us because he had had a personal meeting with Pete Hegseth the previous week, during with the secretary for war had reiterated Trump’s claims that Nato forces had been a waste of space in Afghanistan and that the US troops had fought alone. More than ⁠160 ​offshore rig workers plan walkout amid rising tensions between unions and oil companies

North Sea workers are preparing to strike at oil rigs across the ageing basin over the coming weeks in a sign of growing tensions between trade unions and oil companies.

The Unite union said on ⁠Monday that more than ⁠160 ​offshore rig workers would take part ⁠in a 24-hour ​strike from Wednesday that could “severely disrupt” UK fuel supplies.

A 48-hour strike starting on Tuesday was already planned by workers at oil services company Wood Group contracted to Harbour Energy’s Britannia, Jasmine, Judy, Lomond and North Everest platforms.

Trade union leaders are scheduled to continue pay talks with the Apache energy company through the Acas mediation service on Wednesday. But Unite expects the 24-hour strike to go ahead at 6am that morning because, it says, the company has shown “no willingness” to resolve the dispute.

The strike will include workers employed at five Apache oil platforms linked to the Forties Pipeline System (FPS), which is responsible for about 30% of the UK’s oil production. Unite has claimed that a halt in production could lead to a sharp drop in pressure across the pipeline system and disrupt UK fuel supplies.

A spokesperson for Jim Ratcliffe’s Ineos, the owner of the Forties pipeline, did not respond to a request for comment.

North Sea oil companies have been on a collision course with trade unions in recent years as many cut investments in their UK assets, blaming the UK’s energy policies and tax regime.

The industrial action comes ahead of the budget on 28 October and an imminent decision on the fate of the controversial Jackdaw gas project, as the UK faces fresh concerns over its energy supplies this winter because of the global fuel crisis caused by the wars in the Middle East and Ukraine.

Texas-based Apache plans to end all its North Sea operations by the end of 2029, blaming the “onerous financial” impact of the government’s windfall tax, which means oil companies pay a total tax rate of 78% on their profits.

A spokesperson for Apache said it plans to use experienced contractors to continue production during the strike. It added that even if all five platforms were unable to operate, the company would not expect an impact on other oil companies using the Forties pipeline.

The company added: “Our offer provides a 4% pay increase for employees in the bargaining unit, whose earnings already place them among the highest earners in the UK and whose offshore rota averages 153 working days a year.”

Harbour Energy, the UK’s biggest producer of North Sea oil, has also blamed the UK’s tax regime for its decision to scale back investment in UK waters. It said late last year that it would cut 100 offshore jobs, having reduced its workforce by about 600 since 2023.

Wood Group said that only eight of the 150 employees contracted to the affected Harbour platforms took part in strike action earlier this month and that the action did not disrupt operations. A third 48-hour strike is planned for 3 November, according to Unite and trade union RMT.

The Guardian view on France’s protests: a polarised country is in a perilous political moment

The Guardian Mon, 19 Oct 2026 17:30:02 GMT

The scenes of social unrest and violence at the weekend are an ominous portent, ahead of elections which may deliver a far-right presidency

In Emmanuel Macron’s book Revolution, published ahead of the 2017 presidential election that he went on to win, he promised to restore hope to a country that was losing faith in its future. As Mr Macron’s lame-duck second term enters its last phase against a quasi-insurrectionary backdrop of torched public buildings and looted shops, the failure of that political project appears total.

The worst scenes of urban violence for years overshadowed a weekend of protest that gravely undermined what is left of the French president’s authority. As police lost control of the streets, more than 2,000 shops were ransacked. Far-left groups targeted town halls and local buildings, and engaged in pitched battles with the police, whose disastrously heavy-handed response to last week’s high school protests has succeeded only in escalating tensions.

In a statement on Sunday evening, Mr Macron rightly condemned what he described as episodes of “unbridled violence”. On the far right, Marine Le Pen is already exploiting a national sense of dismay to present herself as the law-and-order solution to the crisis. But the shocking actions of a minority should not obscure the significance of the vast, peaceful demonstrations that took place throughout France on Saturday. Calls to unite the student protests and the yellow vest movement, which disrupted Mr Macron’s first term over cost of living issues, mobilised up to 800,000 people.

The root cause of the unrest is a widespread perception that France’s social contract is broken. The young feel let down by an underfunded and unequal education system, and are fearful of the future impact of AI and the climate emergency. As is increasingly the case across Europe, they no longer trust mainstream politicians to find answers. The scale of the weekend protests showed that gen Z’s discontent has merged with that felt in the country’s neglected towns and banlieues, which have suffered repeated economic shocks since the Covid pandemic.

The obtuse and stubborn response from Mr Macron has been to double down on a cost‑cutting agenda to reduce France’s public debt, in order to appease the financial markets. But in an era where the asset-rich have continued to flourish, and the wealthiest have done best of all, to argue that that there is no alternative to spending less on schools and healthcare won’t wash. The economist Thomas Piketty pointed out during last week’s student protests that the boom in private wealth means that, despite the size of its public debt, “France has never been richer”.

Mr Macron’s reckless decision to call a snap election in 2024, which cost him his majority, left him a diminished political figure. His biggest subsequent error has been to haughtily persist with the economics of austerity, despite clear evidence of deepening political polarisation and rising popular anger. With each week that passes, the social consequences appear more ominous, ahead of presidential elections in six months’ time.

The latest polls suggest that the far right’s huge lead is widening ahead of that contest. Meanwhile, the hard-left leader Jean-Luc Mélenchon continues to outscore progressive rivals, though the numbers suggest that he would heavily lose a runoff against Ms Le Pen. In an increasingly febrile atmosphere, France is heading towards a seismic reckoning in May. Alarmingly, the civil strife witnessed at the weekend may only be a foretaste of what is to come.

The Guardian view on Trump and Putin: Ukraine’s future is not theirs to bargain away

The Guardian Mon, 19 Oct 2026 17:25:02 GMT

Russia wants America and China to decide Ukraine’s future without Kyiv. Europe must challenge this dangerous return to diplomacy of the strong for the strong

Does Vladimir Putin know exactly how to play Donald Trump? The history of chummy phone calls, high-profile meetings and attempts to bring Russia in from the cold certainly suggests that Moscow’s thuggish ruler has a hold on this American president. If Mr Trump agrees to negotiate Ukraine’s future with Mr Putin and China’s Xi Jinping without Ukraine at the table, he will have handed the Russian leader a victory before talks begin. The message will be that strongmen are ruling the world and determining the fate of weaker nations.

Ukraine has the right to determine its future. That right cannot be waved away by a self-serving Russian proposal, however much it indulges Mr Trump’s belief that world affairs should be settled by powerful men. The scales are falling from European eyes. Trumpian America is raising doubts about whether it will help deter aggression or even honour its Nato commitments. If Washington now rewards Moscow and pressures Ukraine to accept a raw deal, it would be a betrayal. European governments would wonder where America might be in the future when their own security is threatened.

The Wall Street Journal laid out how Mr Putin is hoping to secure a diplomatic prize that dwarfs any US benefits. Mr Trump needs to bring down diesel prices before crucial midterm elections. So the Russian president has offered him a deal that helps the White House claim it is addressing such costs, despite most analysts saying that it won’t. In the same conversation, Mr Putin suggested a summit to end the war in Ukraine that would elevate Moscow and exclude Kyiv. China could also gain recognition as a diplomatic mediator, while Europe would be left out of discussions about ending a war on its continent. Reports suggest that the three leaders could meet at next month’s Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in China.

American presidential power is meant to be constrained by law and democratic institutions. Mr Trump’s diesel deal appears to violate US law barring imports of Russian ‌energy until Moscow ends its aggression against Ukraine. More Republicans should find the courage to stand up to their bullying president. While doing so, they might also ask why the order to limit a satellite system used by Ukraine ​for battlefield communications and drone operations reportedly came from the White House. Heated denials from the US secretary of state, Marco Rubio, are no substitute for answers.

A transatlantic breakdown in relations between European powers and the US is not inevitable. Mr Trump’s national security strategy last year called Europe “strategically and culturally vital”. But it also demanded that the continent take responsibility for its own defence. European governments must prepare to meet that challenge.

History doesn’t repeat itself, but it often rhymes. Were Mr Trump to embrace Mr Putin’s trilateral summit, it would echo the Three Emperors’ League that brought together Germany, Austria-Hungary and Russia in 1873. Germany sought to isolate defeated France and contain Austro-Russian rivalry, while monarchies sought to defend themselves against revolution. The original arrangement quickly unravelled. Revived in 1881, the league collapsed in 1887 as Vienna and Moscow failed to reconcile their Balkan ambitions. Agreement between powerful rulers provides no guarantee of a lasting settlement. Ukraine’s future cannot hang on bargains struck to stroke the egos of powerful men.

‘Money and medals over safety’: Nassar judge warns gymnasts are still being failed

The Guardian Mon, 19 Oct 2026 17:22:38 GMT

Larry Nassar’s sexual abuse crimes came to light 10 years ago

Survivors gather at world championships to call for reform

The judge who sentenced the former USA Gymnastics team doctor Larry Nassar to up to 175 years in jail in 2018 for the sexual abuse of more than 250 women and girls has condemned the lack of meaningful change in the decade since Nassar’s crimes were exposed.

With the World Gymnastics Championships taking place here this week, Judge Rosemarie Aquilina said human rights must be prioritised over the desire for sporting success.

“Nassar was 10 years ago and there have been very few changes that are meaningful,” said Aquilina, who insisted on all 169 impact statements being heard in her courtroom after Nasser’s guilty plea.

“I’m not looking for little changes that a lot of people get credit for, I want meaningful change, a lot of meaningful changes, and we’re just not there yet, not in sports, not in life, not in the courtroom, not in the classroom or in the legislature.

“I have to ask why? It’s the same answer: it’s money, medals and notoriety over the safety of children and safety is a human right.”

Aquilina joined activists, survivors and advocates from Gymnasts for Change International (G4CI) in Rotterdam, who gathered to question why the level of change has been inadequate and what can be done.

Claire Heafford, a survivor of abuse within the sport and the chief executive of G4CI, said: “We’re still in a place where survivors aren’t being listened to and where the scale of the reform hasn’t met the scale of the revelations.”

Heafford puts the unwillingness to engage with systemic change post-Nassar as “institutional fear, blinkeredness, and the fact that people who work in sport are not very creative”.

She said: “It’s incredibly difficult for anybody in the system who wants to create change to do so if there’s resistance above them. It’s incredibly difficult for people in the system to feel empowered as change makers when you’re in such fixed hierarchies.”

The event was timed to reflect an opportunity for genuine change as World Gymnastics appoints a new secretary general with Nicolas Buompane stepping down at the end of the year.

Minky Worden, of Human Rights Watch, said the reckoning sport faced since Nassar took the wrong form. “On the one hand, you can measure progress in athlete voice and advocacy, in some whistleblower protections, in safeguarding rules across sport – though the rules are there, but the implementation is not,” she said.

“Then, on the other hand, you can measure it in the impact gymnastics had in all other sports. I’ve interviewed hundreds of survivors in about 50 sports, winter and summer. Ten years on, just the scale and the severity and the duration of the abuses by the so-called Olympic doctor Larry Nassar caused a reckoning across sport. But the reckoning often took the wrong shape, it took the shape of defence.

“Except, this is not a small problem, it is a severe problem and any fair assessment would have to say that sport, broadly speaking, including gymnastics, retains the exceptionalism the Catholic church and schools once had.

“There was a time when it was really hard to get rid of the abusive priest or teacher because they were moved around to different jurisdictions and continued abusing. That is why the scale and the duration of those abuse catastrophes was so great. Sports still has the same problem.”

The former elite acrobatic gymnast Eloise Jotischky, who became the first person to win a civil case against British Gymnastics for the abuse she experienced between 2016 and 2018, which included inappropriate weight management techniques and verbal abuse, said there have been some changes, but the issue is with implementation.

“There’s still a lot to be done. For example, British Gymnastics have come out with a number of policies, they’ve got their hydration policies, they’ve got their weight management policies. That’s brilliant, but let’s implement them. It’s the implementation that matters because if you don’t implement them and if you’re not monitoring them then what’s the point?”

Kim Shore, of Gymnasts for Change Canada, who is a survivor of abuse within the sport and an independent safe sport advocate, wants World Gymnastics to adopt and implement huge cultural reforms if things are to improve. “There’s a crisis of abuse across sport in Canada and yet we’ve seen really no reform and I would say that same lack of action, that same apathy is happening at World Gymnastics,” she said.

“Sure, they’ve taken some steps, but they could post new rules anywhere that say: ‘No more weighing of gymnasts. No more gymnasts returning to competition without a doctor’s note. No more coaches moving from one country to another country, if you’re banned in the US, you can’t just take a gymnast from Mexico to the Olympics.’

“They could have a whole list of rules and regulations, even if they don’t have any sort of legislative jurisdiction in an area, that’s still going to influence the culture because as soon as the leading body says we’re not weighing gymnasts any more, then when the weighing gets done those coaches know they’re breaking the rules.

“If World Gymnastics would come out with a whole list of cultural reforms and started to normalise those within the national federations and then give them backing so that the national federations can go to the clubs all the way down to grassroots, I think we would see faster reform and less resistance.”

World Gymnastics, USA Gymnastics, Gymnastics Canada and British Gymnastics have been contacted for comment.

Funding social care is a collective responsibility

The Guardian Mon, 19 Oct 2026 17:18:11 GMT

Roger Steer says the solution is to adopt the NHS model, Janet Dubé suggests an audit, while Sally Byers says language that respects people living with dementia is crucial

Polly Toynbee asks a seemingly difficult question and discusses a knotty issue (In Liverpool I saw the tough choices Louise Casey faces on social care – starting with who will pay?, 13 October). Her question is framed as an issue of individual choice inviting the response: “Not me if I can avoid it.”

The responsible answer is, of course, all of us – collectively. It is an uninsurable risk that can only be solved equitably and efficiently as a collective solution. By entangling the issue of funding with provision of services, moral clarity is lost. Issues of matching funding distort and influence the level of care provided and ensure that progress toward resolving the question of who determines the need for care is delayed.

The solution is to fund social care in the same way as the NHS was envisaged: as a right, free at the point of need, and funded out of general taxation as part of annually managed expenditure, like pensions and social security, as needs are presented and professionally agreed.

The Treasury has the ways and means, and nothing more needs to be discussed. The additional costs as a percentage of GDP are small and affordable by reference to other countries.

The issue of affordability is exaggerated out of all proportion by politicians who are afraid of being accused of raising taxes. In fact, because of the very high economic multiplier effect of boosting spending on low-paid workers, it is certain that it will pay for itself without impacting government deficits (unlike defence spending).

Andy Burnham knows this, and needs to overrule his cautious advisers. This is his big chance to demonstrate leadership. People don’t vote for ditherers. Roger Steer Sheffield

Thank you, Polly Toynbee, for your article about your visit to Liverpool with Louise Casey. Ms Casey is clearly right when she says: “If it’s public money, it should mainly be publicly run.”

I am old enough to recall the 1970s Tory privatisation of social care, and I remember sales of council facilities being forced through by rate-capping. Blatantly paying staff in the private sector less and lowering their standards and conditions of service was supposed to save money. I wasn’t aware at the time of the massive shift of public money into private establishments. The fact that the state’s bill for residential care increased more than twentyfold within seven years is scandalous, and should have been at the time.

Was the Tory government from 1979 the most ideologically driven UK government ever? Surely it is not too late to carry out an “audit” of the transfer of public assets to private individuals and companies? Until Ms Toynbee’s article, I would have suggested starting with council housing or water boards. Now I think social care is the place to start, soon. Janet Dubé Peebles, Scottish Borders

Polly Toynbee’s description of people with advanced dementia as having “glazed stares or sleeping mouths agape” and “that terrible human vacancy” is deeply troubling. Such language dehumanises people and reinforces the stigma surrounding dementia.

People living with dementia deserve, like everyone else, to be treated and spoken about with respect and dignity. I suggest she consult the guide to language for journalists produced by the Dementia Engagement and Empowerment Project, published in 2014 and written by people with lived experience of the impact of careless descriptors. Sally Byers Sheffield

We need to stop disinformation in UK political adverts. Here’s a chance to do so

The Guardian Mon, 19 Oct 2026 17:17:33 GMT

Alex Tait on a proposed amendment to the representation of the people bill, and Dr Joseph Mullen on Russian interference in the Brexit referendum

Andy Burnham’s comments about Russian interference in Brexit (Report, 11 October) and the warning by the MI5 chief, Ken McCallum, against exaggerating its impact (Report, 13 October) risk overlooking another serious threat to electoral integrity: disinformation from our own political parties and campaigners.

Foreign interference deserves scrutiny, but misleading factual claims in electoral advertising are unregulated, unlike in commercial advertising. We have four sets of rules to ensure an advert for a packet of sausages is accurate, but none for the most important advertising of all – ads that influence how we vote.

With our fragmented five-party politics producing increasingly close elections, misleading advertising can be decisive. Brexit was decided by a 51.9%-48.1% vote split. Our research into May’s local elections found that 41.4% of wards in England were won by margins of less than 5%, with nine decided by a single vote. We also identified misleading electoral advertising in some of the closest contests.

Regulating factual claims in electoral advertising was a key recommendation of the House of Lords select committee on democracy and digital technologies in 2020. The representation of the people bill, currently going through parliament, offers an opportunity to act. An amendment covering the same scope attracted 37 MPs as sponsors in the Commons, and we are working with peers in the Lords to take it forward. Burnham signed up to our voluntary code for honest electoral advertising in 2024, which forms part of the proposed amendments.

We should tackle foreign interference, but we can’t continue to ignore the disinformation put out by our own political parties. Alex Tait Reform Political Advertising

The head of MI5 confirming that Russia did try to interfere in the Brexit referendum is highly significant to the result. The vote share achieved by the leave campaign was 51.9%, as against 48.1% for the remainers. This was a majority of just 3.8%. If Russian interference swayed just 2% of voting intentions, this would erode the much-vaunted majority of the leave group, and remainers would emerge as victors. MI5 should carry out an impact assessment of Russian interference using the most up-to-date AI, and attempt to quantify shifts in voting patterns. This would go a long way towards introducing a new referendum. Dr Joseph Mullen Former senior lecturer, University of Manchester

The cinema, punk music and swimming helped me through grief

The Guardian Mon, 19 Oct 2026 17:17:15 GMT

Rachel Walsh responds to an article by Georgina Elliott in which she describes the comfort she felt sitting alone in the cinema after losing her brother

I could relate to Georgina Elliott’s finding comfort and relief in the dark at the cinema (The one change that worked: numb with grief, I sat in the dark, surrounded by strangers – and began to heal, 12 October). After my mum died, I felt like a balloon floating further and further from my life, incorporeal and ghostly.

The cinema was a world within the world to live someone else’s life, experience their triumphs and adventures, and escape the sharpness of my own painful reality.

Punk gigs also offered me relief from grief, their raw honesty stripping away at this distance, bringing me back to an immediacy that I could cope with, and giving me a feeling of solidarity and acceptance. I could go alone, not talk to anyone if I didn’t feel like it, yet still be accepted as a member. It was OK to be broken there – no one was trying to pretend anything was fixed, and that gave me relief.

Later, swimming helped me recover. Being enveloped in water took me out of my physical numbness and buoyed me up, escaping the weight of grief pressing me down.

To be weightless was freedom. To swim out into the sea and look at the vastness of the sky, and be alone with my thoughts, infused me with a peace. And a power. I felt strong swimming and moving through water. I recovered something frozen in me, a connection with the world, with my own power in it. I felt held and comforted there, as if by a parent’s love. Rachel Walsh Dublin, Ireland

Houthi attack kills 53 in biggest single loss of life since Yemen civil war reignited

The Guardian Mon, 19 Oct 2026 17:15:23 GMT

More than 200 mostly young people said to be injured after ballistic missile attack on training camp for government forces

At least 53 people have been killed in a Houthi ballistic missile attack on a training camp for Yemeni government security forces, making it the largest single loss of life since the country’s civil war reignited in September.

The attack on al-Alam camp in the southern Shabwa province was said to have injured more than 200 others, mostly young recruits, and was described as a disaster by the country’s UN-recognised government. The injured were taken from the police and army training camp in the Jardan district to a hospital in the local capital, Ataq, where pleas for blood donations were made.

There will be an inquiry into how so many troops were left so exposed to a Houthi attack. In mid-September, the group began a fresh push on forces backing the UN-recognised government by pushing south along the Red Sea coast to try to take control of the Bab al-Mandab waterway.

Reliable assessments of the death toll in the fighting over the last month are hard to gather, but it is running into the many thousands. A Saudi airstrike on Sunday killed nine, including five children and two women.

Rashad al-Alimi, the president of the UN-recognised government, said those killed on Monday were new recruits, and he vowed an immediate hard response. He said the incident “affirmed that targeting the recruits reflects the Houthi militias’ approach of resorting to cowardly terrorist attacks whenever they face pressures or their Iranian-backed sabotage plots falter”.

On Monday he phoned the UN secretary general, António Guterres, to ask for the UN to classify the Houthis as a foreign terrorist organisation.

The Shabwa provincial authority said: “Targeting recruits constitutes a military escalation and a blatant assault on the province’s security.” Its governor, Awad bin al-Wazir, visited the wounded in hospitals, and called for extra air defences, saying troops were fighting across six fronts.

The killings underline the dangers of large numbers of troops gathering in one place within reach of the Houthi ballistic missile arsenal. The training camp was struck by three ballistic missiles while the recruits lined up in formation.

Houthi forces have also cut the road between government-run Shabwa and the Houthi-run Bayda governorate.

The Houthi military spokesperson said: “Our armed forces targeted the Saudi enemy’s mobilisations in al-Alam camp, which is run by Saudi officers in the eastern regions. The targeting resulted in the fall of dozens of dead and wounded from the Saudi enemy’s mobilisations, including Saudi officers.

“We warn the deceived ones against responding to the Saudi enemy’s calls to lure them with his defiled money to the pyres of death, and to exploit them instead of his soldiers who are indifferent to their lives.”

A Yemen government spokesperson said the site struck was not a military target linked to the current fighting but “a training centre where new recruits in the internal security forces of Shabwa governorate receive training and qualification programmes.”

They added: “This reveals the criminal nature of this assault, which targeted young people in the preparation and qualification phase to carry out their security duties, far from the frontlines.”

Separately the Houthis claim to have hit the anti-Houthi Giant Brigades of southern Yemen in six strikes in the areas of al-Suqya and Ras al-Ara. Southern forces are said to have been making progress in edging Houthi forces out of control of the area around the Bab al-Mandab strait, the narrowest waterway taking ships from the Red Sea to the Indian Ocean.

Fighting is also under way as Houthis try to mount a siege of Taiz, where citizens have been calling for greater air protection. In the city there seems to be a determination not to capitulate, but conditions are deteriorating as Houthis close access points.

It is not clear whether the Houthis have decided to slow the pace of attacks on Saudi airports and energy installations, or they are running low on munitions.

The Saudi Aramco headquarters was struck last weekend and some airlines have said they will not yet resume using Riyadh airport. The airport reopened at the weekend after being attacked this month.

Egypt’s parliament has postponed a vote on whether to send troops to Saudi Arabia despite extending the debate to a second day as MPs demanded more than two minutes each to speak. The vote is now likely to be held next week.

A two-thirds majority is required, and some opposition parties have signalled their intention to vote against or abstain. Disputes centre on the extent of the mission and whether it will involve sending troops into Yemen to help Saudi Arabia, and whether Egyptian troops inside Saudi Arabia would become targets for Houthi attacks.

The delay also gives the Egyptians time to see if Iran can persuade the Houthis to hold back, and for Saudi Arabia to confirm the renewal of badly needed loans to Egypt.

Egypt has resisted any ground intervention in Yemen, dating back to the 1962-67 war, when Gamal Abdel Nasser sent troops to back the republicans in North Yemen against the Saudi- and British-backed royalists. The incursion was intended to be minimal, but escalated to as many as 70,000 soldiers. Estimates of Egyptians killed range from 10,000-26,000.

Cheltenham jumps into action after fixing its troublesome hole

The Guardian Mon, 19 Oct 2026 16:41:47 GMT

Home of National Hunt racing has undergone extensive work on its drainage system in preparation for new season

There is little chance to catch your breath as the racing seasons turn, and just six days on from an exhilarating Champions Day at Ascot, Cheltenham will open its gates on Friday for the first card of the 2026-27 campaign.

Racing will return to the spiritual home of National Hunt racing after an abrupt curtailment to Cheltenham’s latest season, to allow for extensive work on the track’s drainage system following the discovery of a significant hole in the racing surface on Trials day in late January.

The festival meeting in March went ahead as planned six weeks later, but the Jockey Club, which owns the course, announced soon afterwards that both the popular mid-April meeting and the hunter-chase card in May had been sacrificed to allow sufficient time for remedial work to take place.

More than a kilometre of drainage has since been replaced or upgraded, and both the Old and New courses also received a thorough examination with ground-penetrating radar, which showed no additional causes for concern.

“We’re really pleased with how the track has responded to the significant drainage works that we completed over the summer months,” Jon Pullin, Cheltenham’s clerk of the course, said on Monday.

“Our decision to cancel the last three racedays of last season in order to maximise both the time to carry out the work and for the ground to recover was certainly the right one.

“Everyone knows how long, hot and dry our summer was and the team here have been working tirelessly, just like grounds teams all over the UK, to irrigate and prepare the track ahead of our season opener.”

The Showcase meeting was once little more than a loosener after the long summer break to ease Cheltenham back into the swing. As a two-day midweek meeting at the turn of the century, it attracted a total of 16k racegoers.

Like most of the non-festival days at Cheltenham, though, its popularity has increased steadily over the last 20 years, to the point where the 21,113 crowd for the Saturday card last year was more than three times the attendance for the Flat card at Doncaster the same afternoon featuring the Futurity Trophy, the final Group One of the year.

Cheltenham races so sparingly over the winter that there is no longer any such thing as a minor day at the track, in the main part of the season at least. The loss of three cards in April and May was a small price to pay to ensure that the ground was right for the return of racing in October.

As one problem with the going is apparently solved, though, another, less tractable issue remains, both for Cheltenham and for National Hunt racing more generally.

Cheltenham has already been forced to abandon the cross-country race at the November meeting because of firm ground, and the race is just the latest in a series of cancellations over jumps in recent weeks. Kempton, Exeter, Ludlow, Fakenham, Warwick and Wincanton have all been forced to abandon meetings due to unsuitably fast ground, while Chepstow’s Welsh Racing Festival from 9 to 11 October ended up as an all-hurdles meeting.

Cheltenham, of course, has a watering system, but even that has its limitations. The going ahead of this week’s meeting is now officially good, having been good, good-to-firm in places on Sunday, but the taps are now off due to an unsettled forecast.

A new fortnightly newsletter covering the intersection of sport and the climate crisis

after newsletter promotion

“We had 8mm of rain overnight last night [Sunday into Monday] and expect some further rain tonight into tomorrow,” Pullin said. “As a result, and in light of the uncertain forecast for the end of this week, we’ve stopped watering. We’re good ground all over currently but we’ll have to wait and see how much rainfall we get on Thursday and Friday before I can say with any real confidence what we’ll be when the tapes go up on Friday.”

Cheltenham’s struggle to maintain attendance at the festival meeting has been well-documented in recent years, though last season’s meeting saw a modest but very welcome increase in the crowd figure after three years of steady decline. But that has been at least partially balanced by the increasing popularity of the non-festival meetings, including a remarkable turnout of 44,900 on New Year’s Day this year that was just 232 below the total for the second day of the festival meeting.

The festival experience has clearly been a tricky sell since the post-Covid high of 2022, but the core Cheltenham experience – the atmosphere, the setting and, above all, the excitement and competitiveness of the racing – has remained in high demand.

To maintain that all-important competitiveness, though, the track needs big fields with fit, in-form horses and improving youngsters and novices moving up from further down the pyramid. If this year’s long, dry summer is becoming the rule and not the exception, the base of the pyramid could steadily erode.

The next scheduled fixtures at Exeter and Wincanton are the biggest events of the year at both tracks, and form a mini-festival – the West Country Weekend – on 6 and 7 November featuring the Haldon Gold Cup and the Badger Beers Chase. Since both tracks have already lost cards this season – Exeter, in fact, has cancelled two – there must be serious doubt about both days if the current dry weather continues.

The long, dry summer was a boon for Champions Day at Ascot, which has often been staged on deep winter ground. For the country’s smaller jumps tracks in particular, however, the climate crisis could increasingly been seen as a potentially existential threat.

Journalists forced to flee homes after Tommy Robinson shared images of where they lived online, court told

The Guardian Mon, 19 Oct 2026 16:36:42 GMT

Far-right activist is charged with two counts of harassment causing fear of violence to two MailOnline reporters

Journalists and their family members had to flee their homes after “bullyboy, intimidatory tactics” were deployed by the far-right activist known as Tommy Robinson, a court has been told as his harassment trial got under way.

Robinson, 42, whose real name is Stephen Yaxley-Lennon, was alleged to have targeted journalists from the Daily Mail and Mail Online by circulating images of their homes to millions of online followers and in effect encouraging them to join in making threats.

He is charged with two counts of harassment causing fear of violence to two MailOnline journalists, Andrew Young and Jacob Dirnhuber in 2024, which Robinson denies.

Dirnhuber, a senior editor at the Mail, and his partner had to leave their home, while Young and his family were provided with a close protection officer after the alleged campaign of intimidation by Robinson.

Robinson, a former member of the British National Party (BNP) and co-founder of the English Defence League (EDL), is accused of harassment causing fear of violence through X posts and direct messages. He is also alleged to have made a telephone call on 5 August 2024 in which he is accused of telling Young he would visit his house, saying: “I’m coming to get you.”

Opening the case for the prosecution on Monday at Southwark crown court, barrister Ben Holt told the jury Robinson could have chosen to complain to a press regulator after the Mail reported on his alleged role as an “influencer” encouraging the violence that broke out after the Southport murders in July 2024.

The paper’s coverage included photos of Robinson reclining on a sunlounger, a phone in hand, while on holiday in Cyprus, where a team from the Daily Mail had located him. Members of the jury were shown an image of a front page which included a photo of Robinson and the headline: “Stoking Race Riots from his Sunbed.”

“This trial is about the defendant’s reaction to this, what he perceived to be, unnecessary intrusion into his holiday,” said Holt.

“On social media, to millions of followers, he circulated images of their homes. His supporters, followers, got involved, threatening the journalists. Understandably, you might agree, they were scared, in some circumstances being forced to leave their homes.

“That is what this trial is actually about. The prosecution say this defendant, using bullyboy, intimidatory tactics, threatened the journalists. He sent photographers to their home addresses. He put pictures, albeit redacted, of them out on his timeline on X for the enjoyment and appreciation of his followers.

Holt took the jury through Robinson’s reaction on X to the Mail’s coverage, which was said to have changed in tone from being “reasonable” and “concerned” to “retaliatory”.

Holt said that it was was inevitable “and would have been known” by Robinson that his online followers and supporters “would pick up the baton and attack” those he was talking about.

Examples given included tweets from an X account using the name The Secret SpAd, which posted the home address of Young while the journalist was still in Cyprus. It was posted with the comment: ”Please be sure to congratulate him.”

When Young returned home from Cyprus on 6 August, his wife and daughters told him that a man in a grey Audi had parked outside their home. The man was confronted by the journalist’s daughter but ignored her, and a report was made to police. A further report was made of a man sitting under a tree, pointing his camera at the house.

Holt told the court: “Mr Young was concerned. His main concern was that while (Robinson) himself might not harm him, one of his many supporters online may seek revenge on him or his family.”

The court heard that a third journalist who was involved the mail’s coverage, George Odling, also felt the need to leave his family home after becoming concerned with the publicity surrounding his colleagues.

Ted Verity, the editor-in-chief of the newspaper, provided evidence to police of a voicemail he received from an individual who identified himself as Tommy Robinson, who allegedly told him: “I’ve already located every fucking one of you.”

A video posted by Robinson’s X account was also played to the court, in which he accused the Mail of having “doxxed” his family and children.

In the video, he sad: “You broke up my family holiday. Is it fair that I do that to you? You know I know the locations to where you are. To any other journalist, I will find you. So please, think: is it right?”

The trial was adjourned until Tuesday morning.

Masts removed from bomb-laden WWII ship in Thames in bid to avoid explosion

The Guardian Mon, 19 Oct 2026 16:21:06 GMT

American warship sank in 1944 with approximately 1,400 tonnes of munitions onboard

A sunken US wartime ship in the Thames estuary holding enough unexploded bombs to devastate a Kent coastal town and send a tidal wave through London has been made slightly safer, ministers have announced.

Engineers have removed the masts of the SS Richard Montgomery – a second world war cargo ship that sank in 1944 with approximately 1,400 tonnes of munitions onboard – without triggering the kind of feared explosion that has kept the wreck under constant guard for decades.

The work was carried out because of concerns that the masts, which had remained visible above the water near Sheerness, could collapse in on the deadly cargo and blow up the ship.

The potential effects of an explosion after 82 years under water have divided expert opinion. Some believe it could cause a small tsunami, throw debris 3km into the air, and “level Sheerness”, according to a New Scientist report in 2004. A government report in 2000 said it was widely accepted it would “put property and the local population at risk”.

The exact contents of the ship’s three holds are unknown but a defence agency report estimated there were almost 300 2,000lb (900kg) blockbuster bombs and more than 2,000 cluster bombs.

Keir Mather, the maritime minister, told the Commons on Monday that work had now been completed, with all three masts successfully removed in “complex project requiring specialist programme, engineering and risk management expertise”.

Mather said that the masts had put “significant load on the structure and their removal has reduced that risk and supports the long-term safe management of the site.”

He said work was completed ahead of schedule and below forecast costs, an estimated £9.5m. The masts have now been delivered to a maritime museum, the Historic Dockyard Chatham, “in recognition of the historic significance of the SS Richard Montgomery and its role in supporting the allied forces’ efforts during world war two”.

The wreck would “continue to be subject to continuous monitoring and control via the established exclusion zone”, he said.

A shipping exclusion zone has long been in place around the SS Montgomery, and since 2025 a no-fly zone has been in place – a development that could have been awkward had Boris Johnson’s proposed Thames estuary airport gone ahead.

Although the risk of an accidental major explosion is now deemed remote, local people have been alarmed by incidents in recent years, including the occasional close proximity of cargo shipping, and a paddleboarder who uploaded pictures to social media of himself leaning on the protruding masts.

Secrets, lies and a shock A-list cameo: how You Can See Everything became the film of the year

The Guardian Mon, 19 Oct 2026 16:17:48 GMT

Nathan Fielder’s secretive Elizabeth Holmes documentary has become a sold-out smash hit and might make Oscars history

Spoilers ahead

If there is one moment that sums up You Can See Everything, the new A24 documentary on Elizabeth Holmes that until this weekend was shrouded in spoiler-averse secrecy, it is, perhaps surprisingly, the one everyone already knows: co-director Nathan Fielder, the droll comedian known for deadpanning subjects into submission, sitting eye to eye with Holmes, the unblinking fabulist of Theranos infamy. In tight zoom, saturation turned up – Fielder’s arched brows and Holmes’s oceanic blue eyes as stark as two magnetic poles – he asks her: “Are you being real right now?”

That question hangs over much of the colossal three-hour movie, particularly a claustrophobic first half that has made headlines since the film’s existence was announced in September. That first half – essentially, the only part of the movie anyone respecting spoiler guidelines and/or the theatrical experience could talk about – takes place entirely in 2023, when Fielder and his co-director Lance Oppenheim, along with a small crew, embedded with Holmes, her husband, Billy Evans, and their two small children in the run-up to her prison sentence for fraud. We watch as Fielder, over a few surreal weeks in a beachfront rental, attempts to puncture Holmes’s indomitable facade of faultlessness. It’s not exactly comedic, this chess game between three norms-ignoring people, but it can be quite funny: TV’s grand illusionist, an absurdist auteur who will go as far as actually obtaining a 737 pilot’s license for the bit, stymied by a world-class fabricator, with her poorly dissembling husband on the side. This section resembles, in feel, the pull of an internet wormhole: the closer you zoom in on a subject, without outside context, the more sense devolves. Was Holmes “being real”, for instance, when she told Fielder, with seemingly complete sincerity, that she has never told a lie in her life? Or when she continued to insist, despite plain reality, that Theranos devices could perform 1,000 diagnostic tests?

It’s at once astounding how many people took her seriously, given how obviously mendacious she and her husband appear, and also understandable: the more time you spend with her – the more time you spend watching Fielder spend time with her – the more magnetic the force of her delusions. Or is it manipulations? Or both? There is no one correct read on what, exactly, she’s thinking. “I know what you’re feeling,” an obviously irritated Evans tells Fielder after he bristles at Holmes’s indistinction between the meanings of can perform and could theoretically perform 1,000 diagnostic tests. It is a relief, and one of the best lines of an extremely rich text, when the comedian immediately shoots back with his own irritation: “No, you don’t.” The fundamental unknowability of another person, even a known liar, is fascinating, but also its own dead end.

If the first half had been released as a standalone film, it would probably have generated some attention and then faded as an artefact of a particular era of Silicon Valley celebrity, a briefly fascinating but inconclusive stunt. But luckily for us – and the theatrical box office, where You Can See Everything had the most successful opening weekend for a documentary in over 20 years – Fielder and Oppenheim kept filming. You Can See Everything is, essentially, two films in one: an elevated true crime documentary, and then an experiment unraveling the preconceptions of a documentary. It’s the back half of this immense movie, which picks up in 2025, after Holmes has spent some time in prison, makes You Can See Everything the film of the year – a formally ambitious feat that not only pushes the boundaries of nonfiction cinema but speaks to our destabilizing present of endless, inescapable manipulation.

There’s a reason You Can See Everything currently holds a rare close-to-perfect score on Rotten Tomatoes, is among the highest-rated films all time on Letterboxd and has solid odds to become the first doc to ever be nominated for a best picture Oscar. In the second half of the movie – stop now if you haven’t seen – Fielder recruits a shockingly game (and possibly awards-worthy) Amanda Seyfried, star of The Dropout, the 2022 Hulu series on the Theranos debacle. At first, it seems as though Seyfried is participating in her own stunt: how funny and improbable, to see the actor who won an Emmy for playing Elizabeth Holmes watch footage of Holmes watching Seyfried play Holmes. Two very famous people, confronted by famous representations of themselves. Whose reaction is genuine?

But Seyfried thrillingly becomes part of the very Fielderian pursuit of emotional truth through arcane artifice. Borrowing logic from his groundbreaking HBO series The Rehearsal, Fielder inserts Seyfried into an escalating series of re-enactments, trying to wring some clarity out of his real interactions with Holmes, then out of their own reactions to the simulations. Seyfried oscillates between a conviction that The Dropout was a work of fiction grounded in fact, and that its liberties may have violated another person. Never have I seen an actor really dig into what it means to play a real person like Seyfried here, grappling with her various responsibilities – to Holmes the person, to Holmes the character, to story, to facts, to herself – in real time, shifting with each new piece of info or tilt of perspective.

The Dropout, for what it’s worth, was the best of a series of scam shows from 2022 that tried to turn the rise and fall of inflated 2010s tech companies such as Uber or WeWork into entertainment. (One of the film’s best punchlines is simply observing that Evans, with his “LASERS” license plate and obsession with a new Theranos “device”, continues to push Theranos 2.0 … at a WeWork). You Can See Everything coincidentally arrives amid a new wave of Hollywood attempts to make sense of tech world, from Aaron Sorkin’s dreadful The Social Reckoning to Luca Guadagnino’s OpenAI film Artificial to Alex Gibney’s colossal doc Musk, that feel insufficient to the magnitude and lunacy of the moment. By being neither bound to representation nor straightforward journalism, You Can See Everything gets to what we might call the “emotional truth” of this era – and not just because Evans, a professed Charlie Kirk fan seemingly radicalized by his Musk-owned X timeline who commissioned an AI hologram of his wife, emerges as a very 2020s villain, a tech bro with a possible drug problem and a god complex. Layer by layer, Fielder and co deconstruct the underpinnings of their storytelling, from Evans’s original deal to profit from the film to his possible loyalty toward a woman he has evident chemistry with. Truth, in fact, is dependent on what you’re shown.

This is the pinnacle of Fielder’s longstanding effort to invert assumptions of “reality” on screen. A former producer on Canadian Idol, he’s a student of reality television, a misnomer we readily accept: of course, we know, there is no true reality on TV. But documentary tends to court the benefit of the doubt, as if their presentation did not reflect the makers’ own biases and motivations. The joke is in the title; You Can See Everything is itself a lie – we cannot. Choices are made, things are not shown. Omniscience is impossible.

But we are, in this advent of AI, training to scan everything as manipulated. “Are you being real right now?” applies as much to celebrity bodies as to meme-motivated foreign wars as to the Instagram dog videos sent by my mom as to what, exactly, is going on with Elizabeth Holmes. We’re in uncharted waters now, the type best navigated collectively – such as with a theater full of other people, attempting briefly to make sense of the nonsensical, working with material delivered by the biases and motivations of other people, all vying for our attention. At what point, in this hall of mirrors, do you trust? I emerged from You Can See Everything unnerved: you maybe never know, but you still have to try.

Farage claim that £5m was reward for Brexit was ‘not press office line’, close aide says

The Guardian Mon, 19 Oct 2026 16:16:23 GMT

Exclusive: Undercover footage of Dan Jukes raises fresh questions about Reform leader’s statement that £5m gift was for security

Nigel Farage undermined his own claims that a £5m gift was for security when he referred to the money as a reward for Brexit, according to one of his closest aides.

The apparent admission came in undercover footage seen by the Guardian in which Dan Jukes says that it is “priced in” for Farage to profit from politics.

The footage raises fresh questions about the party leader’s statements that the gift was solely for security purposes.

The Reform UK leader is awaiting the outcome of a parliamentary watchdog investigation into whether or not the £5m from the crypto-billionaire Christopher Harborne, first revealed by the Guardian, should have been declared under parliamentary rules.

Farage told the Sun on 14 May: “And this [£5m] was given to me on an unconditional basis, completely unconditional basis. But frankly, it was given as a reward for campaigning for Brexit for 27 years.”

Now, previously unpublished footage from the undercover reporting group Verbatim, shared with the Guardian, has revealed a conversation between Jukes, a longtime close aide of Farage, and an undercover reporter.

“That was not the line to take from the press office,” Jukes said of Farage’s admission that the funds were a political reward, appearing to suggest that it was an on-air accident.

The subject of Farage’s funds arose when Jukes quipped that if a US limited liability company could not make a donation because of electoral law, perhaps the reporter posing as a donor could just make him a £5m unconditional gift instead.

After discussing if Jukes could think of any ways other than secret polling – foreign-funded polls that appeared to be orchestrated by Reform officials but which were not publicly attributed to the party – for the party to benefit from money from a US LLC, Jukes replied: “I’m happy to take a £5m personal, unconditional gift, of course.”

The undercover reporter said: “That seems like it’s [the £5m] been quite tough.”

“I’m a realist and I bat straight and it’s a little bit awkward,” Jukes said, appearing to admit that Farage was not meant to change his explanation from the £5m being intended for security costs to say it was a reward for Brexit.

“That was not the line to take from the press office,” Jukes said. “So I think now the line is it was a thank you for Brexit to pay for security so he is safe for the rest of his life.”

The undercover reporter suggested that people did not mind if Farage “makes a few bob [from politics]”.

Jukes replied: “Well it’s a bit priced in with our Nige, isn’t it, no one’s voting for him to be the pope.”

If the funds were not given unconditionally but rather as a way to circumvent donation rules, as the footage appears to suggest, it could also trigger questions about whether it was a payment for work and therefore subject to tax.

Jukes left Reform after the original Verbatim/Channel 4 investigation was aired. He had worked closely with Farage for more than a decade.

An internal Reform investigation concluded that neither Jukes nor another senior party official, James Orr, had broken laws that ban foreign donations. A police investigation is ongoing.

Harborne has previously said of the gift to Farage that it was “to support Nigel’s security not just now, but for the rest of his life”. Lawyers for the crypto-billionaire have previously said he “expected nothing in return” and “did not envisage Mr Farage returning to politics”.

The timeline for the gift is disputed.

Lawyers for Harborne have said the gift was made on 5 April 2024.

According to financial industry sources, some of the £5m was not received until the end of May, just before Farage announced on 3 June that he would stand as an MP.

The Guardian has also reported that Farage told senior Reform figures he would need “a million a year” to cover lost earnings if he stood for parliament in the 2024 general election.

Farage has given a wide variety of reasons for accepting the £5m including that it was for his security and a reward for Brexit. He has refused to say how much, if any, of the £5m has been spent on security, adding it was nobody’s business what he did with the money and he could “spend it on Ferraris” if he wanted.

A spokesperson for Farage did not address several of the points put to them by the Guardian, including the claim that Farage had deviated from the press office line by admitting the £5m was a reward for Brexit.

Farage’s spokesperson said Jukes “accurately describes that the gift was for his security for the rest of his life”.

Lawyers for Jukes referred back to a previous statement: “This was entrapment over a prolonged period of time by individuals, using selective editing, who had their own agenda to discredit Reform UK.”

They added that Jukes denied any wrongdoing and pointed to the outcome of Reform’s internal investigation.
