After the ITV exposé, see Reform’s fixation with ‘hate preachers’ as the stinking hypocrisy it really is

The Guardian Mon, 19 Oct 2026 10:00:06 GMT

Far-right extremism and rhetoric is coming from activists and unvetted councillors, but party leaders who peddle fear and rage can’t escape blame

Who are the hate preachers radicalising rightwing extremists? As the head of MI5 warns that anti-migrant haters are increasingly considering terrorist attacks, it is surely a question we must ask. After all, the role of hate preachers in Islamist terrorism has long been debated.

After the London Bridge Islamist terrorist attack in 2017, Nigel Farage demanded that Sadiq Khan – “as the first Muslim mayor of London” – declare that he would do all he could “to work with the Muslim community to drive out the extremist preachers from our mosques” and to fight radicalisation in schools and prisons. More recently, he suggested that Muslim parents in the United Arab Emirates feared sending their children to study in British universities “given the risk of radicalisation here”. His colleague Suella Braverman agrees. “There should be zero tolerance for hate preachers in mosques or radicalising imams in prisons,” she says.

And what of Robert Jenrick, Reform UK’s self-styled shadow chancellor, who warns of “terrorist influencers and radicalising inmates” in prisons and demands “complete zero tolerance on hate preachers”?

Yet on the very day of MI5’s warning, Jenrick declared that Royal Marines would be deployed to turn back migrants in the Channel – and that “if they need to use lethal force, then they’ll be able to do so”. Here was one of Britain’s most prominent politicians injecting violence into our already deeply toxic debate about immigration.

Farage sought to backtrack on Jenrick’s behalf, claiming force “would be used only if soldiers were fired at” and insisting that Jenrick had been “utterly misconstrued”. This made little sense: the Home Office said last year that it had no record of firearms being brought in via small boats over the previous seven years.

Not that long ago, there was supposed to be a strict demarcation between the mainstream right and extremists. No longer. Consider the ITV investigation, screened last night, that exposed Reform councillors describing Asian families as “parasites” and Black children as “animals”. Another spoke of training young men to round up migrants “street by street, house by house”. One spoke of holding asylum seekers in “concentration camps”. Another Reform figure spoke of criminals facing “Sunday morning rose garden executions”. Some of these individuals have since stood down. But while the leaders of Reform have not yet plunged to such extreme depths, what effect might their own words have on impressionable people?

Consider that last week, Jenrick appeared on the YouTube channel of former GB News presenter Dan Wootton, a supporter of both Tommy Robinson and the anti-migrant activist Daniel Thomas, the latter of whom he calls “a British hero”.

Take the anti-migrant protests outside hotels housing asylum seekers. Last August, Jenrick turned up to such a demonstration in Epping, Essex, where far-right activists were also present, praising the “peaceful, patriotic protesters”. A month earlier, following clashes which left eight police officers injured, Braverman insisted the protests had been “largely … peaceful”. Farage, meanwhile, warned that Britain was close to “civil disobedience on a vast scale” and said he understood the anger in Epping: “You bet your life I do.”

Asked about Thomas’s group, Patriot Platform, Jenrick sympathised with masked protesters, arguing that, without a face covering, “you can lose your job, you can be cancelled”. When he was pushed on whether he would accept Robinson supporters into Reform, Jenrick’s response was telling. “Ultimately [it’s] not my call who comes into the party, that’s for Nigel and others in the party to determine,” he said. “But look, I want to build as broad a coalition as possible of people who share my values, who want us to fix this country.” How to square this with Jenrick’s denunciation of Islamist hate preachers?

Sign up to Matters of Opinion

Guardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and more

after newsletter promotion

In the recent past, Reform politicians – Farage, Jenrick and Braverman among them – have described migrants arriving in small boats as an “invasion”. It is the language of war: a nation under siege, an enemy to be repelled. It is hardly a leap for fearful people to conclude that those who resort to violence are not really dangerous extremists, but patriots defending their country.

We can hardly forget that Farage called for “pure, cold rage” in response to alleged police failings over the murder of Henry Nowak. Hours later, violence erupted on the streets of Southampton. He increasingly embraces the language of white resentment, claiming that “anti-whiteness is institutionalised into every aspect of public life”, calling diversity policies a form of “social cleansing” and warning of white Britons becoming a minority by the end of the century. Such rhetoric echoes the “great replacement” conspiracy theory, which argues that white people are being deliberately displaced by mass immigration.

Reform’s home affairs spokesperson, Zia Yusuf, meanwhile, describes Conservative and Labour politicians as “traitors to their country”, warning – without elaboration – that a “reckoning is coming”.

None of these statements constitute a direct incitement to violence. But taken together, they can conjure up a terrifying picture in impressionable minds: a nation and a people under attack, its own political leaders conspiring in its destruction and time running out to save it.

This can’t be divorced from rightwing media outlets echoing and amplifying such rhetoric. We’ve already had the far-right uprising of August 2024, when racist mobs assaulted people of colour in the streets, attacked mosques and migrant-owned businesses, and tried to burn down hotels housing asylum seekers. We’ve had far-right terrorist attacks, such as the neo-Nazi attempted murder of an Eritrean man in 2024, the firebombing of an immigration centre in Dover in 2022, the attack on the Finsbury Park mosque in 2017 and the murder of Jo Cox a year earlier.

None made a dent on the national discourse. It has only become cruder, more toxic and more inflammatory. So, with all we know, time to ask again. Who are the hate preachers radicalising rightwing extremists?

Owen Jones is a Guardian columnist. His latest book, The Fall of the West, is out now. To support the Guardian, order your copy at guardianbookshop. com. Delivery charges may apply.

Blue for poor, yellow for posh: the London maps exposing centuries of terrible housing

The Guardian Mon, 19 Oct 2026 07:00:22 GMT

From rent strikes to squatting, a new show reveals how people have managed to keep a roof over their head in London – and the mould and astronomical rents that persist

Charles Booth’s pioneering poverty maps of Victorian London show a vivid colour-coded warren of streets, alleyways and slums tightly packed together. Those marked black and dark blue were classed as being “very poor”, defined by “chronic want”. The light blue ones were poor – “18s to 21s a week for a moderate family”. Pink streets housed those who were “fairly comfortable”, and those where the wealthy lived were marked in yellow.

The maps by the British social reformer are the 19th-century equivalent of the modern-day indices of deprivation, which rank every geographic area of the UK by its level of social and economic disadvantage. Comparing the two shows how much has changed in the past 150 years – but also what hasn’t. Historical slums have been cleared away and housing conditions have generally improved, but extreme poverty and extreme wealth continue to live side by side in the capital.

Booth’s maps form the backbone of a new exhibition at Senate House library titled A Place to Call Home, which charts the history of housing and poverty in London over the past 200 years. “We may not have the same sort of slums that we used to in Victorian times but there are still issues with living conditions for many people living in rented accommodation,” says academic librarian and curator Mura Ghosh. “These issues are on a continuum – continuity and change underline the whole thinking behind this exhibition.”

A collaboration between the University of London and the London School of Economics (LSE), the exhibition looks at the turbulent timeline of housing over the past two centuries, including wartime and postwar redevelopment, the building of estates and changing housing policy, as well as eviction and squatting. People will be able to view Booth’s maps alongside a laptop displaying the current indices of deprivation, so they can see how conditions in their own postcode have changed over time.

The curators have also picked out individual stories from Booth’s notebooks detailing interviews he conducted with ordinary working Londoners, such as a chorus girl working at Drury Lane theatre who talked about how much her tights cost. “We wanted to bring out these stories of individual lives in London because that’s what people can empathise with and feel connected to. They’re talking about a city 140 years ago, but there will still be things people find relatable,” says LSE curator Indy Bhullar.

One of the exhibition’s rarest objects is a set of pamphlets from the Hampstead Tenants’ Defence League from 1936-39. Some of the earliest examples of collective tenant resistance, they document protests, rent strikes, opposition to slum clearances and challenges to the local council. “It’s quite a unique piece of history, and also utterly unexpected to find in an academic library,” says Ghosh. “They’re beautifully illustrated, and constructed from homemade paper and staples.”

The exhibition shows how the burgeoning collective resistance movement solidified over the subsequent decades. There’s a 1974 squatters’ handbook with practical and legal advice on how to squat, including how to change the locks, do your own plumbing and resist bailiffs.

“Collective action, rent strikes and protests, and encouraging people not to feel hopeless about the future – that’s an important message because people often feel like they’re alone in their housing situation,” says Emily Chu, a fellow curator and academic librarian at Senate House library. “The exhibition shows that working together sometimes creates a much bigger impact and a louder voice the government can hear.”

Moving towards the present day, there will be audio recordings of interviews with people from St Mungo’s who have experienced homelessness, and discussion of how high rents and poor housing conditions persist into the present day. About 27% of Londoners live in relative poverty after housing costs are factored in, the highest rate in England, with high rent and housing expenses the primary driver of poverty in the region. London has disproportionately high rates of damp and mould in social housing compared with other English regions – eight of the 10 local authorities in England receiving the highest volume of complaints are in the capital.

The curators hope visitors will share their own experiences of this on the comment wall. They also call for groups who are campaigning on housing issues today to keep and donate their materials so the history of housing action can be continued.

A Place to Call Home: Poverty and Housing in London is at Senate House library, London, 23 October to 5 March 2027

This carnival of protest on the streets of Delhi has shaken Narendra Modi like nothing before

The Guardian Mon, 19 Oct 2026 07:00:22 GMT

The singing, dancing and sheer joy in the face of police brutality at the protests led by the Cockroach Janta party show people no longer fear India’s regime

In July, as supporters of the Cockroach movement took to Jantar Mantar, the designated protest site in Delhi, incensed over exam-paper leaks and demanding the resignation of India’s education minister, the rest of the nation realised that for the first time since the Bharatiya Janata party (BJP) came to power in 2014, the curse of inertia and the grip of fear had been smashed irrevocably. Prime minister Narendra Modi’s image of invincibility has been punctured.

People in India have been conditioned to believe in an idea of intense slow-burn protests that eventually bring change – but the Cockroach Janta party (CJP) has shown us that the revolution can be fast-tracked.

This time the Cockroaches are demanding the resignation of India’s chief election commissioner, Gyanesh Kumar, following reports in the Indian Express in late September that he had pushed through a purge of voter rolls. Round one of the Cockroach protests came to an end because the BJP was willing to sacrifice the education minister. Round two does not allow for such scapegoating. If Kumar goes, Modi must go too – it would be an open admission that the electoral system has been compromised.

The response of the BJP so far has been hysterical. The repressive apparatus of the state was out in full force: detentions and arrests of journalists, protesters being roughed up and beaten, an internet blackout in the capital. The Cockroach leader Abhijeet Dipke’s bravado in announcing his protest plans paid unexpected dividends the first time around. The second time, the continual broadcasting on social media by the three Cockroach leaders seemed like a lack of experience in organising and strategic thinking. Police forces detained them on touchdown at Delhi airport on the morning of the protest. They alleged that thousands of their members faced preventive detention or were not allowed to reach the capital city.

So at protests on 10 October, the CJP leaders were conspicuous by their absence. Only leftwing and Congress-allied student organisations, prominent gutsy young activists (Neha Bora, Aishe Ghosh, Gurmehar Kaur) and their elected political representatives held the ground and faced the worst of the police brutality.

The absence of the Cockroach leadership on the ground notwithstanding, the protests continued in pockets, eventually reaching a crescendo on 12 October. Heeding a call by Rahul Gandhi on behalf of the Congress-led opposition bloc, the streets of Delhi were filled in an act of defiance the like of which I have not witnessed in my lifetime. The state, however, seemed to have got the memo beforehand. The Delhi police and security forces numbered 90,000, 45 metro stations were closed in the inner city and trains to Delhi were cancelled. Student activists travelling to the capital were picked up en route from their railway carriages.

The following day, a small group of Cockroaches were arrested entering Jantar Mantar, which the Delhi police had banned from being used as a protest site. Two of the group’s leaders, Saurav Das and Ashutosh Ranka, were detained and subsequently sent to jail for five days.

Despite the high-handed approach of the police, the people are still clamouring for battle on the streets. Every screengrab, every video, every reel reinforces the feeling that we are witnessing a carnivalisation of the protests. The songs, the slogans, the sudden bursts of dancing, the satirical placards, the sheer joy of the crowds: this is Mikhail Bakhtin’s carnivalesque. What is the cause for such celebration? This: the state is evidently in retreat. People have begun to treat power as something to be ridiculed.

One of the most popular slogans has been Jab jab Modi darta hai, police ko aage karta hai (“Whenever Modi is afraid, he pushes the police forward”). The regime’s undiluted dread was most visible at Connaught Place in central Delhi on 16 October, when the CJP had called on people to gather at Central Park for a flag-waving celebration. The New Delhi Municipal Council shut down the park for two days and an elaborate fortification followed. The park was cordoned off, security personnel formed a human chain along the metal railings and 220 companies of the Central Armed Police Forces were deployed alongside the Rapid Action Force and the Delhi police.

Cockroach leader Abhijeet Dipke and communist student leader Neha Bora were both detained as they made their way towards Connaught Place. Neither was allowed to contact lawyers until late into the night, and lack of knowledge about their whereabouts caused panic online. Bora was released from detention the following morning, and Dipke could walk free on conditional bail.

For over a decade, the regime crushed students and dissenters by branding them anti-national and punishing them under the draconian Unlawful Activities (Prevention) Act. The genius of the Cockroach protest lay in something very simple – how could the state frame the waving of the Indian national flag as an anti-national activity? We now have a government that is not confident of its own legitimacy; it views the tricolour as a weapon when it is in the hands of its citizens.

The powerlessness of the state could also be seen in its desperation to police the online space: it summoned Meta officials over the summer and imposed an internet shutdown earlier this month. For a party that coasted to power with post-truth propaganda on WhatsApp, its undisputed dominance on X and heavy investment in keeping social media influencers on its payroll, the algorithms (or their oligarch owners) may well have turned. It is impossible to capture the entire social media ecosystem with threats and purchasing power alone.

Sign up to Matters of Opinion

Guardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and more

after newsletter promotion

For the regime, it is a losing battle against the newfound visual grammar that has defined a wave of protests around the world: nothing is as seductive as young women defiantly clashing with uniformed police, or an opposition leader who climbs the barricades and waves the national flag. The German philosopher Walter Benjamin wrote about the tendency for fascism to lean into the aestheticisation of politics – today, looking at Delhi, he would be pleased to report back that the aesthetic can also be snatched back by the masses.

On 12 October, after the mass mobilisation, Gandhi addressed the media by saying: “This is tandav, Lord Shiva’s dance. There is no planning here”, and “This is the wedding procession of Shiva, anyone can join in”. These references to Shiva are a calculated manoeuvre. It is a nod to India’s majority Hindus who, time and time again, have been sold the lie that their sole protector is Modi.

Modi recently went Bhajan clubbing – a kind of rave setup with remixed Hindu devotional music – in a desperate attempt to establish his gen Z connections. But he may find the rug pulled from beneath his feet. Modi’s base rewarding the BJP election after election for weaponising their faith did not secure jobs for the next generation. And now it is their own children who are at the receiving end of the state’s violence.

Saving India cannot happen without pulling Hindus out from the vicious grip of extremist Hindutva. This is one unforeseen outcome of this protest and the wider movement. Whether it topples the government or not, it has shown it can unite people against the divisive force that is the BJP.

Meena Kandasamy is a poet and writer based in Chennai

My critics think speaking fluently is vital for fee-paying pupils, but not for anyone else. Here’s why I reject that

The Guardian Mon, 19 Oct 2026 06:00:23 GMT

We are accused of dumbing down, but that’s nonsense: this is levelling up. All the evidence shows helping children articulate improves their life chances

Lucy Powell is UK education secretary and deputy leader of the Labour party

Private schools don’t leave confident communication to chance. They teach it. Debating, public speaking, presentations, interview preparation. It’s all part of the deal. And parents paying the fees would soon have something to say if it wasn’t. They know that being able to speak up, make your case and hold your own can open doors. I want that for every young person, wherever they grow up and whichever school they go to.

This matters now more than ever. Young people are more connected than they’ve ever been, yet too many feel isolated and unheard. Social media is transforming their friendships and relationships. Artificial intelligence is changing the world they will work in. And in an age dominated by screens and algorithms, the human ability to connect, communicate and make yourself heard has never been more important. But the ability to find your voice should never depend on your parents’ income or the school you attend.

Spoken communication is not a soft skill or a bolt on. That is why we are strengthening oracy across the curriculum, from primary to post-16, in all types of lessons and subjects. Being good or not good at these skills affects whether a young person can get ahead. Yet critics have called our proposals a sign of “dumbing down” and a departure from high standards. This is hypocrisy. Support for developing these skills has stretched across political divides for years. It’s what we want, but also the wish of Conservatives, such as ex schools minister Nick Gibb and former culture minister Lucy Frazer.

I do not accept a two-tier system where confident communication is seen as essential for children whose parents can afford school fees, but optional for everyone else.

Raising standards means giving children knowledge, and the confidence to use it, hold their own, make their case, seize opportunities and succeed in work and life. And the evidence supports this. The Education Endowment Foundation identifies oral language approaches as among the most effective interventions available, with particularly strong benefits for disadvantaged pupils, delivering six months’ worth of additional progress in primary school and five months in secondary school.

Earlier this week, author Michael Rosen welcomed a rebalancing towards speaking as a key component of how we use language, calling it “a great bridge between the mind and the page”, and the basis of our thinking.

And former general secretary of the Association of School and College Leaders, Geoff Barton, now chair of the Oracy Education Commission, pointed to high-performing systems in Japan, Singapore and the Netherlands, where pupils in maths, for example, are expected to explain their reasoning, listen to others and defend their approach. Far from lowering standards, he said it makes them better mathematicians.

Employers understand this too. When they talk about work readiness, they mean being able to articulate yourself, work with others, respond to feedback and deal confidently with customers and clients. A recent Chartered Management Institute survey found managers concerned about gaps in workplace readiness, specifically highlighting gaps in communication skills.

The evidence has not changed, the politics has. Because this was never really about standards. It was about who gets the chance to succeed. And if we’re serious about social mobility, raising standards and tackling the fact that one in eight young people are not in education, employment or training, we cannot pretend that the ability to communicate, persuade, present ideas and work with others does not matter.

The one change that worked: I deleted Instagram – and embraced the joys of a truly private life

The Guardian Mon, 19 Oct 2026 05:55:20 GMT

I’d become obsessed with appealing to my invisible audience. But since I ditched the app a year ago, my quieter moments have taken on brilliant new meaning

I first downloaded Instagram when I was 17 and became hooked on it the way most people fall in love: slowly, and then all at once. For a long time, I never considered myself a social media addict. I self-righteously refused to download TikTok, declared Snapchat to be for “children”, and posted less regularly on Instagram than half of the people I followed.

As I went through my university years, however, certain changes crept up on me. I began to swap reading – or essay-writing – for hours spent curating new posts. On my way home from lectures (or later, from my work as a journalist), I would spend ages trying to take the artsiest, most perfect picture of that evening’s sunset for my story – as if the people who followed me were eagerly awaiting yet another photo of one of the Earth’s rotations. What usually followed was a night of reloading my feed to see how many people had reacted to my post – or worse, hadn’t reacted at all.

It wasn’t until a trip to Sri Lanka last year that I realised how far my obsession had gone. My partner and I spent two weeks travelling through Negombo and Kandy, having dinner in front of the Indian Ocean and visiting ancient heritage sites that I will probably never see again.

This would have been memorable even without a third guest: my inner Instagram monologue. It commented on everything I saw in those two weeks, debating the merits of each photo I took and the possible captions (or music, or filters) that could accompany it. On one of our last days, we hiked up Sigiriya, an incredible rock fortress that has been inhabited since prehistoric times and is one of the most remarkable places I have ever seen.

My first thought upon reaching the top? This has to go on my story. Already, I was imagining how it would look on Instagram. I dutifully made several posts upon my return to London, which were accompanied by hours of anxious scrolling and reloading, wondering why more people weren’t liking or commenting on my feed. Did they think I was annoying? Boring? Ugly? Had I been ungenerous with my own likes and comments, causing my followers (a grand total of 400) to band together to punish me? Should I delete the post? Redo it?

Within two days, I couldn’t take my own thoughts any more. I decided to delete Instagram from my phone for a month, reset my habits, and then return with a hopefully healthier mindset.

Yet in its absence, certain realisations became unavoidable. I came to see how much of my photo-taking was driven by wanting to appeal to an invisible audience, most of whom I hadn’t spoken to in years. In that first month, I started to take photos for myself and my own memories instead. It made me feel like my experiences could belong to me again.

One month turned into three, then six – next month, it will have been a year since I took that first step. In my Instagram days, I expended a great deal of energy comparing the most normal parts of my life to the seemingly wonderful lives of others. Without the app, I was able to direct this energy into other parts of my life. That’s not to say I became productive every minute of every day. I didn’t. But the background noise decreased substantially. I read more, finished writing my first novel and started another.

It has been liberating to live my life privately again. You may laugh, because I’m hardly a public figure, but I discovered how joyful it can be to reconnect with your anonymity and do activities knowing that it’s no one’s business whether you liked them or not.

Now, moments matter because I’m enjoying them, or sharing them with someone I care about – not because they have been liked and validated by a hundred other people. I remain fully present for each of them, without disappearing halfway through into an Instagram rabbit hole. My life feels smaller in some ways, but also much more like my own. Whether the Insta-verse has noticed my absence, I couldn’t say. Do I care? Thankfully, not any more.

The housing crisis is now global. It shows just how undemocratic our nations have become

The Guardian Mon, 19 Oct 2026 05:00:21 GMT

When we can’t even afford to rent or buy somewhere to live, we have to ask: did we give the financial sector too much power?

Leilani Farha is the former UN special rapporteur on adequate housing

In the summer of 2021, I visited a homeless community in a park in Toronto, Canada, and spoke to one of the residents. He was living in a tent in the shadow of brand new skyscrapers, and had been homeless for about five years. At one point he swivelled around, pointed up at a crane on the skyline, and said: “Who are they building those for? Definitely not for me.”

He was right. And he captured something experienced by ordinary people around the world: the growing conviction that the housing system is no longer tethered to their needs. What he was pointing at is not just a housing crisis. It is a crisis of democracy.

Democracy promises that our living conditions are shaped by all of us, regardless of our station in life. Yet decisions about housing have been systematically removed from democratic control and handed to financial actors such as private equity firms, pension funds and real-estate investment trusts. Working hand in hand with governments and banks, these actors have decoupled the price of housing from what ordinary people earn. They’ve transformed our homes into a toy for wealthy investors. I call this alliance Housing Inc.

The tools available to the large financial actors driving and profiting from the housing crisis are not available to the rest of us. They hire armies of lobbyists to squash rent-control laws. They fund political campaigns. They rotate in and out of government positions. They are in the rooms and hallways where decisions are made.

Even governments trying to fight the growing influence of the financial sector in housing face intense pressure. In Copenhagen, after the private equity giant Blackstone bought up apartment blocks across the city, renovated them and, in some cases, doubled the rent for new tenants, the Danish parliament passed legislation barring new owners from raising rents on renovated apartments for five years. While this “Blackstone law”, as it was commonly called, was a brave measure, it was weaker than the government had wanted. Kaare Dybvad, then Denmark’s housing minister, had proposed a 10-year freeze. Faced with fury from landlords and pension funds, and needing rightwing party votes to pass it, he cut it to five.

The average tenant, the person experiencing homelessness, the young person locked out of the housing market – what do they have? They have a vote. That is all.

And the vote changes less than we are promised. As the economist Yanis Varoufakis has argued, elections no longer determine economic policy. Governments of the left and the right come and go, and regardless of who is in power, rents keep rising, because the economic model always stays the same: money flows to wherever the returns are highest, which means into unproductive assets such as real estate, and away from the public investment that would actually house people. We can change our governments. We cannot, it seems, change the economic policies they all adhere to.

Who decided that financial firms could use our homes as investments? Not the public. Consider the bundling of mortgages into securities, which laid the groundwork for the 2008 financial crisis, or the decision in more than 40 jurisdictions to exempt real-estate investment trusts from corporate income tax. Both happened out of public view, shaped by governments and financial actors, with no public debate.

The same thing happens with other kinds of housing investment. Take short-term rentals in Athens. While democracy may have been born there, it hasn’t always thrived. After the global financial crisis, Greeks were held to brutal austerity measures against their will. Property values collapsed, wages fell and ordinary families struggled to make ends meet. For many property owners, renting to tourists through short-let platforms such as Airbnb became a lifeline – a way to generate income from an asset that had lost most of its value.

But what began as a survival strategy for families became an investment strategy for foreign buyers. The government introduced a “golden visa” programme in 2013, offering residency to any foreigner who bought Greek property. Thousands did – not to live there, but to convert apartments into short-term rentals, banking on Greece’s tourism industry as a good investment. As foreign capital flooded in, long-term housing became scarcer, rents spiked and neighbourhoods such as Exarchia and Koukaki began to change beyond recognition. Athenians protested and their government responded by sending in the riot police and steamrollering dissent to defend its decisions.

What’s on offer in terms of genuine civic engagement for the people most affected by the housing crisis tends to be defanged, inadequate or inaccessible. Tenants who speak out about poor conditions risk eviction, and they need landlord references for their next place. People holding down multiple jobs just to pay their rent don’t have time for city council meetings, or surveys and questionnaires that lead nowhere. When people have no means to participate in decisions about their own housing, they feel abandoned by government. This creates a vacuum that rightwing populism is perfectly designed to fill.

Which brings us back to democracy’s promise. Can it be a democracy when a place to live is governed not by human beings and their needs but by financial firms and profit, pricing people out of their homes and onto the streets? Around the world, people are forcing that question into the open.

In Madrid, 87-year-old María del Carmen Abascal (better known as Maricarmen) had lived in the same flat for 71 years when the investment firm that owns it demanded she pay €2,650 (£2,280) a month instead of €500. On 23 September, after earlier attempts had been blocked, police cleared hundreds of her neighbours from the doorway and she was evicted. That evening, thousands took to the streets of Madrid. Within days there were tens of thousands, a protest camp had filled the Puerta del Sol square, and demonstrations had spread to cities across the country.

Sign up to Matters of Opinion

Guardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and more

after newsletter promotion

Six days after the eviction, the Spanish government passed emergency decrees extending rental contracts and shielding vulnerable tenants from eviction. People called it the “Maricarmen decree”. Three days later, parliament struck it down. The parties of the right had voted against it, one of them calling automatic lease renewal an “expropriation of property rights”. Maricarmen passed away not long after.

In Berlin in 2021, more than one million people – 59.1% of valid votes – backed a referendum to take the homes owned by the city’s largest corporate landlords into public ownership. The result was non-binding, and successive governments have ignored it. So Berliners used the one tool they had, blunt as it was. On 20 September this year, Die Linke, which had campaigned on the promise to carry out the referendum, won the state elections and became the largest party in the city’s parliament for the first time. One day later, before a government had even been formed, Germany’s chancellor, Friedrich Merz, announced that he would fast-track a national law banning the “expropriation” of housing. Berliners had voted for a change in economic policy on housing, and the chancellor then made it clear that this was not theirs to decide.

But the movement had known better than to rely on the broken promise of democracy. Last year, it wrote an expropriation law itself, so that it could be passed by a willing government – or, failing that, put to a second, binding vote. In its own words: “ Alles muss man selber machen” – we have to do everything ourselves.

That is what it takes to reclaim democracy.

Leilani Farha is the 2026 CBC Massey lecturer. This piece is based on her new book: Housing Inc.: A Global Takeover and Our Fight for Home. She is the former UN special rapporteur on adequate housing and the global director of the international human rights organisation, The Shift

Trump Blitzes Through Deep-Red States Amid Fears About G. O. P. Enthusiasm

The New York Times October 19, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

The president’s swing is taking him to states including South Carolina and Kansas that were not seen as competitive just a few months ago.

By Emily Davies and Jonathan Swan

Emily Davies reported from Washington and Jonathan Swan from Wichita, Kansas.

President Trump has embarked on a campaign swing across a remarkably conservative swath of America in a six-day blitz that began Monday, trying to boost Republican turnout in places the party did not view as competitive just a few months ago.

Leanne Abraham/The New York Timess

With just two weeks to go until the midterm elections, Mr. Trump’s itinerary reflects how worried the G. O. P. is about its prospects for holding onto the House and Senate, and winning governor’s races nationwide.

Traditionally Republican strongholds have become battlegrounds this cycle. Polling in these places shows that Mr. Trump’s policies on tariffs and the war in Iran — and their effect on the prices of gas, diesel and groceries for everyday Americans — have gravely threatened the party’s fortunes.

The president started his barnstorm in Kansas, with plans to pass through the Carolinas, Florida, Iowa and Georgia. He will stump in five House districts he won in 2024 by more than 20 points, and for the most part in states with unusually competitive Senate races.

Notably, he is staying away from traditional battleground states such as Maine and New Hampshire, where Republican candidates have distanced themselves from the president in hopes of winning over more moderate voters. His choice appears to signal a political strategy that focuses not on persuading swing voters but on shoring up support from the base that powered his rise.

“He goes where the battles are,” said John McLaughlin, a longtime pollster for Mr. Trump. “And this is where the battles are.”

In a more favorable political environment for Republicans, the party would be looking to pick up a Senate seat in Georgia and defend one in North Carolina, in addition to using the president to defend its Senate seat in Maine.

But Mr. Trump and his political team have all but given up on the first two states, and have accepted the president’s inability to help Senator Susan Collins, the Republican incumbent in Maine, two advisers to the president said in interviews. This cycle, the White House sees Texas, Ohio, Iowa and Michigan as the battlegrounds, they said. Michigan represents the rare setting this year for a competitive seat held by a Democrat.

“This idea that he’s going to red states, well yeah that’s where the races are right now, which tells you all you need to know,” one of the advisers said. “But also we’re playing to a national audience in terms of motivating Republicans.”

The swing will also allow Mr. Trump’s political operation to generate good “pictures” to use in advertisements beyond his actual itinerary, the adviser said.

“We play to visuals,” the adviser said. “And if we’re in a congressional district that’s next door to a competitive congressional district, what difference does it make? It’s all the same people, it’s all the same media.”

Mr. Trump remains his party’s most effective motivator a decade after he descended a golden escalator at his namesake building in midtown Manhattan to announce his first bid for the White House. Yet his popularity has dipped to historic lows, with about 37 percent of Americans approving of how he is handling his job.

The Republican National Committee, in announcing his travel, said the itinerary is intended to shore up the party’s vulnerable candidates. But the president is also known to go where he will find adoring crowds, and the midterm blitz through ruby red America provides him ample opportunity for that experience.

Mr. Trump will start the week in a House district in Wichita, Kansas, that backed him over former Vice President Kamala Harris two years ago by more than 23 points. He will then travel to Greenville, North Carolina, which, under the state’s new congressional map, would have broken for him by 14 points, before swinging through Clemson, South Carolina, to a district that he carried by a whopping 43 points. Mr. Trump will end the week with stops in deep-red Sioux City, Iowa, and Fort Myers, Florida, before a final rally Saturday in Macon, Georgia.

Next week, he will rally in Lubbock and Waco, Texas, said Republican National Committee Press Secretary Natalie Baldassarre.

Vice President JD Vance, who has also embarked on a campaign swing this month, has taken a similar approach. He kicked off the week in North Carolina, and will end it in a district in Nebraska that backed the president by more than 50 points.

Kevin Madden, a Republican strategist who worked for the campaigns of former President George W. Bush and Mitt Romney, called the White House’s posture “defensive.”

“Two of the most valuable assets on any campaign are money and time,” Mr. Madden said. “Where you are spending your money and where you are spending your time in the last two weeks says a lot about your strategy.”

It isn’t just the last two weeks. This fall, the president has campaigned in the southeast corner of Oklahoma, the reddest part of one of the reddest states in the country, and swung through Western Nebraska, Northern Kentucky and Mobile, Ala., the latter being where he held his first presidential campaign in 2015 and began building his vaunted MAGA base after drawing some 30,000 supporters to an open-air football stadium.

Nebraska and Kansas should be slam dunks for his party, even in years when Democrats do well. His Friday night visit to Dalton, Ga., was perhaps most symbolic of the party’s dire view of its position: The city sits in the heart of a congressional district once represented by Marjorie Taylor Greene, the longtime Trump ally who broke with him over the Epstein files and the war in Iran.

The approach relies on motivating less reliable voters whom Mr. Trump has shown a singular ability to motivate. At rallies over the past month, he has pleaded with them to pretend he is on the ballot. So far, the results have been mixed.

At Mr. Trump’s rally last week in Youngstown, Ohio, entire sections of the arena remained empty. But some voters who had watched from home said the event had given them more confidence in Senator Jon Husted, the Republican of Ohio in a tough race to retain his seat against Sherrod Brown, the Democrat.

“What Husted said at the rally,” said Steve Zawilinsky, a pastor who watched the rally on TV, “that is what I wanted to hear.”

Reid J. Epstein contributed reporting.

Emily Davies is a political correspondent for The New York Times.

Jonathan Swan is a White House reporter for The Times, covering the administration of Donald J. Trump. Contact him securely on Signal: @jonathan.941

Trump Urges Voters to Focus on Him. Republican Ads Tell a Different Story.

The New York Times October 19, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

Only a small fraction of recent G. O. P. broadcast and streaming ads mention the president, according to a Times analysis of ad data.

By Bayliss Wagner

At rallies across the country, President Trump has implored voters to “pretend I’m on the ballot” in the midterm elections.

But on the airwaves, his party is sending the opposite message.

Less than $1 of every $100 in Republican television ad spending on House and Senate races from Sept. 9 through Oct. 17 has gone toward commercials that mention the word “Trump,” according to a New York Times analysis of broadcast and streaming ad data and transcripts from the media tracking firm AdImpact.

Mr. Trump’s approval rating is well under water, putting Republicans in a difficult spot in battleground contests that could decide control of Congress.

Note: Data includes only broadcast and streaming ads aired between Sept. 9, 2026 and Oct. 17, 2026.

Source: AdImpact

Lazaro Gamio and Bayliss Wagner

Democrats, in contrast, have spent $20 out of every $100 on spots mentioning Mr. Trump during that period, which covers much of the final sprint before Election Day. They have run heavily against the president, opposing the war with Iran, tariffs, cuts to health-care spending and the handling of the Epstein files. Many other Democratic ads do not mention Mr. Trump by name, but are critical of his policies.

The starkly divergent strategies reflect one of the defining dynamics of the final weeks of the campaign season. Republicans are increasingly trying to distance themselves from the president’s unpopular agenda, while Democrats are hoping to tie them to it.

“When the president’s approval rating is in the 30s, that’s not generally something that’s helpful for a campaign that needs to get to 50 percent of the vote,” said Whit Ayres, a Republican pollster and strategist.

The current dynamic differs sharply from the primaries, when Republican candidates, eager to appeal to the base and demonstrate their fealty to Mr. Trump, spent a much larger share of their ad dollars on commercials mentioning the president— $55 of every $100, according to the Times analysis. (AdImpact uses artificial intelligence to transcribe TV ads.)

“Voters blame what they’ve done for the pain that they’re feeling, so Republicans don’t want to own that,” said Jesse Ferguson, a Democratic strategist. “But you don’t get to start the fire and then get credit for calling 911.”

He added that Republicans “need a time machine, not an ad buy.”

Amount spent by each party on ads mentioning President Trump.

Source: AdImpact

Minho Kim and Bayliss Wagner/The New York Times

Battleground Republican Senate candidates and their allies have largely steered clear of mentioning Mr. Trump in recent ads. And when they do talk about him, it frequently comes with a catch.

Senator Dan Sullivan, the Alaska Republican running for re-election in a tight race, said in an ad released on Oct. 7 that he “voted to force Trump’s D. O. J. to release the Epstein files.”

Other Republicans have tried a more indirect strategy. Former Representative Mike Rogers, the Republican Senate nominee in Michigan, sought to distance himself from Mr. Trump’s trade war with Canada in an ad first aired on Oct. 10.

“Canada is not our enemy,” Mr. Rogers said in the ad. “We need to end this tariff war now. As Michigan’s senator, I’ll bring both parties together to lower your prices.”

Democrats, meanwhile, have spent most heavily on anti-Trump attack ads in states the president lost or that he won narrowly in 2024, including Maine, Georgia, Michigan and New Hampshire, according to the Times analysis of AdImpact data.

In an ad run by allies of Senator Jon Ossoff, Democrat of Georgia, a woman stands at a gas pump and blames Mr. Ossoff’s Republican challenger for the spike in prices caused by the Iran war.

“Mike Collins sides with Trump and we pay,” the woman says in the ad. “We can’t afford him in the Senate.” (Mr. Collins has blamed the Biden administration’s environmental policies for higher energy prices.)

In Republican primaries, where loyalty to Mr. Trump was a major factor and candidates competed to be seen as most supportive of the president, Mr. Trump’s name showed up in more than half of all Republican broadcast and streaming ad airings. His name has appeared in just three out of every 100 ad airings for the general election, according to the analysis of AdImpact data.

Democrats also spent heavily on Trump-related ads in their primaries, which were often contests over which candidate would oppose the president most fiercely: Roughly $50 of every $100 in ad dollars in House and Senate races went to TV spots mentioning the president.

Now, both parties have modulated their approach.

In August, Josh Turek, the Democratic Senate nominee in Iowa, started airing an ad in which he vowed to work with anyone, “including President Trump,” to fix the country’s “broken immigration system” and “secure the border.” Mr. Trump won Iowa three consecutive times.

In her own pivot, his Republican opponent, Representative Ashley Hinson, announced she was running to be Mr. Trump’s “top ally in the United States Senate” last year; now, she argues she can pass legislation regardless of who is in office.

“Working across the aisle isn’t always easy,” she says in an ad mentioning Mr. Trump and Democrats, “but it’s how you get results.”

While Republican candidates have not centered Mr. Trump in their midterm ads, his administration has recently promoted him in taxpayer-funded television spots. A judge ordered last week that the ads be taken down.

We've seen evidence of some Republican candidates distancing themselves from Trump, including by scrubbing his name from their websites, criticizing his policies and, in one case, demanding that a billboard about his endorsement be taken down. This data shows how widespread that distancing is in a medium both parties rely on heavily to communicate with voters.

Bayliss Wagner is a political reporter and a member of the 2026-27 Times Fellowship, a program for journalists early in their careers.

Mr. Khalil had recently graduated from Columbia when he was arrested by ICE agents and became the face of the Trump administration’s crackdown on pro-Palestinian demonstrations.

By Ann E. Marimow

Reporting from Washington

Mahmoud Khalil, the Columbia University graduate arrested last year by Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents amid campus protests, appealed to the Supreme Court on Monday in an attempt to prevent his deportation.

Mr. Khalil, a legal permanent U. S. resident who is married to an American, became an early and high-profile example of President Trump’s crackdown on pro-Palestinian demonstrations on college campuses.

His case presents the justices with another test of the Trump’s administration’s aggressive efforts to deport people who are in the country both legally and illegally.

The administration has said that Mr. Khalil’s prominent role in protests at Columbia against Israel’s war in Gaza and his continued presence in the United States spreads antisemitism and is at odds with Mr. Trump’s foreign policy goals. Mr. Khalil has denounced antisemitism and said that criticism of Israel is not inherently antisemitic.

Mr. Khalil had recently gotten his master’s degree from Columbia when he was arrested in March 2025 and detained on the basis of a determination by Secretary of State Marco Rubio that his presence in the United States undercut the national interest. Mr. Rubio cited a rarely used provision of a statute that gives the secretary of state sweeping power to expel foreigners.

A district court judge found that the law cited by Mr. Rubio was most likely unconstitutional and ordered Mr. Khalil released, but the Trump administration has continued to try to deport him, resulting in a series of legal maneuvers in different courts.

Mr. Khalil’s appeal to the Supreme Court comes after the U. S. Court of Appeals for the Third Circuit cleared the way for him to be arrested again and potentially deported.

If the Supreme Court lets that decision stand, it will likely not end the wrangling over the legality of the administration’s moves, but it could remove one of the remaining obstacles preventing Mr. Khalil from being deported. The justices will now decide whether to hear his case, a process that could take months. If they agree to review it, they would then schedule oral arguments likely in the spring and issue an opinion by the end of the court’s term in late June or early July.

Mr. Khalil has argued that the attempt to deport him violates his free speech rights. The appeals court decision did not address that question but instead dealt with a more technical dispute over which court has the authority at this stage in the litigation to review the constitutional issues in his case.

Mr. Khalil has said that his case should be heard in federal court; the Trump administration has said the case should be heard in immigration court, which is controlled by the executive branch and overseen by the Justice Department.

Judge Michael E. Farbiarz of the District Court of New Jersey sided with Mr. Khalil and ordered him released. But a closely divided appeals court agreed with the administration and said the district court had not been the proper venue to weigh his petition for release. The matter, the court said, should have initially been addressed by an immigration court.

In their filing Monday, Mr. Khalil’s lawyers told the justices that immigration law gives the federal courts the authority to review an immigrant’s constitutional challenges to punitive and retaliatory detention.

“The federal government jailed Mr. Khalil for his speech,” one of the lawyers, Alina Das, director of N. Y. U.’s Immigrant Rights Clinic, said in a statement. She urged the Supreme Court to uphold the power of federal courts to “free people from retaliatory detention and prevent the weaponization of the immigration system to punish dissent.”

The Trump administration has separately asked the Supreme Court to review the case of Badar Khan Suri, a postdoctoral fellow at Georgetown University whom officials have accused of promoting Hamas and tried to deport. D. John Sauer, the solicitor general, has asked the justices to reverse an appeals court ruling siding with Mr. Suri.

The court could decide to consolidate the two cases, which raise similar legal questions.

Monday’s request from Mr. Khalil, a Palestinian who was born and raised in a refugee camp in Syria, comes as he has been traveling the country to promote his memoir, “No Land to Stand On.” The book recounts Mr. Khalil’s harrowing experience of being arrested in the lobby of his New York apartment building and held in a detention camp in Louisiana. Mr. Khalil was held there for months and missed the birth of his child.

His case in immigration court has continued on a separate track. In April, an immigration court affirmed that Mr. Khalil could be deported, an unusually quick decision that was also characterized by other abnormalities.

Mr. Khalil can appeal the ruling of the immigration court to the conservative U. S. Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit, potentially providing another avenue to eventually seek Supreme Court review.

Jonah E. Bromwich contributed reporting.

Ann E. Marimow covers the Supreme Court for The Times from Washington.

Connections: Soccer Edition

Connections Coach

OpinionGuest Essay

Credit... Lukas Verstraete

Supported by

By Michael Brendan Dougherty

Mr. Dougherty is a senior writer at National Review.

“Pretend, please, that I’m on the ballot,” President Trump has been pleading with Republicans in midterm campaign stops. He has a point. With him on the ballot, in 2016 and 2024, Republicans fared much better than they expected. In 2018 and 2022, without him, they stumbled.

But two things can be true at once. Mr. Trump is the party’s great unifier, and going into 2026, he’s the party’s biggest drag.

G. O. P. candidates can read polls as well as anyone, and those in the toughest races are reacting almost in real time. Representative Ashley Hinson in Iowa, Mike Rogers in Michigan and Senator Jon Husted in Ohio have broken with the president on some issues, and all three have called for an end to the fighting in Iran.

The midterm outlook for Republicans may be poor, and Mr. Trump’s unpopularity may be dragging the party down. But by smashing the former consensus in the party, he has allowed new elected figures and influencers to start building a different G. O. P.

The Dallas midterm G. O. P. convention may have looked like yet another event to focus attention on Mr. Trump as the main attraction and the biggest draw. But we actually got a glimpse of the post-Trump road ahead. We saw figures who disagree with Mr. Trump, and with one another, to one degree or another.

That cacophony of voices representing itself as Republican would have been unthinkable before Mr. Trump. And it is this collection of voices — the mismatched set of impulses and ambitions on display — that may very well represent the future of the Republican Party.

It will be a big tent, and bring in people who didn’t feel welcomed in the G. O. P. before and who may even disagree on some issues — and yet a party with the real potential to grow into a majority. Yes, it will have to transition from one focused around the strong personality and charisma of Mr. Trump to a coalition. It doesn’t lack for potential leaders who could fit that model.

So 2026 may be rough. But in the years ahead, that party may be electorally stronger than what preceded it, even if it is far more diverse and fractious than the old one.

There is a model for what this kind of Republican Party can become. The New Deal Democrats were the most dominant political coalition of the 20th century. That party joined urban Catholics with Southern segregationists, farmers with union workers and, increasingly, Black Americans as well.

A restive coalition, it was held together by patronage and shared enemies. Southern committee chairmen in the House and Senate with seniority shaped the New Deal to fit their region and constituents. Political machines in Chicago, Kansas City and New York turned relief jobs and money into votes from Catholic and Jewish immigrants. Unions organized workers as a matter of loyalty to one another, not to New Deal intellectuals. Farmers got price supports and rural electricity.

The New Deal coalition was undone by historical upheavals like the civil rights era, the Vietnam War and the social revolutions of the 1960s that would split the party. But the long, multifarious life of New Deal Democrats shows that a looser coalitional arrangement can dominate electorally, and even manage enormous internal cultural differences and contrasting priorities for decades.

Before Mr. Trump, the Republican creed was easy to state: smaller government, lower taxes, free trade and global leadership. The party isn’t going back to it whole. Nor does what’s coming look like a contest between two ideologically grouped sides, the Tea Party-style libertarian populists and the conservative nationalists.

That’s too simple and neat. Many nationalists are against wars. Take Vice President JD Vance and Senator Josh Hawley of Missouri. Though he supports the president publicly, Mr. Vance is widely reported to have advised against the Iran war. Both suspect NATO can be a debit on American sovereignty, not just a force multiplier. Mr. Hawley voted against Swedish and Finnish membership in NATO. Libertarian types believe the government is too intrusive in Americans’ lives, and the MAHA movement says regulators are captured by corporations. They are united by suspicion of the state. At the Dallas midterm convention, programming moved through the party constituencies hour by hour: “America First” trade police, school choice and opposition to gender ideology in youth sports, chronic disease and “corporate influence in public health agencies.” Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. drew cheers for praising his uncle Ted Kennedy’s authorship of Title IX. John Fetterman, a Democratic senator, sent a video introducing and praising a Republican Senate colleague, Dave McCormick, vowing to “defend the steel way of life” in western Pennsylvania.

Or take the example of glyphosate, a controversial pesticide used on millions of acres of farmland. For years, Mr. Kennedy has railed against its overuse. When the Trump administration declared glyphosate production a matter of national security, Florida Representative Anna Paulina Luna was behind an amendment to strip a liability shield for pesticide makers from the farm bill. She was joined by Chip Roy from the Freedom Caucus. It is another glimpse of party members not walking in lock step but clashing over ideas and positions.

Almost every Republican wants to restrain the reach and ambitions of government, but they no longer agree on where. Just look at how the September outcry about Flock cameras scrambled Republicans. Some Republicans defended them as a tool for law and order, others an unholy alliance between Big Tech and big government against our rights and privacy. Senator Hawley, who chairs the Judiciary Subcommittee on Crime and Counterterrorism, opened an investigation into the company in August, and ripped it in a televised hearing.

Take data centers. A Fox News poll in July found that 70 percent of voters opposed building data centers in their area. Mr. Trump and Mr. Vance defend them, but Mr. Rogers, the Republican Senate candidate in Michigan, backed a moratorium on new ones. Senator Husted supported them in his state but also introduced a bill to shield residents from higher electricity costs.

Debate and negotiation give even the losers a stake in the party. They may not win this time, but there will be other opportunities to fight for their cause. And the contestation over ideas makes a party seem to voters like it is more engaged with the vital questions about the future of the country.

Over a decade ago, Peter Harris, a political-science professor at the Colorado State University, said that the problem with the G. O. P. was that it was “not diverse enough.” He meant ideologically, but he also believed that a little less party discipline and more internal debate would change the demographics of the party. He noted that figures like the stalwart libertarian Senator Rand Paul of Kentucky or the evangelical culture warrior Senator Ted Cruz of Texas serve an important function as “outriders.” These figures, he said, would flummox the party establishment but “excite and engage large numbers of young Americans, racial minorities and others not usually tempted by the G. O. P. brand.”

Mr. Harris was right: The outriders — none more so than Mr. Trump — dragged in exactly those voters. In a New York Times/L2 analysis, between 2020 and 2024, Republicans gained 2.4 million registered voters, while Democrats lost 2.1 million. Democrats lost ground in voter registration in 30 states in that time period. Similarly, Gallup’s three-year trend showed Republican identification broadening among groups that don’t fit into the traditional business wing or the evangelical wing: Hispanics, voters under 30, lower-income Americans. Republicans gained among Catholics and African Americans, too.

This G. O. P. coalition is under strain in 2026. The most dramatic break is among Hispanic voters. In a New York Times report on polls, Democrats lead among Hispanic likely voters on the generic congressional ballot by 35 points. The same pollsters found Kamala Harris, then the vice president, ahead by only seven points in their final 2024 surveys. Republican gains among young voters are also in jeopardy. Polling by Echelon Insights found Mr. Trump’s net approval among 18 to 34 year olds at minus-44 in August.

Voters soured on Mr. Trump for familiar reasons: the deaths of Lorenzo Salgado Araujo and Renée Good, among others, in ICE encounters, an Iran war that drags on and pushes up energy prices and inflation. What ties these complaints together is that Mr. Trump has governed less like the outsider who ran in 2016 and more like the party he had come to change. He signed tax cuts with a Republican Congress and made the market a measure of his success. Instead of draining the swamp, he has presided over a Washington where graft now looks rampant.

But this isn’t a simple reversion to the old status quo either. It looks more as if younger voters and Hispanics are at the volatile edge of longer-term trends. Hispanic voters may swing toward Democrats this year, but as a TelevisaUnivision executive said recently, Latino voters “aren’t locked into one party.” Gallup, meanwhile, found that a record 45 percent of adults called themselves independents in 2025.

These trends are the environment the party sits in now — and they suggest the party has room to grow.

The potential leaders of a future Republican Party seem to be pulling in different directions. This just so happens to be the physics of building a big tent.

Mr. Vance is the likeliest nominee for the 2028 presidential election. His recent book about his conversion to Catholicism puts economic concern for families at the center of his conservatism. Traditional conservatives regularly denounce him for his views on “America first” foreign policy and trade restrictions. Mr. Trump himself noted that Mr. Vance had a “philosophically” different view on Iran, code for advising against it. His more populist views probably work to his advantage in a general election.

Still, even if a Fox News Poll shows that 70 percent of voters are at odds with Mr. Trump on data centers, Mr. Vance has defended the buildout as essential for our competition with China. In Dallas, Mr. Vance acknowledged the discontent and heterogeneity in the Republican coalition, telling voters he wouldn’t ask for agreement on every issue.

Although some cast them as antagonists, and they may have some disagreements on foreign policy, Secretary of State Marco Rubio is quite similar to Mr. Vance. Both were initially hostile to Mr. Trump and eventually became loyal to him and began to echo him on trade and re-industrialization.

Gov. Ron DeSantis of Florida, who has generally been seen as more acceptable to the traditional business-friendly wing, is taking a stance on artificial intelligence that is more populist than Mr. Vance’s. He pushed hard for A. I. regulation in Florida, barring data centers from passing infrastructure and electricity costs on to residential ratepayers. Mr. Hawley is also fighting Mr. Cruz in the Senate over a federal A. I. moratorium.

The older Reagan-Bush Republican Party may get the closest thing to its own champion in Gov. Brian Kemp of Georgia, who not only hews to the conservative movement’s orthodoxy on taxes and small government but whose political persona has been shaped by his clashes with Mr. Trump over the 2020 election. A Kemp nomination would represent the return of the repressed.

Still, Mr. Kemp’s own survival in the Trump era is instructive. The state party accepted him even though he refused an explicit demand from Mr. Trump. In Mr. Kemp there is a lesson: There is a way for competent politicians to survive big internal battles, manage a fractious coalition and still win.

There are also the many well-known figures and influencers who have become influential in various parts of the G. O. P. coalition and the wider new media world that now surrounds it.

Tucker Carlson is a wild card. He has all but sworn a vendetta against President Trump over the war in Iran. Mr. Carlson’s current passion over issues of foreign policy regularly drives him to describe America, or its politicians, as being enslaved to the ambitions of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu of Israel or his government.

Mr. Carlson also shows that the party’s coalitional openness is a two-way street. It’s one thing to cheer when Senator Fetterman crosses over to cheer a Republican senator. It’s another to watch the party’s most influential podcaster praise a Democrat — something Mr. Carlson did when he said he wouldn’t vote for Mike Rogers in Michigan at gunpoint and lauded the agenda of the Democratic nominee, Abdul El-Sayed, as “literally Trumpian.” A coalition loose enough to let Mr. Fetterman in the front door is also loose enough to let Mr. Carlson escape.

The MAHA moms and the wellness right look to figures like Jillian Michaels, a fitness trainer and a TV personality. There’s the manosphere in its varieties, from extreme misogyny to more mainstream “save our boys” concerns among parents who see their sons failing to thrive in school. There are the national populists who tune in to Steve Bannon’s “War Room.” And there are people Mr. Bannon denounces, like the tech bros and A. I. optimists on the “All-In Podcast.”

There are the foreign-policy restrainers who think the liberal world order is a threat to America’s independence and solvency, and there are the hawkish diaspora groups from Iran, Venezuela, Ukraine and Cuba who want the G. O. P. to press harder on foreign policy. And there are still the stalwarts: gun owners and pro-lifers.

Yes, Mr. Trump’s personal charisma and the way he could turn any controversy into one about himself rather than the substance have papered over these differences for a decade.

When the midterms end, the party will go through a rambunctious primary in 2028 — and eventually it will rally behind a nominee. Throughout, the G. O. P. will disagree about tariffs, A. I. and foreign policy.

What will unify this fractious coalition after Mr. Trump is a common enemy in the liberals of the credentialed class. That class staffs the very institutions — such as universities — that Americans have come to broadly distrust. The G. O. P. will continue to cast its antagonist as a national H. R. department: intrusive, entitled and not really more qualified than you, just empowered.

Republicans must beware of a big vulnerability of coalitional politics: factional capture. In the past, the G. O. P. has suffered when it could be caricatured as a party beholden to the country club or as the political wing of an evangelical tent revival.

Democrats are now suffering from this very problem with the dominance of their college-educated faction and their values. Their influence on the party is disproportionate to their numbers.

The most important battle line between the parties in the years ahead might come down to a simple question: who can appeal to normal people? Winning that competition requires, at the very least, demonstrating that your party isn’t hostage to one faction and threatening to rule everyone by its norms.

But it bears noting that normal people can seem politically weird. The same person can be paranoid about Flock cameras and enthusiastic about A. I., antiracist but gender-critical, distrust the Food and Drug Administration but want food additives to be better regulated.

A coalitional party doesn’t exhaustively try to resolve those contradictions, just contain them and draw what is useful from them without letting one faction or figure try to speak for 330 million citizens.

Mr. Trump shattered the image of the G. O. P. as a vehicle dominated by the conservative ideological movement. Now the post-Trump Republican Party is freer to rebuild itself again as a more fractious coalition.

The traditional stalwarts for small government are still in there, and still have influence. But the party is no longer in their grip. They may find that the party lasts longer and goes a little harder under conditions of anarchy.

Michael Brendan Dougherty is a senior writer at National Review.

Houthi Strikes Kill Dozens in Yemeni Desert Military Camp, Officials Say

The New York Times October 19, 2026

Houthi-Saudi War

Advertisement

Supported by

The Iranian-backed militia struck with ballistic missiles deep in government-held central Yemen, in what appeared to be among the deadliest attacks of the renewed war.

By Saeed Al-Batati and Ismaeel Naar

Saeed Al-Batati reported from Al Mukalla, Yemen, and Ismaeel Naar from Dubai, United Arab Emirates.

The Iranian-backed Houthi militia killed dozens of Yemeni soldiers in a strike on a desert camp in the middle of the country on Monday, officials said, in what appeared to be one of the deadliest attacks since their war resumed.

Col. Majed al-Nuzaili, a spokesman for the Yemeni armed forces, said in a statement on social media that the Houthis had fired three ballistic missiles at the camp, Al Alam, which is in Shabwa Province. They hit what he described as a training center for security and police recruits. He told a Saudi-owned broadcaster, Al Arabiya, that at least 47 people had been killed and 53 others wounded.

Saba, a Houthi-run news agency, said the group had struck what it called Saudi “troop buildups” at the camp and made no mention of recruits.

“The number of martyrs is very high and is expected to rise,” Fahd Al-Khulaifi, the deputy governor of Shabwa Province, said in a telephone interview. He said there were dozens of casualties, some of whom were being transferred to the government-held cities of Aden and Al Mukalla.

The Saudi-led military coalition that is fighting the Houthis in Yemen has not commented on the strike.

The Yemeni government and the Houthis, a rebel group from the country’s north, have been at war since 2014, when the militia seized the Yemeni capital, Sanaa, which it still holds.

Graphic footage published on social media and verified by The New York Times shows multiple bodies and blood on paved ground at Al Alam. At least 15 bodies can be seen as the camera pans the military camp, with clothes and sandals strewed around.

The scale of the attack underscored the rapidly intensifying war in Yemen, which erupted earlier this year after the United States and Israel attacked Iran, the Houthis’ main patron.

Last month, the Houthis seized swaths of strategic territory on Yemen’s Red Sea coast in a lightning offensive, gaining greater control over a crucial choke point for global trade. In recent weeks, forces affiliated with the Yemeni government have mounted a counteroffensive to retake the territory, backed by Saudi warplanes.

Colonel al-Nuzaili said on Monday that Yemeni forces had carried out hundreds of attacks on Houthi positions over the past day, and claimed to have “neutralized” more than 500 Houthi fighters.

The Houthis have not commented on those claims, but on Sunday, an official for the group said that Saudi warplanes had launched 110 airstrikes in Sanaa on that day alone. There were more than 30 casualties in the attacks, Yahya Saree, a Houthi military spokesman, said on social media, describing the majority of them as women and children. The Saudi government did not immediately respond to questions about Mr. Saree’s claims.

As the fighting has ground on, the Houthis have demonstrated their ability to hold out against the government’s forces, and have launched offensive strikes deep within government-held regions. On Friday, the Houthis struck the Yemeni government’s headquarters in Aden, killing five staff members and security officers.

The conflict has increasingly spilled onto Saudi soil, with the Houthis attacking infrastructure and oil facilities in the kingdom. Repeated attacks on an airport in the Saudi capital, Riyadh, have killed at least 17 people and injured more than 330 others since the beginning of this month, according to the Saudi authorities.

Saudi Arabia further restricted flights to and from its main airport in Riyadh this weekend, saying that none would be allowed to arrive or depart without explicit permission. The change was made in an official notice that took effect on Saturday night local time, with no end date.

Organizers of the Future Investment Initiative summit, Saudi Arabia’s marquee investment conference scheduled to kick off on Oct. 26, said on Monday that the event, nicknamed “Davos in the Desert,” will be postponed until 2027, underscoring how strikes on the kingdom are endangering its economic diversification plans. “We will announce the new 2027 dates very soon,” the Future Investment Initiative Institute said in a statement.

Rashad al-Alimi, who leads Yemen’s internationally recognized government, the Presidential Leadership Council, promised a “decisive response” to the attack on Monday, saying the deaths would not stop the government from protecting citizens and rebuilding state institutions. His comments were reported by the Saba news agency.

The Houthis’ long conflict with the Yemeni government and its allies paused in 2002 with a cease-fire, but tensions resurfaced over the summer after the Houthis accused Saudi Arabia of carrying out an airstrike on Sanaa’s airport and retaliated by imposing a blockade on Saudi maritime traffic.

The recent surge in violence has alarmed countries in the region, and Saudi Arabia has been lobbying its allies for help in recent weeks in the face of the Houthis’ attacks. President Trump rebuffed Saudi appeals last month to launch U. S. strikes against the Houthis, but the United States is providing significant military support, including intelligence and data to help with selecting targets.

On Monday, lawmakers in Egypt were discussing whether to authorize military assistance to Saudi Arabia, but they adjourned until next week without a vote, according to a report by Egyptian state media.

The country’s National Defense Council, whose chairman is President Abdel Fattah el-Sisi, announced in a statement on Sunday that Egypt would provide “all necessary and possible forms of support” to defend the kingdom but did not specify what that would entail.

The return to fighting in Yemen has exacerbated an already dire humanitarian situation there.

In the government-held city of Taiz, hundreds of thousands of people remain trapped between the Houthis and government forces. Taiz has taken in more than 100,000 displaced persons, according to the United Nations’ International Organization for Migration, and local health officials have said that fuel and medical supplies are running low.

Shuaib Almosawa contributed reporting from Sanaa, Yemen, Niraj Chokshi from New York, and Sanjana Varghese from London.

Ismaeel Naar is an international reporter for The Times, covering the Gulf states. He is based in Dubai, United Arab Emirates.
