France to Impose Curfews After Nationwide Rioting

The New York Times October 19, 2026

Unrest in France

Advertisement

Supported by

Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu defended police efforts and pledged to restore order as government ministers acknowledged failures.

By Catherine Porter and Ségolène Le Stradic

Reporting from Paris

Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu of France said he had ordered localized curfews for Monday night in some French towns and neighborhoods, as the government moved to reassert control after the worst riots in decades hit cities around the country.

While ministers in Mr. Lecornu’s government acknowledged failures in handling the weekend riots, the prime minister struck a different tone, saying that the police had done a good job against a “shadowy network” of far-left instigators who he said were seeking to orchestrate “a profound disorder in the country leading up to the presidential election.”

“While we witnessed very difficult scenes involving violence against property, no one was killed, and that is a miracle,” Mr. Lecornu said, emerging from an emergency meeting of ministers on Monday afternoon.

He told reporters that a massive police operation was underway — with “practically” 200 investigators in Paris alone working to track down the looters.

“My determination to restore order is absolute,” Mr. Lecornu said, vowing to use “whatever tools are at the government’s disposal.”

He did not provide specifics on where the curfews were expected, saying only they were for places that had been especially affected by unrest and that a map would be provided later on Monday.

Earlier in the day, France’s interior minister, Laurent Nuñez, offered a mea culpa on national radio, saying that the police had been underprepared to deal with the scale of the riots that spun off from the mostly peaceful protests held across the country. Mr. Nuñez said he had offered his resignation to President Emmanuel Macron but that it had not been accepted.

The justice minister, Gérald Darmanin, also acknowledged that the authorities had “undeniably failed” in the face of the violence — the biggest unrest to hit France in years — and said on French television that there had been “a failure in intelligence.”

The government estimated that at least 3,000 businesses across the country had been pillaged over the weekend, double the figure given on Sunday by the federation of commerce and distribution.

Mr. Lecornu said that workers affected by the riots could access partial unemployment payments starting on Tuesday, and that the government was pushing insurance companies to accelerate the process of reimbursements.

“We must enable shopkeepers to get back on their feet very quickly,” he said.

It was unclear if those words would assure rattled citizens and furious mayors, many of whom demanded answers from the national government on Monday.

Benoît Payan, the mayor of Marseille, blamed the government and the police for “delivering” that city, France’s second largest, to “looters and rioters.”

Speaking on French radio, he accused the region’s prefect of inflating the number of rioters that had attacked city hall and local stores, and said that he was seeking “explanations” and “the guarantee that this will not happen again” from the government.

“I want compensation down to the last cent,” he added, saying: “You cannot let a country sink into a political crisis without an answer.”

After sporadic episodes of violence and looting persisted in several French cities on Sunday — including in Paris, where the police chief said 351 people had been arrested — several cities undertook measures aimed at restoring calm on Monday.

Even before Mr. Lecornu said he had instructed prefects to impose targeted curfews in certain places, a few cities had announced their plans to do so.

The authorities in Marseille banned gatherings throughout the city from 12 to 8 p. m. that day, a local official said on social media. In Denain, a small town in northern France, city officials said on social media that a curfew would be in place from 9 p. m. to 6 a. m. through Oct. 25.

The mayor of Coulaines, in western France, made his announcement after the prime minister’s call, saying his town would have a curfew for minors after 11 p. m.

“I think that at the state level, it would be necessary to implement similar measures,” he said in a video posted on social media. “And why not declare a state of emergency if the raids and looting continue?”

Amid calls for calm and order, there were questions about what would happen next.

The students who started a protest movement more than a month ago by blockading their high schools to demand better conditions are now on a two-week vacation. However, other groups have joined the protests in solidarity and to highlight their own grievances, with some seemingly determined to keep the movement going.

A group of university students blocked entrances to the Louvre Museum on Monday morning, preventing it from opening its doors. Students also blockaded the Paris campus of Sciences Po, one of France’s most prestigious universities. The police were called to the scene, according to student unions and a spokeswoman for the university.

Some protesters who took part in the weekend’s huge demonstrations have already called for another mass action next weekend. On Monday, Mr. Nuñez said that police numbers would be reinforced across the country, “particularly this weekend.”

Catherine Porter is an international reporter for The Times, covering France. She is based in Paris.

Ségolène Le Stradic a reporter and researcher for The Times, based in Paris.

Huge Riots and Antigovernment Protests in France: What to Know

The New York Times October 19, 2026

Unrest in France

Advertisement

Supported by

France imposed scattered curfews on Monday after weekend protests over living costs and poor school conditions devolved into riots.

By Amelia Nierenberg and Catherine Porter

Catherine Porter, who reported from Paris, has covered the protests for weeks.

France is cracking down after antigovernment demonstrations in cities and towns devolved into the most destructive riots in decades as riots and looting on Saturday caused nationwide damage and deepened a sense of national reckoning.

On Monday, Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu said he had ordered localized curfews for that night, a sign that the French state was trying to reassert control after the widespread chaos. He said a map detailing the areas under restrictions would be made public by Monday night. Later, local government officials announced curfews in parts of several cities, including Paris, Nice and Lille.

The move came amid an escalating political blame game, which gathered steam on Sunday as the chaos subsided. Mr. Lecornu blamed the far left for the unrest, saying that the French police had done a good job against a “shadowy network” of instigators who he said were seeking to orchestrate “a profound disorder” in France before presidential elections in April.

The main far-left party has repeatedly blamed his government for the discontent. And French citizens are caught in the middle of the finger-pointing as they try to carry on with daily life in cities littered with broken glass and the charred skeletons of burned cars.

The protests have heightened a sense of fiscal and social crisis in France, the European Union’s second-largest economy. And there’s more debate to come: The government is trying to pass an unpopular belt-tightening budget as France heads toward the elections.

The violence was a convergence of a weeks-old student movement seeking better school conditions, an emerging national movement protesting high living costs and opportunistic rioters who used the demonstrations as a cover for looting.

More than half a million people joined some 110 marches throughout France on Saturday, the Interior Ministry said, on the biggest day of protest since the demonstrations began about a month ago. A major union, the C. G. T., gave a higher estimate, saying that 800,000 protesters had turned out.

Amid many peaceful demonstrations, rioters vandalized about 1,500 shops and many symbols of the French state, leading to nearly 2,400 arrests. An arson attack largely destroyed the town hall in Limoges, in central France. In Marseille, the second-largest city, masked people broke into a government building and tipped over a bust of Marianne, a symbol of the republic.

On Monday, the government estimated that at least 3,000 businesses across the country had been pillaged over the weekend.

High school students started protesting last month to express frustration with the condition of their schools.

They have pointed to crumbling infrastructure, overcrowded classrooms, overloaded schedules, a shortage of teachers and staff, and underfunding. Many also called for an overhaul of state-run admissions platforms for higher education and universities that they said were unfairly selective.

Students have blockaded hundreds of schools. They have set fire to, or damaged, at least 24 of them, according to the government. Thousands have been arrested since September and over 1,000 police officers, students and school staff members have been hurt.

The students’ anger has been exacerbated by the police’s forceful response. Prosecutors and a police watchdog are investigating at least 34 cases involving accusations of police misconduct during the protests.

The cases include a 15-year-old boy whose left hand was ripped off, officials said, most likely by the explosion of a police stun grenade; and a 14-year-old boy maimed by a tear-gas grenade that an officer had fired at close range.

This month, labor unions and other campaign groups have increasingly joined the student demonstrations. They have held bigger rallies to express solidarity as well as to protest a broader range of issues.

Some are angry over the cost of living and rising fuel prices that have surged, in part, because of the war in Iran. Farmers have also joined, angry at agricultural costs.

Social media accounts associated with the “yellow vest” protest movement, which emerged in France nearly a decade ago with roadside demonstrations against high gas prices and other issues, have joined calls for demonstrations.

And left-wing parties have also seized on the protests as part of a wider expression of discontent at President Emmanuel Macron, who is limited to two terms and is nearing the end of his time in office.

Such discontent has a long history in France, where student-led protests in 1968 nearly toppled the government and helped transform French society.

On Monday, high-level officials admitted failure.

Laurent Nuñez, the interior minister, offered something of an apology on national radio, saying that the police had been underprepared to deal with the scale of the riots that spun off from the mostly peaceful protests in the country.

He said he had offered his resignation to Mr. Macron but that it had not been accepted.

Gérald Darmanin, the justice minister, also acknowledged that the authorities had “undeniably failed” in the face of the violence.

On Sunday, far-right leaders and the centrist government blamed the far left for the chaos. They pointed in particular to a major far-left party, France Unbowed, that they said had provoked the unrest.

Mr. Lecornu, the prime minister, accused party leaders of sowing distrust among student protesters about the police and said some rioters were members of the “ultra-left.”

France Unbowed has rejected that accusation, and its leader, Jean-Luc Mélenchon, has blamed the government for actions that he said had made the unrest more likely.

Mr. Mélenchon said on social media that Mr. Lecornu was “responsible for the chaos” because of “incompetence or a worst-case strategy to create a party of order that would make people forget his failure in public finances.”

Mr. Lecornu did not respond to that accusation.

As of the weekend, high school students were on a two-week vacation. Some of the groups that joined the demonstrations in solidarity appeared determined to keep protesting.

Some protesters who participated in the huge demonstrations over the weekend have called for another mass action next weekend.

The government is trying to signal that it is ready: On Monday, Mr. Nuñez, the interior minister, said that police numbers would be reinforced, “particularly this weekend,” around France.

Reporting was contributed by Lynsey Chutel, Ségolène Le Stradic, Giulia Imbert and Zane Irwin.

Amelia Nierenberg is a Times reporter covering international news from London.

Catherine Porter is an international reporter for The Times, covering France. She is based in Paris.

The New York Times October 19, 2026

Artificial Intelligence

Advertisement

Supported by

A Saudi military official paid for the OpenAI engineer’s wife and infant son to fly out of the United States a day after his arrest, according to a court filing. The Saudi government also offered to cover his bail.

By Emmy Martin

Reporting from Phillip Burton Federal Building and U. S. Courthouse in San Francisco

A member of the Saudi military paid for the wife and infant son of the engineer charged with planting a hidden recording device at OpenAI to fly out of the United States the day after his arrest, federal prosecutors said in a court filing on Sunday.

The flights were among a number of new details about the ties of the former OpenAI engineer, Abdulrahman Alfozan, 35, a Saudi national, with Saudi officials, according to the filing. Among other things, Mr. Alfozan had been in frequent contact with a member of the Saudi royal family who tried to recruit him to work in Saudi Arabia, the filing said.

In May, the royal family member wrote to Mr. Alfozan, saying “Saudi needs you more” than the United States. Mr. Alfozan replied “100,” according to prosecutors. But Mr. Alfozan said he would not leave OpenAI until he could collect the company stock he had been promised, which was worth $2.2 million when he was hired, according to the filing.

The Saudi government also offered to pay Mr. Alfozan’s bail. In a letter to his lawyer, dated Oct. 14, the Saudi consulate in Los Angeles said it was ready “to cover the full amount of the bail bond” required for his release. Mr. Alfozan’s lawyer filed the letter with the court as part of the request that he be released.

The revelations follow OpenAI’s disclosure this month that it had found a hidden recording device in one of its offices in San Francisco and had traced it back to Mr. Alfozan, who appeared to be planning to place more recording devices in sensitive areas of the artificial intelligence company’s offices. He was arrested by the Federal Bureau of Investigation on Oct. 9 and charged with trying to secretly record conversations using an electronic device.

Mr. Alfozan has been in jail since then. He is scheduled to appear in federal court in San Francisco at 11 a. m. Pacific time on Monday, when Magistrate Judge Alex G. Tse will decide whether he stays in jail while the case moves forward.

The incident has fueled concerns about the security of leading A. I. labs like OpenAI, which create advanced A. I. models that are among the most closely guarded secrets in the U. S. technology industry.

(The New York Times sued OpenAI and Microsoft in 2023, accusing them of copyright infringement of news content related to A. I. systems. The two companies have denied those claims.)

Prosecutors said in the filing that Mr. Alfozan’s motive might have been to enrich himself or to aid a foreign government, “or both.” Prosecutors said their investigation was continuing and “may result in additional serious charges.”

Mr. Alfozan’s wife, identified as Lujain Alassaf, and son left the United States about 36 hours after his arrest, on a one-way, business-class flight to Doha, Qatar, which was booked and paid for by a Saudi military official, according to the filing. An earlier one-way flight to Jeddah, Saudi Arabia, booked and paid for by the Saudi government, was canceled, prosecutors said.

Mr. Alfozan’s wife, whose U. S. student visa recently expired, told F. B. I. agents that her husband planned to return to OpenAI after two months in Saudi Arabia but that he, too, intended to eventually move there permanently, according to the prosecutors.

The Saudi Embassy in Washington did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

After searching Mr. Alfozan’s home and phone, investigators found electronic parts similar to those in the recording device that was planted, as well as photos of a different concealed device and photos of technology in another conference room used for sensitive meetings, according to the filing.

In court papers filed ahead of Monday’s hearing, Mr. Alfozan’s lawyer, William Pernik, said his client had deep roots in the United States. Mr. Pernik submitted more than 50 letters of support, along with records showing that Mr. Alfozan had applied for U. S. citizenship and was scheduled for a naturalization interview in November. He had also been scheduled to begin two months of paternity leave from OpenAI in October that was set to end in December.

Prosecutors argued that the Saudi government’s help was itself a reason for concern. They said Saudi Arabia has no extradition treaty with the United States and pointed to a previous case in San Francisco in which, they said, the Saudis helped arrange a next-day flight to Saudi Arabia for an employee of Twitter (now known as X) after the company confronted him in 2015 about accessing user data. The employee, Ali Alzabarah, was later charged with spying for Saudi Arabia but has not been arrested. Another employee involved in the scheme, Ahmad Abouammo, was convicted in 2022.

Emmy Martin is a reporter covering the technology industry from San Francisco and a member of the 2026-27 Times Fellowship class.

The police in Long Beach, Calif., said they were called by ICE for backup and found a man who was bleeding and handcuffed.

By Madison Malone Kircher

A California man whose family said he was a U. S. citizen was hospitalized in Long Beach over the weekend after an altercation with Immigration and Customs Enforcement left him pinned to the ground in handcuffs.

The encounter in Southern California on Saturday is the latest mistaken detainment as ICE arrest numbers across the country continue to rise.

It was unclear on Monday what led to the encounter, how it unfolded or whether the man was still in the hospital. But officers with the Long Beach Police Department arrived at the scene after being called in for backup by ICE, which reported that vehicles were being vandalized and that there was a person “in need of medical attention,” according to a statement from the police.

Officers then took a bleeding, handcuffed man to a nearby fire station, where they removed his handcuffs and later took him to a hospital, the statement said. The police said they were not involved in immigration enforcement and did not make any arrests at the scene.

The police declined to further comment and directed questions to the Department of Homeland Security, which did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

The man, Ricardo Gonzalez, was riding an e-bike when he was struck by an unmarked vehicle, according to Leslie Gonzalez, his daughter, in a post on Instagram. She said in a message to The New York Times that her father was a U. S. citizen but declined to answer more questions, citing concerns for her family’s safety. But in her post, Ms. Gonzalez wrote that her father had been “tased” and pinned to the ground. Mr. Gonzalez did not respond to an interview request.

In clips posted to social media, Mr. Gonzalez appears immobilized on his stomach by officers wearing ICE vests.

“My arm is broken, stop!” he yells, asking for medical assistance as officers handcuff him, restraining his arms behind his back.

Mr. Gonzalez is one of many U. S. citizens who have been mistakenly detained by federal immigration agents in operations that are part of the Trump administration’s deportation campaign.

In September, agents held a U. S. citizen in suburban Chicago. The man suffered injuries to his head, neck and teeth in the confrontation. This month, ProPublica reported that hundreds of U. S. citizens have been detained by immigration officers under the current administration, inadvertently caught up in federal operations. (During President Trump’s first term, a U. S. citizen was awarded a $55,000 settlement after she was wrongfully detained by ICE.)

There has also been a recent spike in ICE arrests of people with no criminal record even as Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin continues to emphasize that the agency is targeting “the worst of the worst.”

In Long Beach, videos of the encounter involving Mr. Gonzalez show a chaotic scene on a neighborhood street, with onlookers yelling at law enforcement. In other clips, a woman is shown being handcuffed by ICE officers and put in a car.

“That’s my wife, and that’s a U. S. citizen,” a man is seen yelling in one of the videos, using expletives.

Mayor Rex Richardson of Long Beach said that he had spoken to Mr. Gonzalez on Sunday but that he did not have information about the woman in the other videos.

Mr. Gonzalez had called 911 on Saturday, the mayor said, adding he did not have details about how the altercation unfolded.

By the time police officers arrived, Mr. Gonzalez was being detained, Mr. Richardson said. The mayor’s team was still gathering documentation from Saturday and working to verify what happened. His office plans to submit a complaint to D. H. S., he added.

“This is his neighborhood. He’s a father, he’s a dad,” Mr. Richardson said of Mr. Gonzalez. “The reality is, you know, that wasn’t what he expected that day. He didn’t expect that his children were going to see him cuffed and on the curb. He simply just wants his kids to be safe,” the mayor added.

On Instagram, Mr. Richardson wrote that ICE did not belong in his city and that the agency’s activities had undermined community safety.

Mr. Richardson added that his team was concerned about the timing as California begins early voting.

“No one should feel intimidated or afraid to exercise their right to vote,” he said.

Kitty Bennett contributed research.

Madison Malone Kircher is a Times reporter covering internet culture.

Fire at Starlink Center in Lithuania Was Sabotage, Officials Say

The New York Times October 19, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

The fire, which did not seriously damage the network, came after similar incidents in Bulgaria and Poland involving the satellite internet provider, a key defense tool for Ukraine’s armed forces.

By Lara Jakes

Lara Jakes covers NATO and has written extensively about hybrid warfare in Europe.

The authorities have thwarted what they called attempted sabotage against the Starlink network in Lithuania, the latest in a string of apparent attacks in Eastern Europe against the satellite internet provider. The service is used by NATO countries and is crucial for Ukraine in the war against Russia.

Prime Minister Mindaugas Sinkevičius of Lithuania said the attack occurred around 2 a. m. on Sunday, targeting antennas and a control unit at a data center company where Starlink infrastructure is installed.

Mr. Sinkevičius said at a news conference that “flammable liquids and Molotov cocktails” had been used, according to the local news media.

The control unit caught fire, but it was quickly extinguished after a security guard spotted the flames. The antenna was not damaged, and the head of Lithuania’s National Crisis Management Centre said Starlink service was not disrupted. A search for potential suspects is underway.

European officials have blamed a spate of recent, unconventional attacks on Russia, and Mr. Sinkevičius said in a radio interview that he saw the attack in his country as part of the same pattern, though he offered no evidence.

Bulgaria’s prime minister said last week that Starlink antennas near the country’s capital had recently been attacked. He did not give details, citing a pending investigation. Bulgarian authorities are seeking a European arrest warrant for two suspects in the case who have left the country, according to prosecutors.

Last month, a fire at a Starlink station in central Poland damaged supply equipment and a generator. German authorities arrested two Turkish citizens last week in connection with the fire, which Prime Minister Donald Tusk of Poland called “another act of hybrid warfare.”

The Polish control station is an internet hub not just for Poland but also for communication services in Ukraine, according to Krzysztof Gawkowski, Poland’s deputy prime minister.

It was not immediately clear how deeply the recent attacks had affected Starlink’s network. SpaceX, the company led by Elon Musk that provides the service, did not immediately respond to requests for comment on Monday.

While the authorities in all three cases have yet to determine who is responsible for the attacks, some officials have suggested that Russia could be targeting Starlink as a new front in its shadow war against NATO countries that support Ukraine.

Russia has for years been accused of launching cyber strikes against critical infrastructure like energy facilities and government networks; planting explosive packages on cargo planes; jamming navigation systems on commercial flights; and sending surveillance drones over military bases in Europe. Moscow has generally denied the accusations as “Russophobic.”

By their nature, the hybrid strikes are difficult to trace back to a perpetrator, and most incidents have been hard to pin down. Still, last month, Berlin directly attributed to Moscow a recent explosive-laden but faulty drone at the Leipzig-Halle airport, in eastern Germany, that was found near Ukrainian transport planes.

More recently, drone attacks on commercial ships in Black Sea zones that are considered Bulgarian and Romanian waters have been widely blamed on Russia. NATO’s North Atlantic Council, the military alliance’s decision-making forum, is expected to discuss the Black Sea attacks at a regularly scheduled meeting on Tuesday.

Starlink is a service of SpaceX that provides internet connectivity across much of the world, including Europe, from satellites in lower earth orbit. A military-grade version, Starshield, was developed for the U. S. government, which has made it available to Ukraine.

The Ukrainian armed forces have relied heavily on the two services for battlefield communications, to carry out drone attacks, and to thwart Russian attacks.

But Ukraine has reported in recent days that its access to Starshield had been restricted.

President Trump, who is in a deepening feud with President Volodymyr Zelensky of Ukraine, has denied ordering the restrictions and has said that he did not think Mr. Musk had done so either. Mr. Musk has suggested that any restrictions came from the Trump administration, which has been pushing Ukraine to agree to a peace deal that it fears could benefit Russia.

Still, some European advocacy groups have called for governments to cancel their contracts with Mr. Musk’s businesses.

“Ukraine’s ability to defend its people, and Europe’s ability to support it, must not depend on arbitrary decisions by a single company or on the political will of Donald Trump,” one group, Renew Europe, wrote in an Oct. 14 letter to Ursula von der Leyen, president of the European Commission.

Ryan Mac, Boryana Dzhambazova and Tomas Dapkus contributed reporting.

Lara Jakes, a Times reporter based in Rome, reports on conflict and diplomacy, with a focus on weapons and the wars in Ukraine and the Middle East. She has been a journalist for more than 30 years.

The Future Investment Initiative, a centerpiece of Saudi efforts to diversify its economy from its reliance on the energy industry, was set to begin next week.

By Humza Jilani

Reporting from Dubai, United Arab Emirates

Saudi Arabia’s marquee investment conference will be postponed until 2027, its organizers announced on Monday, underscoring how missile and drone strikes on the kingdom are jeopardizing its economic diversification plans.

“We will announce the new 2027 dates very soon,” the Future Investment Initiative Institute said in a statement.

The event, nicknamed “Davos in the Desert,” was scheduled to kick off next Monday.

In recent days, event organizers had offered some speakers the opportunity to address the conference by video link, while they also internally discussed the possibility of hosting a fully remote conference. But they decided on Monday to postpone the event entirely.

The decision is a blow to Saudi Arabia’s efforts to project calm amid escalating missile and drone attacks from the Iranian-backed Houthi militia in Yemen. The increasingly brazen strikes have undermined efforts that Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, Saudi Arabia’s de facto leader, has made to recast the oil-dependent kingdom into a hub for global tourism, business and sports.

The Future Investment Initiative summit, which last year drew over 8,000 participants and featured prominent business and financial leaders as speakers, including Larry Fink of BlackRock and Jamie Dimon of JP Morgan Chase, is Saudi Arabia’s premier venue to pitch its post-oil plans to the world.

But deadly strikes on King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh this month have killed at least 13 people and injured hundreds of others, forcing the facility to close and causing thousands of flight cancellations.

Saudi Arabia further restricted flights to and from its main airport in Riyadh this weekend, saying no flights would be allowed to arrive or depart without explicit prior permission. The change was made in an official notice that took effect on Saturday night, local time, with no end date.

Before the FII Institute and the authorities decided to postpone the event, many had already canceled their plans to attend while others who had planned to attend were rerouting their travel through neighboring Bahrain.

The conference is the highest-profile event among a number of others, including the Urban Cycling World Championships and a summit between Persian Gulf and European leaders, that have been postponed or canceled since fighting renewed between Houthi rebels and Saudi Arabia this year.

Riyadh hosted the WPC Energy Congress, an international energy summit, last week, but many high-profile delegates, including the chief executives of Exxon Mobil, Shell, Chevron and BP, pulled out before the event because of security risks and travel disruptions.

The French 14-Year-Old Whose Face Was Maimed by a Tear Gas Grenade

The New York Times October 19, 2026

Unrest in France

Advertisement

Supported by

The police’s treatment of the student last month sheds light on how a wave of school unrest evolved into national protests that spilled into widespread riots on Saturday.

By Ségolène Le Stradic

Reporting from St.-Ouen-l’Aumône, France, Ségolène Le Stradic interviewed witnesses and verified footage of the confrontation.

As police officers tried to disperse students amid unrest outside a school in a Parisian suburb last month, they approached a 14-year-old boy who was lingering near the school entrance.

Their initial interaction is unclear, but soon the teenager was in a heated argument with the police. As it escalated, a male police officer shoved him with a tear gas launcher, according to video footage verified by The New York Times. Then a female officer hit him with her baton, according to prosecutors, the footage and a teacher who witnessed the altercation.

The boy kicked at the female officer, according to the footage, the prosecutors and the teacher, Mathieu Moreau.

The male police officer, standing roughly two yards from the boy, fired a tear gas grenade at his face, breaking his jaw and destroying many of his teeth.

The boy, whose family has identified only as Eden, was unavailable for an interview because he has not been able to speak since a surgery the day after the incident, according to his lawyer, Elsa Marcel. The male officer, who has not been named, said he fired a tear gas grenade because he believed the female officer was at risk, according to prosecutors who interviewed him. He has been suspended and placed under investigation. The interior ministry declined to comment on the incident.

The officers’ actions stirred a national outcry. They were seen and cited by some protesters and others as an incident that helped to explain the anger and intensity of the student demonstrations that began in late September and then evolved into a nationwide protest movement that on Saturday led to some of France’s worst riots in years.

The student demonstrations were initially focused on improving conditions in high schools, including by improving crumbling facilities and hiring more teachers. Those protests often turned violent as participants set fire to or ransacked at least 24 schools, according to the government, leading the police to respond with force. Officers arrested roughly 8,000 people at the high school demonstrations and often used contentious crowd control methods, such as stun grenades, that spurred accusations of police brutality.

Instead of dampening the unrest, the police’s actions against teenagers like Eden helped to galvanize both students and adult citizens across the country, giving them another reason to protest.

That culminated in huge demonstrations across France on Saturday, with people of all ages protesting a range of social grievances, including police violence against students.

Those demonstrations came hand in hand with yet more street unrest as rioters seized the moment to loot shops and set fire to government buildings.

Now, the police stand accused of being too weak to prevent the violence on Saturday — and too heavy handed in its handling of the protests that led to the riots.

Addressing that contradiction, Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu said on Monday: “For the past three weeks, we’ve been hearing that the police are killing or injuring people. And then, for the past two days, we’ve been asked, ‘What is the police doing?’ A very French kind of schizophrenia.”

The government has defended how the police handled the student protests in the buildup to the weekend chaos, noting that officers were often forced to contend with violent unrest.

“We’re walking a fine line here because this is a difficult situation to handle,” Laurent Nuñez, the interior minister, said at a recent hearing in Parliament. “When demonstrations take place peacefully, there are no police arrests.”

Critics of the police counter that even against that backdrop, officers have been extraordinarily harsh in their approach to a movement led by teenagers. Prosecutors and France’s police watchdog are investigating at least 34 accusations of police misconduct during the weeks of protests.

Cases include a 15-year-old boy whose left hand was blown off, the interior ministry said, most likely by the explosion of a police stun grenade; a 16-year-old boy hospitalized, prosecutors said, after an eye injury “consistent with being struck” by a kind of rubber bullet; and a 17-year-old boy whose hand was destroyed by a grenade, according to prosecutors.

Concerns about police conduct at protests have repeatedly surfaced in recent years, especially between 2018 and 2020 during the “yellow vest” movement when several demonstrators, protesting high gas prices and other issues, lost eyes after being shot by officers with rubber projectiles.

Experts say the number of incidents is the result of the police increasing their use of heavy-duty weaponry that is inappropriate for crowd control.

“We’re talking about numbers that should prompt the government to re-evaluate the use of these weapons,” said Sébastian Roché, a professor at the National Center for Scientific Research who researches the police and has documented injuries caused by police weapons since the 2000s. “What’s happening is the transposition for a teenage population of a law enforcement approach that has evolved over the past 10 years.”

Mr. Nuñez said at the parliamentary hearing that it was “excessive” to describe the police response as “repression,” but has suspended the police’s use of a certain kind of stun grenade at student protests.

Eden’s face was maimed just weeks after he enrolled at Lycée Château d’Épluches, a vocational high school in St.-Ouen-l’Aumône, just north of Paris. The school trains students — almost all of them boys from underprivileged backgrounds — to be car mechanics and truck drivers.

Less than a month after Eden began studying there, unrest broke out at schools across the country as students demonstrated against dilapidated buildings, overloaded schedules and absent teachers. The protests soon reached Château d’Épluches, where the number of students has risen to 630 from 480 in 2014, without a comparable increase in resources to accommodate the increased enrollment, according to teachers, including Mr. Moreau.

Like at many schools affected by the protests, the students gathered outside the school’s entrance, set fires in the street outside and refused to attend class.

The police often responded with tear gas, according to residents, teachers and students.

One resident, Massira Tazi, said, “They’re protesting for what they need, but they shouldn’t be breaking things or setting fires.”

Another, Nisrine Bensmaine, said the police had still been too harsh. “They’re minors, after all,” she said.

Prosecutors investigating the police officers said that Eden was among the demonstrators. According to Mr. Moreau, Ms. Marcel and texts reviewed by The Times that Eden sent his mother, the boy was not involved in the protests.

“There are blockades, I’m heading home,” he wrote to his mother after arriving at the school on Sept. 25.

“OK but please, take care of yourself,” she replied.

“Yes mom,” he wrote.

On the day of his injury, Sept. 28, confrontations between the police and students began after boys lit fireworks in a nearby park, according to Mr. Moreau. That prompted officers to spray tear gas, he said.

Mr. Moreau was trying to usher the students into the school, he said, when a bottle was thrown at the police. The teacher approached the police and pleaded with them not to retaliate, he said. The officers sprayed more tear gas, he said, dispersing most students.

While prosecutors said Eden was “one of” the demonstrators, without giving further detail, a video that Eden sent his mother during the clashes shows the teenager was watching from next to a parking bay, roughly 50 yards from the unrest. The prosecutors and the police have not accused him of lighting fireworks or throwing the bottle.

Eden did not immediately leave the area when the police fired the gas, according to Mr. Moreau, who spotted Eden from a distance.

Mr. Moreau said the police then approached Eden and forced him to stand up — leading to a scuffle that was captured on camera by several bystanders and also later described by prosecutors.

The prosecutors did not say how the scuffle started but described a standoff in which the officers repeatedly tried to push Eden back as he kept moving toward them.

After the female officer struck him with her baton, Eden kicked at her thigh — at which point the male police officer, “carrying a tear gas launcher known as a ‘Cougar,’ fired horizontally at the young man, who was standing facing him,” the prosecutors wrote in a statement.

The officer believed he had “only a fraction of a second to protect her and his team,” the statement added.

Eden will take at least six weeks to recover, according to a medical record reviewed by The Times that shows the boy is at risk of long-term chronic pain and restricted movement in his jaw.

Eden’s mother, who spoke on the condition of anonymity out of fears of retribution, said that Eden often wrote messages to her asking if he would ever get his old face back.

Her lawyer, Ms. Marcel, has asked prosecutors to consider charging the police officer with attempted murder.

“He’s going to have to undergo extremely invasive surgeries. He’s completely unable to speak or eat normally. His jaw will be completely immobilized for several weeks,” Ms. Marcel said in an interview. “Obviously, this is compounded by intense psychological trauma — he could have died.”

The interior ministry said it could not comment on the case while the police watchdog’s investigation was ongoing.

Mr. Moreau, the teacher who witnessed the scene, said he and his colleagues were left asking what could have justified the police response to Eden.

“Why? I mean, why?” Mr. Moreau said. “What danger did he pose at that moment?”

Reporting was contributed by John Ismay from Washington, Monika Cvorak from London, and Jonathan Baran from New York.

Ségolène Le Stradic a reporter and researcher for The Times, based in Paris.

Judge Grills Witnesses About Decisions Behind Trump’s Golf Course Plan

The New York Times October 19, 2026

Trump Administration

Advertisement

Supported by

The Justice Department clashed with Judge Ana C. Reyes over testimony by several government witnesses about the chain of decisions surrounding East Potomac Golf Links.

By Zach Montague

Reporting from Washington

A hearing about the fate of the East Potomac Golf Links in Washington turned into an icy standoff on Monday as a federal judge went to extraordinary lengths to learn who has been responsible for decisions about the property and whether plans to overhaul it have been kept from the court.

A day after President Trump announced that his administration would transform the municipal course into a professional golf venue, Judge Ana C. Reyes summoned a constellation of officials to testify about whether the government has been plotting the renovation even while swearing in court that no decisions had been made.

While the stakes of the case are relatively low — the fate of one municipal golf course on a spit of land not far from the monuments in Washington — it has taken on symbolic importance as the latest blowup between Mr. Trump and the federal courts. It is proving to be a test case for how far Mr. Trump is willing to go to get his way on a project that he has made clear is important to him.

Judge Reyes asked several senior officials to testify on Monday about a decision to cut down hundreds of trees at the course after providing only a few hours of notice. She had requested notice of major changes at the course, so she could consider whether the proposed actions would be legal, given a challenge from a preservationist group trying to halt the project.

The Justice Department responded by alleging that Judge Reyes, an appointee of President Joseph R. Biden Jr., has shown bias in the case and asking her to recuse herself. She declined.

Facing an army of lawyers from the Justice Department, including the department’s third most senior official, Judge Reyes made clear that her patience was running thin. She said the government’s position that the tree removal was part of routine maintenance — not in preparation for a renovation that Mr. Trump has now trumpeted on social media — made little sense.

“There is no universe in which all of this just coincidentally happened at the same time,” she told the lawyers. “There just isn’t.”

In his Sunday post, Mr. Trump announced that the course would close for a 14-month renovation on Nov. 15. On Monday, he followed up to say that work was scheduled to begin immediately.

Judge Reyes has ordered the administration to halt all tree removal until at least Oct. 26, but she is considering a more expansive block on work at the site.

The hearing opened with drama, as Judge Reyes asked all of the Justice Department officials present, including junior lawyers and nonpolitical career lawyers, to raise their hands if they agreed with a filing that had been submitted on Sunday by Stanley E. Woodward Jr., the associate attorney general. If they did, she said, she would order them to add their names to it as well.

That document tried to square the government’s courtroom statements with Mr. Trump’s social media commentary. It argued that federal agencies were still studying the plan and that cutting trees on the property did not amount to a determination about the future of course.

“The plan is not final because the Park Service has not completed its review and the details of the proposal are subject to change during the review process,” it said.

Mr. Woodward told Judge Reyes that her request was “inappropriate.” He added that he would instruct his colleagues not to do as she had ordered.

“I’m the one who’s going to say how we move today, not you,” she fired back.

She then ordered Mr. Woodward to explain in writing by later on Monday why the Justice Department did not have to follow her direction.

The hearing continued with testimony by Gregory Wischer, a deputy chief of staff at the Interior Department, who was involved in meetings about improving East Potomac Park as part of larger “beautification” efforts in Washington.

Facing questions from Abbe Lowell, a lawyer representing the group suing to stop the renovation, Mr. Wischer testified that taking down the trees was a basic aesthetic decision. A 2019 report that proposed restoring the course’s original layout had recommended tree removal, he testified.

“We were just trying to find ways we could clean up the course,” he said.

Mr. Wischer’s testimony on Monday played out against a backdrop of Mr. Trump’s conflicting public statements.

Mr. Trump has attacked Judge Reyes as “a crazed lunatic whose courthouse tapes will reveal, may be insane.” The Justice Department had requested that audio be released of a hearing she conducted last week, in which she angrily took the Trump administration to task for removing trees with minimal notice.

In denying the administration’s request that she step away from the case, Judge Reyes pointed out that she had consistently rejected what she described as premature requests by the preservation group suing that she block work at the course.

Instead, she wrote that she had approached the case as a “pragmatist” who had urged the parties in July to hammer out an agreement on their own, rather than pre-emptively halt work by court order. She had instead asked the government to provide notice before undertaking major work at the course.

“Between February 13, when this case was filed, and October 11, the court had not barred the government from taking any action in East Potomac, including tree removal,” she wrote.

“It is easy to weaponize selective quotations to bring a baseless recusal motion,” she added. “But it is much harder to meet the demanding legal standard against a full record. By any objective measure, the government fails to meet the standard for recusal.”

Zach Montague is a Times reporter covering the federal courts, including the legal disputes over the Trump administration’s agenda.

Latest Climate Report Warns of Major Upheaval to California Way of Life

The New York Times October 19, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

The dire projections come from the state’s Climate Change Assessment, which analyzes the impacts of changing weather patterns on the nation’s most-populous state.

By Soumya Karlamangla

Reporting from San Francisco

In just a few decades, summers in California will not only be much hotter, but will also stretch for months longer. Floods will become more widespread and extreme. Exposure to wildfire smoke will kill thousands more people every year.

Those are the dire projections of California’s Fifth Climate Change Assessment, a report produced by California every few years that analyzes the impacts of changing weather patterns on the nation’s most-populous state.

The future laid out in the report, which was published on Monday, touches on familiar warnings: more wildfires, bigger storms, longer droughts. But it illustrates in unsettling detail just how quickly the climate is being reshaped, and reveals what is likely to be major upheaval to long-established ways of life in California.

According to the report, average temperatures are likely to increase in California by about 4 degrees Fahrenheit by the middle of the century. Current warming in California is unprecedented compared with the past century and estimates for the past millennium, the report shows.

More and more, warm weather will arrive in California earlier in the year and persist later, with summer conditions lasting for 135 days on average by the middle of the century, compared with an average of 90 days between 1981 and 2010, according to the report. That prolonged summer will have widespread impacts, including on fire risk, tourism, agriculture and wildlife.

The warmer conditions will also mean a 40 percent reduction by midcentury in California’s snowpack in the Sierra Nevada, which feeds the state’s reservoirs. What once fell as snow will instead fall as rain and immediately become runoff. This will lead to more severe droughts, according to the report.

Many Californians have already lived through the beginnings of these trends. The state this year logged its warmest August on record. And several of the most destructive fires in state history have happened in the last decade, including the wildfires last year in Los Angeles that were among the costliest disasters in U. S. history.

Abby Edwards, senior deputy director for the Governor’s Office of Land Use and Climate Innovation, which produced the assessment, said she hoped the report would alert communities and decision makers about where to focus their efforts as the climate continues to change.

The report, which weaves together existing and new, state-commissioned research, contains multiple scenarios based on different greenhouse gas emissions levels in the coming years, as well as recommendations for how to adapt to changing climate patterns.

“The future is not predetermined,” Ms. Edwards said in an interview.

The report comes as the Trump administration has been undermining California’s position as a national leader in environmental protection. As the world’s fourth-largest economy, California’s environmental regulations have influenced car and consumer goods manufacturers, and many of the state’s green policies have been adopted by other states in what’s known as the “California effect.”

Among the recent moves from the Trump administration: It ordered an oil company to restart a pipeline off Santa Barbara that caused one of the state’s largest oil spills in 2015; it announced $75 million for a new coal export terminal in Oakland that city officials have tried to stop for nearly a decade; and it has signaled that it could curb the power of the California Coastal Commission, which has been entrusted with protecting the state’s 840-mile shoreline for more than a half-century.

“As the Trump administration turns its back on science, California is doubling down on climate action, on protecting our communities, and on building a safer future,” Gov. Gavin Newsom said in a statement.

The state’s assessments began in 2006 under former Gov. Arnold Schwarzenegger as a way to evaluate the specific threats of global warming on the state. This year’s assessment was the most extensive yet.

Beyond the statistics, the report also laid out how a changing climate could threaten beloved ways of life in California, such as skiing in the Sierra Nevada and going to the beach.

A longer summer means a shorter winter for California, and warmer temperatures are expected to blanket lower-elevation ski resorts with rain instead of snow. The snowpack is expected to fall by 60 percent by 2100.

The report also found that without major intervention, as much as three-quarters of California’s beaches could disappear — either seasonally or permanently — by 2100 because of coastal erosion. In that same time frame, sea level rise is expected to threaten $78 billion worth of property because of coastal flooding.

The state’s agricultural industry is expected to take a major hit as well.

Many crops require a certain number of hours of cold temperature to develop properly, and warmer temperatures could decrease fruit yields in some parts of the state by as much as 40 percent, according to the report.

At the same time, water shortages could mean that the number of acres that farmers irrigate could decline dramatically, including by up to 40 percent in the San Joaquin Valley, a major agricultural hub.

Soumya Karlamangla is a Times reporter who covers California. She is based in the Bay Area.

The Overlapping Plagues Quietly Devastating American Forests

The New York Times October 19, 2026

By Catrin Einhorn

This grove of trees looks idyllic. But hiding in plain sight are threats that could lay waste to this peaceful scene, and upend forests far and wide.

Many of the trees in this photo are infested and will very likely die.

The young American beech has been struck by a microscopic roundworm, first spotted in the United States in 2012.

Another invasive species, a tiny, aphid-like creature, is attacking the Eastern hemlock.

These ash trees are already dead: victims of another invasive insect, the emerald ash borer.

This stand of terminally sick trees is not unique. These days, in the Northeast, it’s rather ordinary.

Supported by

The trees are sick.

Epidemics are escalating, across numerous species, as more and more pests and pathogens invade forests. Their entryway is global trade — in live plants, and in the countless products that are shipped in wooden pallets, crates and other packaging. As trade has boomed, so have the opportunities for tiny stowaways to wreak havoc.

“We’re moving insects and microbes around the world through trade very rapidly, and basically running an experiment” to see which ones will take hold, said Bernard Slippers, a forest pathologist at the University of Pretoria in South Africa.

The attackers have killed billions of trees already, with countless more under threat. In some severe cases, forests are transforming into bleak spaces of brambles and vines.

And the impact extends far beyond the woods. Trees filter water, stabilize the land and clean the air. They absorb and store planet-warming carbon dioxide, fighting climate change. They create the three-dimensional habitat that countless species use for shelter and shade. And they offer something even more foundational.

“Plants are the only thing that take sunlight, carbon dioxide, water, and turn it into biological energy,” said Anurag Agrawal, an ecologist at Cornell University. “Plants, trees are the ultimate source for all of the energy, all of the food on the planet.”

Different tree species offer sustenance at different times each season: Nuts and berries for mammals and birds, pollen for pollinators. Some insects can feed only on certain trees, and when those trees disappear, so do they. Fallen leaves affect the acidity of the forest floor and the water running through it.

Each tree species that drops out leaves a hole. Some are bigger than others.

“You really have this whole cascade of effects that grows exponentially as you lose more and more species,” said Kathleen Knight, a research ecologist with the United States Forest Service.

Scientists are doing what they can to help a growing number of species withstand the onslaught, even as they struggle to understand what it will mean.

While tree species are getting hit all over the world, the northeastern United States has emerged as an epicenter. Scientists attribute that to both the volume of imports and the rich variety of tree species in the region.

The beetle responsible for some of the worst recent damage is tiny, bright green and shimmers like a jewel: the emerald ash borer.

Scientists don’t know exactly when it entered the United States, but by 2002 in the Detroit area, something was terribly wrong with the ash trees. Their crowns died back and their outer bark split apart, revealing strange, serpentine marks underneath. The bright green beetles were found among dying trees.

Less than two decades later, the borer had so devastated North American ash trees that all six of the most prominent species were classified as endangered or critically endangered. Death rates for mature trees are sky high.

Because ashes were common in cities and because they are dangerously prone to falling when heavily infested, local governments have spent billions of dollars removing them. Cities and towns have lost much of their canopy, just as climate change makes urban trees more important than ever.

Each invasion, as scientists call them, brings its own consequences for forests.

At the Mohonk Preserve, conserved land in New York’s Hudson Valley, a stretch of serene forest leads to a sudden starkness. Fallen branches litter the ground. Naked trunks of dead trees stand like giant toothpicks.

The victims here are hemlocks, an evergreen notable for creating dense, year-round shade, cooling the ground in the summer and insulating it in the winter. Hemlocks can grow on rocky slopes that challenge other trees, stabilizing banks. And they cool streams, protecting aquatic life.

Radka Wildova, a senior scientist at the Ecological Research Institute, walked among the grove of dead trees on a recent day. “In 2023 at this plot, the mortality was around 80 percent,” she said.

A tiny, aphid-like insect called the hemlock woolly adelgid is behind this massacre. First detected in Virginia in 1951, it probably arrived on plants imported from Japan. The insect spread slowly in the beginning but has now decimated hemlocks across the Southeast.

In New York, winter cold snaps have helped hemlocks survive longer by knocking back the adelgid populations.

But this hemlock graveyard shows that where conditions aren’t perfect — where there’s less water, more heat, maybe thinner soils — it’s harder for the trees to survive the attack. A warming planet is expected to compound the problem by both stressing the trees and helping adelgids survive.

An hour’s drive west into the Catskill Mountains shows the high stakes.

The forests there are famous for filtering New York City’s drinking water. Instead of spending billions of dollars on water filtration plants, government officials agreed in 1997 to conserve enough land for the forests to do the job.

But near the Neversink Reservoir, one of six that collectively deliver roughly 90 percent of the city’s water, the overlapping plagues affecting hemlock, ash and beech are evident.

Ailing beech trees are victims of one of the most recent outbreaks, which first showed up in Ohio in 2012. Beeches were already suffering from beech bark disease, facilitated by a small insect. Now a microscopic worm native to Japan is attacking their leaves, causing the tissue to thicken and the leaves to drop.

When one species of tree disappears, others can partly fill the ecological gap. The American chestnut, a grand tree that once anchored many eastern forests, has been functionally extinct since around 1950. It was felled by a fungus that was accidentally introduced from East Asia.

When the chestnuts vanished, oaks and hickories broadly took their place. But now they, too, face threats from invasive insects and pathogens.

Another malady, Dutch elm disease, probably arrived with beetles in logs imported for furniture veneers. By 1980, stately American elms had largely vanished from forests and city streets alike.

Their replacement? The ash trees that are dying now.

To survive in a new land, an insect must encounter a climate that meets its needs. Much of northeast Asia aligns perfectly with the northeastern United States. (Infestations happen in both directions. For example, the pinewood nematode, native to North America, is attacking East Asia and Europe.)

The number of highly destructive pests identified by scientists has increased since 1990, as global trade ramped up, said Juliann Aukema, a scientist who helped identify the surge and is now an assistant director of research at the Forest Service.

The direct costs are formidable. In 2011, researchers estimated that bark- and wood-boring insects would cost local governments in the United States around $1.7 billion a year in tree removal, replacement and treatment.

Over the decades, authorities have stepped up measures to prevent outbreaks. In 2002, countries agreed to a global standard that required packaging materials from raw wood to be treated with heat or fumigation and stamped to show that they were safe.

A study later found that infestation rates declined by around a third to half after the agreement was implemented. But compliance is inconsistent, scientists said.

“Material is still coming in infested,” said Deborah McCullough, who studies invasive forest insects at Michigan State University.

And while regulations governing international trade in live plants have also been tightened, plants can still be sick or infested even if they look healthy, scientists said.

At the border, federal inspectors examine shipments determined to be highest risk while also conducting random checks, said Dudley Hoskins, an under secretary at the Agriculture Department. “There will never be a scenario where there’s a zero risk profile,” Mr. Hoskins said. “We do interdict shipments of concern, if not daily, then almost every other day.”

To save individual trees, insecticides can be injected or applied to the soil around the roots. The tree becomes poisonous to insects that try to feed on it, whether or not they’re beneficial.

While effective, the costs add up: One tree might run $150 every few years, for example. Property owners often choose to treat a small number of beloved trees, but protecting a forest can be impractical.

Scientists are racing to find more sustainable solutions.

Standing among the cluster of sick hemlocks near the Neversink Reservoir in the Catskills this June, Nicholas Dietschler, who works with Cornell University’s New York State Hemlock Initiative, popped off the top of a small plastic bottle filled with tiny flies that prey on the adelgid. These are Leucotaraxis argenticollis, a type of silver fly so obscure it doesn’t have a common name.

The flies quickly climbed to the mouth of the bottle, flew out and disappeared into the forest.

“Be free,” Mr. Dietschler murmured.

With oversight from the federal government, several universities and state agencies are trying to fight hemlock woolly adelgid with what’s known as biocontrol, bringing in predators to drive down their numbers. Cornell has released hundreds of thousands of flies and beetles in recent years.

The irony of introducing a nonnative species to combat another nonnative species is not lost on scientists. They acknowledge the risks of unintended consequences.

But scientific protocols have tightened over the years, and many scientists think insect predators could give embattled tree species a chance. Four species of stingless wasps from Asia have been enlisted to fight emerald ash borer, and an imported fungus has helped tamp down the spongy moth, which defoliates oaks and other hardwood trees.

Other scientists have brought breeding to the battlefront. They are focused on finding trees with natural genetic resistance and helping them to multiply.

In 2006, Kathleen Knight was a young Forest Service research ecologist tasked with monitoring the spread of emerald ash borer. Ahead of the insect’s arrival in Ohio, she set up plots of healthy forests and watched the invader rip through, killing the trees in just a few years.

One day, she and her team recorded “hundreds and hundreds” of dead trees in one plot, she said. But on the way back to the car, they stumbled across something stunning.

“We found this really healthy, amazing-looking ash tree,” Dr. Knight said. “And we were just dumbfounded. How did this tree survive?”

As more strangely healthy ash trees were found, she teamed up with Jennifer Koch, a colleague at the Forest Service who had been looking for natural resistance to beech bark disease. The survivors were given a name: “lingering trees.”

When grafts of the lingering trees were exposed to emerald ash borer, a significant number of the larvae died. And when the scientists bred lingering trees with each other, the offspring were also resistant, some even more so than the parents.

“Trees are similar to humans in that they have a lot of genetic variability,” Dr. Koch said. But in the wild, the survivors are so few and far between that breeding is improbable. Their pollen and blossoms are unlikely to find each other.

“We’re helping Mother Nature along,” Dr. Koch said.

She has partnered with groups like the Ecological Research Institute in New York, which has recruited citizen scientists and conservation professionals to help detect lingering trees.

This kind of work can give people hope, said Jonathan Rosenthal, the institute’s director.

When asked what the future holds for forests in the Northeast, scientists struggled to answer. Ecosystems are made up of a dizzying number of variables, all interacting in ways that can be impossible to predict. Climate change makes the forecasting even harder.

“In the coming decades, the eastern forests might look quite different,” Dr. Agrawal said, “with a lot of death and destruction that not only saddens me as a biologist and a lover of nature, but makes me worry about all the things that nature does for us.”

Douglas Main contributed reporting.
