Why Is MAGA Swooning Over Richard Nixon?

The New York Times October 19, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

Guest Essay

By Geoffrey Kabaservice and John Guida

Mr. Kabaservice is the author of “Rule and Ruin: The Downfall of Moderation and the Destruction of the Republican Party, From Eisenhower to the Tea Party.” Mr. Guida is an editor in Times Opinion.

Was Richard Nixon a counterrevolutionary “taken down in a Deep State coup”? A model for the new climate right? Was he also, in some ways, a progressive?

On some parts of the right, Nixon is undergoing a reassessment, or redefinition, known as “Nixonmaxxing.” Young conservatives are celebrating him in Washington and on social media.

With his embrace of tariffs and law-and-order policies — and his insistence that he was unfairly dogged by the deep state — Nixon has some things in common with the current occupant of the Oval Office.

Is this reappraisal of Nixon about the past, or the future, of the G. O. P.? Geoff Kabaservice, the author of “Rule and Ruin: The Downfall of Moderation and the Destruction of the Republican Party, From Eisenhower to the Tea Party,” reflected on these questions in a written conversation with John Guida, an editor in Times Opinion. It has been edited for length and clarity.

John Guida: “Nixonmaxxing” has received a lot of attention this year, but the reappraisal has been a work in progress. For example, in a 2023 video, Christopher Rufo argued that Nixon’s politics represented a counterrevolution against the upheavals of 1968. Was Nixon a counterrevolutionary? What does it mean to call him one?

Geoff Kabaservice: Rufo actually laid out his case for Nixon as a “counterrevolutionary” at great length in his 2023 City Journal essay “Bring on the Counterrevolution.” Rufo’s thesis is that Nixon, particularly in his second term, began to strike back against the “federal agencies” that had been built up by Lyndon Johnson’s Great Society and parts of Franklin Roosevelt’s New Deal.

Nixon aimed to tame the federal bureaucracy by decentralizing power under his “new federalism” approach (which included consolidating federal programs into block grants to states and localities and trying to replace Great Society anti-poverty programs with a guaranteed-income system); to restore “law and order” in a way that would discredit and disempower the left; and to build a “counter-elite” that would supplant the “establishment” that Nixon believed had turned against him. He meant the national news media, elite universities, leading foundations, federal bureaucrats and to some extent upper-class society as well.

Guida: So this was especially a second-term project?

Kabaservice: Nixon definitely intended to take the Republican Party in a more conservative and populist direction in his second term, and present-day conservatives are not wrong to see his rhetoric and intended program as a forerunner of Trumpism. Nixon took significant steps toward recasting the G. O. P. as a working-class party, as Donald Trump briefly succeeded in doing in the 2024 election. Nixon was also, in some ways, an economic nationalist on trade and a proponent of a pro-labor policy — as Trump sporadically has attempted to be.

However, Nixon was a complicated leader who thought and acted in ways we would consider both conservative and surprisingly progressive. He did more than Johnson to desegregate Southern schools and establish federal affirmative action programs, and both Bill Clinton and Barack Obama acknowledged that their national health insurance proposals were built upon Nixon’s innovative 1974 health care proposal.

This complicates the effort to paint him as someone who started the conservative counterrevolution that Trump has carried forward.

Guida: That complication extends to Nixon’s posture to executive power, right? It was his administration that created the Environmental Protection Agency in 1970 as well as other additions to executive-branch bureaucracy (the Consumer Product Safety Commission, for example).

Kabaservice: The E. P. A. is an excellent example of why Nixon is hardly a direct model for today’s conservatives — and one might also add his signing into law of the Occupational Safety and Health Administration, which the right has disliked since its creation in 1970. But Nixon saw both agencies as means of improving the health and safety of Americans, and he was baffled by conservatives’ objections to using the power of government toward that end.

In other ways, however, Nixon seems to have anticipated some of the central claims of what is now known as the unitary executive theory. Nixon used impoundment — withholding congressionally appropriated funds — to prevent money from going to programs he objected to, claiming that the president has independent constitutional authority over execution of the law.

He also, notably, claimed executive privilege during the Watergate crisis, attempting to shield his deliberations (including his secretly taped conversations in the Oval Office) from Congress and the courts. Like Trump, Richard Nixon didn’t believe in a small government in the way past generations of conservatives like Robert Taft had. He wanted a government large and powerful enough to accomplish his goals, which Nixon genuinely conceived as contributing to a more peaceful world and a more prosperous United States.

But in his more vindictive moments, Nixon clearly thought of the power of the state as a weapon with which to strike back at his “establishment” enemies, in ways that prefigured Trump’s attempts to defund elite universities or expel dissenters from the Civil Service. And, as Nixon said to the journalist David Frost in a post-presidential 1977 interview, “Well, when the president does it, that means that it is not illegal.” This is a view for which Trump has considerable affinity.

Guida: Do you see the Trump administration’s direction of the Justice Department as a modern application of that use of government power to strike back at enemies? Or perhaps to intimidate opponents, as in, say, the investigation of Democratic Representative Ilhan Omar?

Kabaservice: Nixon’s “enemies list” was a testament to how he wanted to use the F. B. I., I. R. S. and other government agencies to “screw” his opponents, in ways that again seem to anticipate Trump’s weaponization of the Justice Department.

But it’s important to remember that people who worked for Nixon often saw him as something of a split personality — the good Nixon and the bad Nixon. The bad Nixon wanted to use Machiavellian means to accomplish his ends, even when they went up to the edge of legality and beyond; the good Nixon knew those efforts were illegal and immoral.

So his aides learned to work around what they called his “Alice in Wonderland” moments, when he would order them to attack his enemies in these illegal or unconstitutional ways — only to come back hours or days later and tell them that, after thinking about it, he had decided it would be better not to.

Guida: I’m curious how you think about Nixon and Trump in the context of the Supreme Court under Chief Justice John Roberts. In several decisions — on presidential immunity, presidential control of administrative agencies and more — it has endorsed the unitary executive theory. How do you think about these changes and presidential power?

Kabaservice: The Roberts court obviously has expanded executive power in numerous ways, but it also has struck down Trump’s attempts to bypass congressional authority or the Constitution. One thinks of the court’s ruling against Trump on tariffs, birthright citizenship and his attempts to remove officials without due process.

So in certain ways Trump, like Nixon before him, has been constrained from acting on what he seems to believe is his authority under Article II to do “whatever I want.”

Guida: How would Watergate, or some modern equivalent, go down under the Roberts court?

Kabaservice: I don’t think the Roberts court would countenance Trump forming a “plumbers’ unit” (to use the Watergate term for Nixon’s black-ops team) that would commit burglaries and other crimes in the hopes of plugging leaks and harassing the president’s enemies. Neither would I expect it to countenance the president’s obstruction of justice, evidence of which provided the “smoking gun” that ultimately forced Nixon to resign. However, would a similar scandal even reach the court nowadays? That’s a different question.

Guida: To that point, JD Vance said, about Watergate, “The idea that it would have taken down a presidency is crazy.” What do those remarks reveal about how we view politics today?

Kabaservice: Vice President Vance was more right than wrong when he speculated that if Watergate happened today, it would be a “12-hour news story” rather than a scandal that would bring down an administration. That has less to do with the courts than with the way that our political parties have become intensely partisan and polarized.

Nixon was persuaded to resign when a group of Republican senators came to him and told him he had lost the support of much of his own party. I have a hard time believing that would happen today.

If anything, many conservatives have come to appreciate Nixon more in retrospect because of — not despite — his actions in the Watergate scandal. Trump’s Nixonian willingness to act ruthlessly against his Democratic and deep-state enemies is at the core of his appeal to many of his supporters: “He fights!”

Guida: Will that “he fights!” appeal will be a staple of Republican politics after Trump? Or do you see other paths? For example, Dan McLaughlin wrote for National Review that Ronald Reagan was a better leader than Nixon and should remain the model for modern Republican success.

Kabaservice: Conservatives appreciate that Nixon was hated by what they considered to be all the right people — the anti-anti-Communists, the student protesters, the left-wing professoriate and so on — although the revisionist claim that Nixon was the victim of a “deep-state coup” doesn’t hold water.

Trump supporters also value Nixon as a kind of tribune of working-class people — or as Nixon called them, “the silent majority,” who objected to the disorder and cultural radicalism of the late 1960s. But Nixon was someone who stood at the center of the Republican Party. He didn’t emerge from its right wing — and in fact, the conservative movement began as a protest against the moderation of the Eisenhower administration in which Nixon served as vice president.

Many conservatives had a lifelong sense that Nixon betrayed them when, as vice president, he helped shut down Senator Joseph McCarthy’s anti-Communist crusade.

Guida: Nixon was, in a sense, a party man?

Kabaservice: He can be hard for us to understand because he saw himself as a kind of mediator among the Republican Party’s conservative, moderate and liberal factions, trying to keep them from attacking one another and making sure that each had what he called “a piece of the action.”

Reagan also maintained that big-tent approach to some extent, which is why relatively moderate Republicans like James Baker still played important roles in what was overall a conservative administration. Reagan never had a conservative mutiny because the right saw him as one of their own, and so gave him much greater latitude when he deviated from conservative orthodoxy.

It’s also true that Reagan was more of a party-builder as president — Nixon’s Committee to Re-elect the President shared very little of the money it raised in 1972 with the regular party apparatus — and Reagan validated conservatives in ways Nixon did not.

Guida: How would you rate Nixon, given the complications you convey here, among postwar Republican presidents? From Eisenhower to Trump, how would you rank them?

Kabaservice: I confess to having a great deal of sympathy for Nixon just on a human level. Of all of our presidents, he may have been the most brilliant and the most tormented. Lee Huebner, who served as a speechwriter for Nixon almost up until the end of his presidency, came out with a terrific book recently — “Nixon’s Elusive Totality” — which includes a generous selection of Nixon’s speeches and other statements, including his farewell remarks to the White House staff on the day he left office.

That last, impromptu address reveals Nixon’s genuine idealism about public service as well as his rather self-pitying sense of his own difficult roots in the working class (he said his father would have been considered “sort of a little man, common man,” but “he was a great man, because he did his job”). Nixon exited the national stage as a kind of Willy Loman figure, in a way I find tragic and moving.

In terms of how to evaluate Nixon as a president, you have to give him high marks for his opening to China, which ultimately resulted in making that country a tacit ally in bringing about both the downfall of the Soviet Union and our present globalized economic order. But Nixon’s presidency comes with a lot of asterisks as well, including not only Watergate but his prolongation of the Vietnam War.

I would rank Nixon below Eisenhower in terms of how his actions added to the country’s core strengths, but Nixon had a more difficult assignment in managing the economy as it began to move into the postindustrial era and faced greater overseas competition.

I would rank Nixon above Reagan and George H. W. Bush as an effective government manager, and well above George W. Bush and Trump as a leader able to transform society and move toward a prosperous and peaceful world order.

Guida: So unlike Mr. McLaughlin and I’m sure many others, you would put Nixon above Reagan?

Kabaservice: Reagan restored the morale of much of the country after the setbacks of the 1970s. But he also presided over the continued economic stagnation of the working class and the movement toward uncontrolled deficit spending that poses a serious long-term threat to the national interest.

Guida: The subtitle of Huebner’s book — “It Depends on Who Writes the History” — makes me wonder about historical narratives in the service of shaping politics. Several writers — among them Jonah Goldberg at The Dispatch — have suggested that this reappraisal of Nixon is really about who comes after Trump. It weaves a narrative of a particular type of conservative (a counterrevolutionary and a bare-knuckle political brawler) out of the very real complexity of Nixon that you stress.

How do you think about the construction of these types of narratives, and what makes some of them effective or intriguing (here I’m thinking of “Nixonmaxxing”) while others are forgettable or unconvincing?

Kabaservice: “Nixonmaxxing,” as I first read about it in The Wall Street Journal, really is a kind of vibe more than it is a genuine attempt to rehabilitate Nixon’s legacy or to consider him in his “elusive totality,” to quote the title of Huebner’s book. But history, in a country this divided, is always going to be a contest we wage in the present.

Nixon is an important figure for the Republican Party to think about as it gropes its way toward a post-Trump future. Nixon was a realist — détente was in many ways a recognition of the limits of American power — and at his best he understood that politics in a two-party system has to involve negotiation and compromise with people who disagree with you.

When Nixon listened to his better angels, he remembered that political opponents are still fellow Americans, not enemies to destroy. And Nixon’s legacy ought to be a reminder that if politics is a contest, at times a bitter one, it also has to be played by the rules of the game, including the rule of law and the Constitution.

Geoffrey Kabaservice, the vice president for political studies at the Niskanen Center, is the host of the podcast “The Vital Center” and the author of the newsletter All Things in Moderation and the book “Rule and Ruin: The Downfall of Moderation and the Destruction of the Republican Party, From Eisenhower to the Tea Party.” John Guida is an editor in Times Opinion.

It’s Sliced Cheese on Bread. And It’s Rocking Copenhagen’s World.

The New York Times October 19, 2026

The Danish capital is obsessed with this stripped-down snack, and the city’s top bakeries won’t stop until they’ve perfected it.

The Danish capital is obsessed with this stripped-down snack, and the city’s top bakeries won’t stop until they’ve perfected it.

Real Copenhageners know to eat a bolle med ost open-faced, instead of closed up like a sandwich. Credit...

Supported by

By Amelia Nierenberg

Visuals by Ulf Svane

Amelia Nierenberg, who feels icky after eating both lactose and gluten, braved Copenhagen’s bakeries to report this article.

Copenhagen is famed for its innovative gastronomy and elaborate dishes. But these days its hottest food is its most basic: just bread, butter and hard cheese. And Copenhagen’s top bakeries are in a dead heat to make the best one around.

It’s called a bolle med ost (bun with cheese), shortened by many to BMO, an abbreviation that was entered into the biggest Danish dictionary this year.

Often served open-faced, this sort-of-sandwich is all about the fundamentals — sparer than smorrebrod and a test of how sublime the simple can be. That’s a 180 from the best-known Danish cuisine, which has been foraged, fermented and tweezered into submission over the last two decades.

The BMO has become a calling card for Copenhagen's best bakers. Batch after batch, they experiment with the bread, the cheese and, yes, even the butter as they strive to stand out in a city obsessed with understated excellence. The BMO is hard to mess up, but almost impossible to perfect.

“You can’t pretend with BMOs,” said Anne-Sophie Lahme, a Danish trend researcher who focuses on food. “You can’t fake it. It has to be really, really good.”

Danes grab BMOs almost anytime — after run club, before dates, between meetings. They’re a filling snack and not all that expensive. At many of the top bakeries, they sell for about 45 Danish kroner (roughly $7), in line with other baked goods.

Now, thanks to a phalanx of influencers, tourists have it on their must-try list, along with a cardamom bun and a cinnamon bun.

And where there’s hype, there’s optimization.

Two brothers have written a BMO cookbook with 25 recipes. In June, Burger King released its own “Gourmet BMO,” although this time the “B” stood for burger. And die-hards run Instagram accounts chronicling their search for the ideal specimen. For one popular account, a married couple who are both mathematicians spent months fiddling with an algorithm to fairly compare the bounty.

In July, the Danish newspaper Politiken joined the fray and published a ranking of the city’s 50 best BMOs.

“This is how all Copenhageners tell the quality of a bakery,” said David Dyrholm, the critic who masterminded the list. He’d pitched the project almost as a joke. But to his delight, his editor loved the idea, and Mr. Dyrholm found himself surprised by the variety.

“There are thousands of these being sold every day,” he said. “There’s a lot of money made on this. So why not take it seriously?” Eventually, he ate about 65 bolle med ost, which cost more than 2,000 kroner (about $300).

Because bread is not just bread in Denmark, he had many questions along the way: What type of flour did any given bakery use? Did they mill their own? How long was the ferment? Did they roll the bun in seeds or cornmeal?

And what about the cheese? A beloved Danish cow’s cheese called Gammel Knas? Comté? Should that cheese be presliced or sliced to order? And should the butter be salted? Browned? Whipped?

“I like nerding out about this stuff,” Mr. Dyrholm said, a little sheepishly.

The nouveau-BMOs first appeared a few years ago, in a post-peak-pandemic onslaught of bread-baking. Sourdough starters passed between friends and new bakeries opened, street by street.

At some point, the abbreviation was born, and quickly proved divisive. To skeptics, the nickname sounds a lot like gentrification — dressing up a beloved family food in frippery.

“It is literally just a bun with butter and a slice of cheese,” said Nina Bauer, a Danish food historian.

Claus Meyer, a titan of Denmark’s food scene who co-owns Meyers Bageri, said, “I could not see myself entering a bakery and asking for a ‘BMO.’ ”

Thomas Spelling, the owner of the microbakery Rondo, almost shuddered at the idea. “I would never say that myself,” he said.

But he’s fine with customers calling it whatever they want. The bolle med ost is, hands down, Rondo’s best-selling product, he said. He would never retire it. “It would be like opening a bar and not having draft beer,” he said.

BMOs are also the best seller at Hart, which has 13 locations around Copenhagen and sells some 50,000 each month. “It’s its own category,” said Talia Richard-Carvajal, Hart’s creative director. The chain keeps finessing the recipe, she said, trying dozens of cheeses to find the right one and tweaking the bread, in search for a “glass-shard” crunchy crust.

The cheese Gammel Knas almost tells the story of the trend on its own. By 2024, BMOs had become so popular that Gammel Knas supplies began to run low. Danish newspapers reported a “cheese crisis.” Customers raced to stores.

Gammel Knas needs to mature for more than 24 months to develop its signature crunchy protein crystals. But new bakeries kept opening and demanding more cheese. For months, Sofie Biltoft-Riis, the director of Arla Unika, the company that produces that cheese, was in meetings about how to deal with the BMO skyrocket.

“My phone was ringing day and night,” she said. “The whole country went quite crazy.”

Copenhagen may be reaching a BMO plateau. But the snack is still the best seller at any bakery of repute. No longer as hyped, they’re just part of the fabric of the city.

And locals have perfected eating them. Even though a bolle med ost can be snarfed one-handed, it’s not. At least not by any self-respecting Copenhagener.

I found this out the hard way. I’m from New York City. I can knock back a slice of pizza in a minute flat. So with the first few BMOs I tried, I combined them into a sandwich, and ate quickly and efficiently with both hands.

“That’s the burger method,” said Mr. Dyrholm, the Politiken critic.

Two friends set me straight. “It’s just, like, very, very important that you eat it like this,” said Emma Toft Kromann, holding it open-faced.

“If you see someone eating it like a burger, you know they’re not from here,” added Ophelia Ernland.

A bolle med ost is the elevenses of a city caught between hustle and hygge. It’s a little treat, something to savor, even on the go, even if it’s just bread and butter and cheese.

Amelia Nierenberg is a Times reporter covering international news from London.

The Cover-Up: How a Trillion-Dollar Industry Launders Illegal Gold

The New York Times October 19, 2026

This is an illegal mine in Madagascar. Its gold is banned from the world’s legitimate marketplace.

Thousands of children work in these mines, in violation of international law.

Yet Madagascar’s gold flowed easily to market.

And the world’s gold authority helped cover it up.

Supported by

Times INVESTIGATION

The line between dirty and clean gold is an industry fiction. Wall Street and governments profit off gold from criminals, gangsters and those who exploit children.

By Justin Scheck

Visuals by Lynsey Addario

Reporting from illegal gold mines across Madagascar.

In an industry riddled with abuse, the world’s banks and governments rely on one entity to keep gangsters, warlords and human rights violators from selling gold into the mainstream market.

That group, the London Bullion Market Association, is the self-described “global authority for precious metals.” With the power to blacklist companies, the L. B. M. A. is the closest thing the multi-trillion-dollar industry has to an international regulator.

Governments rely on the association’s stamp as a sign that gold has been mined without human rights abuses, environmental devastation, financial sanctions or criminality. In the most literal sense, the L. B. M. A. sets the gold standard.

But a New York Times investigation found that the association has repeatedly allowed gold into the market that has been mined by criminals, cartel members and children. Refiners lie with impunity about the origins of their gold. The rules are pocked with exceptions and vagaries, and the L. B. M. A. has repeatedly decided not to enforce them.

And in the case of Madagascar, the L. B. M. A. helped change and backdate key paperwork that certified gold as free from abuse.

As prices skyrocketed in recent years and evidence emerged that gold was financing armed groups in Sudan and polluters in the Amazon, the industry perpetuated the notion that it kept such dirty gold out of the mainstream marketplace.

200 miles

MOZAMBIQUE

Betsiaka

Madagascar

Antananarivo

Mozambique

Channel

Mananjary

Africa

Indian

Ocean

The New York Times

The Times investigation shows that the divide between “clean” and “dirty” gold is an industry fiction. There is just gold. And as Wall Street, central banks and investors stockpile and trade the precious metal, they’re profiting off a supply that includes gold from illegal sources.

That matters now more than ever. Two decades ago, when gold sold at about $600 an ounce, it was not profitable to drive mining barges into the deepest parts of the Amazon or use bulldozers to tear up acres of Madagascar rice fields to find gold. The price this year crossed the $5,000 mark. That has made it profitable to mine in inefficient, destructive and politically destabilizing ways.

The industry works like this: Miners and brokers sell raw gold to refiners, which melt it, remove impurities, and form it into bars. The major international marketplace accepts bars only from the 67 L. B. M. A.-certified refineries. Those refiners must document the source of every ounce of gold in every bar. They are subject to independent audits to assure that their suppliers aren’t linked to criminals, child abuse or financial sanctions.

The L. B. M. A. is financed and run by the gold industry’s biggest players, including large refiners, like Asahi, and financial houses such as HSBC, Morgan Stanley, J. P. Morgan and Deutsche Bank.

National governments may regulate mining, but if the L. B. M. A. does not certify the gold, it becomes all but unsellable in the world’s biggest markets.

But for all its talk about being a global authority, the L. B. M. A. is mostly a paperwork collector. The association relies on refiners to inspect the mines and to self-report the details.

One way to see how the association fails to live up to its claims is to compare its public statements with what it says in private.

On the association’s website, its chief executive, Ruth Crowell, declares, “We’re the standard-setting organization that defines how precious metals are refined, as well as traded around the world.”

In court documents in London, where Tanzanians are suing the L. B. M. A. over violence in a mine, the group disavows those very words: “The assertion that the L. B. M. A. is ‘the standard-setting organization that defines how precious metals are refined and traded around the world’ is denied.”

Ms. Crowell wrote in 2024 that the L. B. M. A. was a global authority that sets standards for “85 percent to 90 percent of the global gold production.”

In court, the association says it is “a small, not-for-profit organization” that “does not possess the levels of staff, the expertise or the resources necessary” to be held responsible for what happens in gold mines.

In an interview and written statement, Ms. Crowell said the L. B. M. A. held refiners to “the highest level of international guidelines.” But she downplayed the association’s responsibility.

“The L. B. M. A.’s role is we designate what is acceptable for entry into one market,” she said. It is up to governments to oversee the industry, she said.

With few industry guardrails, gangs have diversified from cocaine into gold. Islamist terrorist groups have gotten into the business. Russia and Iran use gold to prop up their wartime governments.

And a few years back, Madagascar’s central bank decided to capitalize on booming prices by buying and stockpiling gold, including from illegal mines that employ children.

The Madagascar case reveals how the L. B. M. A. failed in its oversight mission, the one on which the entire mainstream gold industry rests.

To see how it happened, I began at the mines themselves. I took a propeller plane from the capital, Antananarivo, and drove three hours through farmland to a mine called Madagold. The mine sits in a dry valley in the northern part of the island, surrounded by a busy market fueled by gold-rush cash.

Miners have worked here for generations, but the increase in gold price in recent years has created a bustling unlicensed operation.

The L. B. M. A. says it bans gold that “is likely to harm the health, safety or morals of children.”

Everywhere I looked, at Madagold and at mines across the country, children were in danger.

Children drank from a wastewater pipe.

Others panned for gold in pools of raw sewage.

These young women say they’ve been mining crocodile-infested waters since they were 10 and 13.

There’s no age requirement. “Anyone can do it,” the owner of one mine told us. “And I keep a share.”

Children in Madagascar’s mines crushed rocks and hauled buckets of ore. Toddlers wandered between 100-foot-deep shafts.

Rising gold prices have fueled such rogue operations around the world. Miners linked to a Colombian drug cartel have sold gold into the U. S. Mint’s supply chain, via an L. B. M. A.-certified refiner. An illegal mine in Papua New Guinea was busy with child workers this month. A manager showed me a receipt. He was selling to a subsidiary of a major L. B. M. A.-certified refiner.

The association says that mines must be licensed and legal, and that they cannot destroy the environment. But illegal mines and environmental damage were rampant across Madagascar.

In the gold-rich northern region of Diana, miners follow no laws, the government’s regional mining supervisor, Firmin Razafindratondra, said. All of the area’s gold mining, he said, is illegal.

Outside Mananjary, on Madagascar’s east coast, miners operated despite government shutdown orders. Excavators turned rice paddies into a giant pit. In the north, workers felled trees in a protected forest to make beams for mine shafts. Such destruction plays out around the country.

“The environment is destroyed,” Elys Karena Hanitriniaina, the governor of another gold-mining region, said.

So there were obvious signs, to anyone who visited, that Madagascar’s mines would be hard-pressed to meet L. B. M. A. standards. Yet the gold breezed onto the market.

Here’s how it happened.

Several years ago, Madagascar’s central bank decided to start a national gold stockpile. Bank representatives bought gold from around the country. Government documents show that some came from Madagold, the mine where children worked and drank from wastewater pipes.

Other gold came, Madagold’s chief executive said, from muddy pits nearby. When I visited, toddlers panned for gold there. Much of the rest came from intermediaries who bought from informal mines.

For that gold to be worth anything, it needed to be “certified L. B. M. A.,” Madagascar’s central bank governor, Aivo Andrianarivelo, said.

So he dispatched his gold chief to Switzerland to find a refiner. Initially, it did not go well. Refiners questioned the gold’s origins and legality, Mr. Andrianarivelo said. “The answer we gave them didn’t give enough satisfaction or trust to the Swiss,” he said.

“Nobody wanted to touch this gold,” said Marc Ummel, a gold-supply-chain specialist at the nonprofit group SwissAid who met with Madagascar’s representative during the trip.

This was an example of the system working.

Small-scale mines are considered red flags. The L. B. M. A.’s rules say that any refiner accepting this gold would be required to conduct mine inspections. Swiss refiners worried that the bank couldn’t even identify all its sources.

Even if it could have, the required inspections would have revealed children, pollution and criminality. “‘It’s impossible,’” Mr. Ummel remembers telling Madagascar’s banker. “You will never be able to find an L. B. M. A. refiner.’”

On that point, he was wrong.

The central bank cut a deal in 2023 with the Istanbul Gold Refinery, one of the world’s biggest L. B. M. A.-certified refiners.

The Turkish refiner’s auditor filed paperwork with the L. B. M. A. claiming that it “does not do any business” with mines that raise red flags, records reviewed by The Times show. That claim freed the company from having to conduct inspections.

In an interview, Mr. Andrianarivelo acknowledged that children worked in Madagascar’s mines and said that his understanding was that they provided support work to miners, rather than hammering rock themselves. He acknowledged, too, that the mines did not follow safety laws. The workers, he said, were “very small and very poor people” who believed that only God, not safety equipment, would protect them.

The raw gold was melted into 12 kg bars at a plant next to Madagascar’s international airport. From there, tens of millions of dollars in gold was shipped to Turkey to enter the legitimate supply.

Normally, once the Turkish refiner filed the paperwork with the L. B. M. A., that would be the end of it. Unless discrepancies surface — from whistle-blowers, journalists or law enforcement authorities, for example — the L. B. M. A. does not typically independently verify that the paperwork matches the reality.

When discrepancies do surface, the refiners seldom face serious consequences.

Three years ago, for example, the L. B. M. A. learned that a refiner had received illegally mined gold from the Amazon. The refiner blamed the supplier, and the association took no action.

When an Australian refiner bought gold tied to child labor and other abuses in Papua New Guinea, the association blacklisted the auditor, not the refiner. The L. B. M. A. said it required the refiner to make unspecified management improvements. But the gold still sold.

And in 2021, emails show, the L. B. M. A. learned that Istanbul Gold Refinery itself had received gold originating from small-scale mines in Mauritania, where forced labor is well documented. The refiner did not disclose this and reported no inspections. The association determined that the refiner had broken no rules.

It was only by chance that anyone at the L. B. M. A. took a look at the Madagascar gold. The European Union happened to be considering certifying the association for a new oversight role. An E. U. inspector noticed the Madagascar deal and began scrutinizing it.

How, the inspector asked, could a refinery process gold from Madagascar yet claim no red flags? UNICEF has reported more than 230,000 children working in the country’s mines. The Justice Department and the International Monetary Fund have documented industry abuses there.

L. B. M. A. staff escalated the problem to a “compliance panel” that included the chief executive, Ms. Crowell. The association could have punished the refiner. Instead, the L. B. M. A. helped cover up the problem.

Association officials worked with the Istanbul Gold Refinery’s auditor to create a new report that made it seem like the refiner had disclosed the red flags from the beginning and had taken steps to scrutinize the supply chain, according to documents and the refiner.

The second report acknowledged that the company bought gold that originated in small-scale, red flag operations. But the report concluded that the mines “do not use child labor.”

The report was backdated, as if it had been filed in real time.

That backdated report remains on the L. B. M. A.’s website, with no indication of any alterations. The document serves as proof that Istanbul Gold Refinery processed only gold that had no connection to child labor or other abuses — claims that are undercut by what I saw in the mines.

A close look at the backdated report shows that, even with the changes, the Istanbul Gold Refinery did not follow L. B. M. A. rules as written. Those rules require refiners who process high-risk gold either to inspect the mines themselves or to use independent third parties to do so. The Istanbul refiner relied instead on the seller, the central bank, to self-certify that no child labor was used.

The rules as written make no allowance for such a self-certification. But Mustafa Salali, the Istanbul Gold Refinery’s compliance officer, told me that, in this case, he relied on the word of a government entity, the bank. As far as he was concerned, he said, everything was by the book because the L. B. M. A. signed off on the audit.

In response to questions about the backdated audit, Ms. Crowell acknowledged “non-conformances” in the process and said that “the chronology of these documents could have been explained more clearly.”

Initially, she said the refinery had been punished by being subjected to a publicly announced compliance investigation. She later said that no such investigation had actually been announced.

She said that the L. B. M. A. had mandated a “corrective action plan” — but the refiner said all it had to do was update the report.

The matter was closed. The gold was certified as meeting the world’s most rigorous standards.

It all worked out quite well for Madagascar’s destructive and exploitative gold industry.

Back when Mr. Andrianarivelo was shopping gold in Switzerland, many companies had turned him away. Now those same refiners are calling him looking to buy gold, he said, because the L. B. M. A. had declared that “there was no issue” with it.

Drone piloting by Andrianotahinarisoa Faraniaina Mamy

I’ve spent more than a year trying to answer a basic question about the world gold trade: Why are there so many destructive and illegal mining operations when most gold is sold on a tightly controlled market with rules to eliminate criminals? What I found is that the global gold trade is essentially unregulated once bullion crosses national borders. Most of the world's supply falls under the London Bullion Market Association—an industry group with the power to bar non-compliant refiners from the majority of the global market.

Justin Scheck is a London-based reporter for The Times.

Lynsey Addario has been a contributor to The Times since 2001. She has photographed many of the biggest conflicts and humanitarian crises of her generation.

How Did Life Arise?

The New York Times October 19, 2026

Photo illustration by Will Warasila for The New York Times

Supported by

Where did it start? How did it grow complex? Why did it get big? Three moments in Earth’s early history when evolution suddenly, inexplicably turned up the dial.

By William J. BroadKenneth Chang and Carl Zimmer

Life on planet Earth is a riot of diversity: ants and elephants, frogs and blue whales, tulips and redwoods, even a branch of the great apes known as humans. Uniting it all is biochemistry, in particular the shared biochemistry of genetic inheritance — DNA and RNA, the universal instruction kits of life.

Tracing these biochemical threads back through time has convinced many scientists that all life descends from a so-called Last Universal Common Ancestor, or LUCA, that emerged between 4 billion and 4.5 billion years ago, after Earth itself congealed from the gas and detritus of a nascent solar system. How this LUCA rose from the primordial stew may be impossible to ever say definitively. No fossils exist to provide a window onto that moment in time, and scientists have no point of comparison: So far, Earth is the only place in the universe known to harbor life.

After that initial “how,” the questions become marginally easier for scientists to address. Here’s what’s known about three of the biggest inflection points in the evolution of life on Earth.

4 Billion Years Ago:

Scientists agree on little regarding the origins of life, including where it might have arisen — at Earth’s surface, or in its watery depths.

“It’s hard to answer these questions,” said Joanna Masel, a professor of evolutionary biology at the University of Arizona. “The evidence is sketchy. So people argue.”

On one side is the primordial soup hypothesis: Life originated from natural chemical reactions in Earth’s primal waters, which formed a broth of organic compounds.

Charles Darwin floated the idea in 1871, when he proposed that “some warm little pond” was responsible for life’s origin. A few simple chemicals and sources of energy, he suggested, such as natural heat and electricity, might have joined together to form molecules “ready to undergo still more complex changes.” These in turn would have led to the first life form: a tiny sack of chemicals able to divide and make copies of itself.

The hypothesis got its first serious test in 1953. Stanley L. Miller, then a graduate student at the University of Chicago, filled a flask with water as well as ammonia, methane and hydrogen, gases that were considered to be abundant in the early atmosphere.

Then, to mimic a lightning strike, he introduced sparks. Days later, the simple molecules had given rise to amino acids, the building blocks of proteins and virtually all planetary life.

But the amino acids never advanced in complexity, and excitement ebbed as scientists rethought the composition of the primordial air. Some years later, researchers detected amino acids in meteorites, which suggested that the building blocks of life may have rained down from the heavens, putting another potential dent in the primordial soup theory.

On the other side of the argument is the watery-depths camp. In 1977, American scientists exploring the Pacific seabed stumbled upon an alien world of volcanic vents and otherworldly ecosystems, including eerie fields of albino tube worms. They drew their energy not from sunlight, which powers surface ecosystems, starting with plants, but instead from chemicals emitted by the hot springs.

As other deep-sea ecosystems came to light, scientists proposed that all life on Earth had perhaps arisen in the depths, nurtured by a warm, steady diet of chemicals and sheltered from the killer rocks and cosmic radiation that bombarded the planet’s surface early on.

In recent years, new discoveries have bolstered both sides of the argument.

In 2009, for instance, John D. Sutherland, a chemist at the University of Manchester, in England, described a new way that the molecules of life, energized by the sun’s ultraviolet rays, could have assembled spontaneously on the surface of a primitive Earth. And in 2017, an analysis of mineral deposits in Australia suggested that surface hot springs had nurtured the land’s earliest signs of life. In 2024, an influential group of scientists voiced strong support for the finding.

Even so, the deep springs theory has also gained new support. This summer, a team led by scientists at Heinrich Heine University in Düsseldorf, Germany, proposed that the warm chemicals available in the deep sea included metals such as nickel, cobalt and palladium. These metals, the researches contend, could have served as catalysts that helped the earliest forms of life build metabolic pathways.

The growing wealth of evidence suggests that, ultimately, both camps of theorists might be right, Dr. Masel said.

“It doesn’t have to be one thing,” she said. “It’s possible that life arose at the hydrothermal vents and also a warm little pond.”

Perhaps, she added, life arose independently in disparate ecological niches that remained isolated from one another for ages.

“It looks like the early events happened really, really fast, which points to ‘first life’ not being the hardest part,” she said. “Maybe the origin of life was easier than we thought.”— William J. Broad

2 Billion Years Ago:

About two billion years ago, a new kind of cell emerged on Earth, one much bigger and more complex than the microbes that had come before. Today, these so-called eukaryotic cells inhabit our own bodies, as well as those of other animals, plants and fungi. How this new brand of cell emerged remains one of biology’s great mysteries.

“Eukaryotic” comes from a Greek term meaning “true nut,” a reference to the nucleus, the compartment in which eukaryotic cells coil their DNA. Eukaryotic cells have many other vital compartments, including thousands of mitochondria, which generate energy. The huge volume of a eukaryotic cell is supported by a scaffolding that can be quickly dismantled and reassembled; it also serves as an internal shipping network, whizzing packages of molecules from one compartment to another.

In contrast, a single-celled microbe such as Escherichia coli is far simpler. No mitochondria, no scaffolding, no nucleus; a nut-free “prokaryote.”

Eukaryotes — organisms composed of eukaryotic cells — all descend from a common ancestor, which in turn descended from ancient prokaryotes. The earliest eukaryotes were single-celled protozoans; their oldest known fossils date back 1.8 billion years. How long before that the first eukaryotes evolved, scientists can’t say.

Living organisms have offered important clues to this transition. In the past decade, scientists have discovered a lineage of microbes known as Asgards that bear many, but not all, of the hallmarks of eukaryotes. For instance, they have a cellular skeleton that helps them crawl, but have no nucleus or mitochondria.

The current thinking is that Asgards descend from the forerunners of eukaryotes. Early Asgard-like organisms acquired some eukaryote features through ordinary natural selection: Mutations altered their cells, conferring advantages they passed down to their descendants today.

But cells evolved by other means, too.

Early eukaryotes lived in close quarters with other microbes, forming ecological partnerships. That intimate contact made it possible for the early ancestors of Asgards and eukaryotes to grab genes from their partners and add them to their own genomes.

This exchange may have started about 3 billion years ago and continued for hundreds of millions of years. Recent studies suggest that the final exchange that gave rise to eukaryotes was the most spectacular. Around 2.25 billion years ago, one species of bacteria took up permanent residence inside Asgard-like cells, using their own metabolism to generate fuel for the cells they occupied. They began to be passed down from one generation of hosts to the next, evolving into our mitochondria.

The broad outlines of eukaryote origins are now coming into focus, but many pages of the story are still blank. Scientists don’t yet know how all the parts that make up the nucleus came together, for instance.

And they don’t know why the merging of microbes apparently gave rise to big, complex cells just once in the history of life. Was there some exquisitely rare set of circumstances that allowed it to happen? Or did evolution conduct other experiments in complexity that ended in extinction long ago?

One thing is clear: Once the eukaryote cell evolved, Earth was never the same. From coral reefs and giant squid to Amazonian rainforests and vast herds of wildebeest on the African savanna, eukaryotes gave rise to all the life we can see, including the one in the mirror.

— Carl Zimmer

580 Million Years Ago:

The advent of eukaryotes set up the evolutionary foundations for coral reefs and herds of wildebeest, but it took life a long time to have a growth spurt.

Indeed, the billion years that followed are often called “the boring billion.” Evolution appeared to stagnate; life stayed almost entirely microscopic. Even the tectonic plates pressed pause, leaving the continents mountainless. Then, about 720 million years ago, the world went haywire.

First, Earth froze over, sealing the planet in an icy shell that blocked sunlight from the oceans and shut off photosynthesis. Except for a 10-million-year thaw in the middle of it, Earth remained a shiny white snowball, not a blue marble, for 85 million years.

Scientists marvel that life did not die out. Instead, after that long era of darkness, it underwent a mysterious jump in size and complexity.

“That is the absolute wackiest interval of Earth history that anyone’s aware of,” said Nick Butterfield, a paleobiologist at Cambridge. “You go in the one end, and it’s this old, dreary, boring microbial world, and you come out the other end after these two massive glaciations, and all of a sudden, there’s animals on the scene, and all the microbes have changed.”

The changes were so striking that in 2006, scientists named a new geological period to encompass them: the Ediacaran. It began around 635 million years ago, with the thawing of “Snowball Earth,” and ended roughly 540 million years ago with the start of the Cambrian Era.

Guy Narbonne, a geological scientist at Queen’s University in Ontario, Canada, has studied fossils of large, soft-bodied animals that lived during the Ediacaran at a site known as Mistaken Point, at the southeastern tip of Newfoundland. The creatures include rangeomorphs, marine animals that looked like palm fronds and could reach the height of a modern-day basketball player. Others were round and the size of coins. Some, perhaps early sponges, were cone-shaped.

For Dr. Narbonne, the story is straightforward: The omnipresent glaciers crushed rocks as they moved across the landscape. When they receded, the sediment washed into the ocean, spurring algal blooms that raised oxygen levels and made possible the greater metabolism required by larger creatures.

“I can’t think of a better way of fertilizing the oceans than to have glaciers melt after the end of a glaciation,” Dr. Narbonne said.

Andrew Knoll, a paleontologist at Harvard, also thinks that oxygen fueled the evolutionary jump during the Ediacaran. But in his view, the timing of Snowball Earth was coincidental; instead, he points to the resumption of plate tectonics at the end of the boring billion, which created Himalayan-scale mountains.

As these eroded, they added phosphorus to the oceans, which seeded blooms of photosynthesizing marine microbes, Dr. Knoll said. Predators evolved and began feasting on smaller organisms, which spurred an evolutionary arms race to get bigger, in order to avoid getting eaten.

But some scientists doubt the oxygen story, including Donald Canfield, a geochemist at the University of Southern Denmark, who performed the analysis that is often cited as evidence of an oxygen increase during the early Ediacaran.

“I’ve had somewhat of a change of mind,” Dr. Canfield said. He now thinks that oxygen levels in Earth’s atmosphere then were low, but significant and steady — about 4 to 10 percent of current levels.

Dr. Butterfield, for his part, thinks that scientists have been looking at the question backward. He proposes that complex animals began to appear before Snowball Earth, not afterward, simply as the culmination of random genetic mutations. This revolution in evolution, he says, upended the food chain, altered the chemistry of the oceans, pulled carbon dioxide out of the atmosphere — and tipped the world into a frozen state. Big life caused Snowball Earth, not the other way around.

“To my eye, the single most insulting, ecologically insulting, thing that has ever been imposed on this planet,” Dr. Butterfield said, “is animals.”

— Kenneth Chang

We've been publishing a series of pieces this month called "Unknowns," in which we head to the frontiers of science, where researchers are grappling with what remains to be discovered. There's no bigger question that the rise of life, so the editors asked three of us--Bill, Ken, and myself--to tackle it.

William J. Broad has reported on science at The Times since 1983. He is based in New York.

Kenneth Chang, a science reporter at The Times, covers NASA and the solar system, and research closer to Earth.

Carl Zimmer covers news about science for The Times and writes the Origins column.

Trump Is Pushing Ukraine to Surrender to Russia, Zelensky Says

The New York Times October 19, 2026

Russia-Ukraine War

Advertisement

Supported by

President Volodymyr Zelensky said he didn’t want to believe that Washington wanted an end to the war at Ukraine’s expense. “But that’s how it looks,” he added.

By Constant Méheut

Reporting from Kyiv, Ukraine

President Trump is trying to force Ukraine to surrender in the war, President Volodymyr Zelensky of Ukraine said in an interview published on Sunday, as a deepening feud between the two leaders drives their relations to new lows.

“I believe steps have been taken to convince Ukraine to capitulate,” Mr. Zelensky told Bloomberg News. He was referring to a string of measures in recent days by the Trump administration that could bolster Russia’s war machine while squeezing Ukraine’s ability to fight.

Mr. Zelensky added that he did not want to believe that Washington was seeking a quicker end to the war at Ukraine’s expense. “But that’s how it looks,” he said.

His comments capped a week in which the leaders traded some of their harshest words yet. Mr. Zelensky said that Mr. Trump had an instinctive affinity for autocrats, a pointed allusion to President Vladimir V. Putin of Russia, while the U. S. leader urged Ukrainians to vote Mr. Zelensky out of office.

Mr. Zelensky on Sunday appeared to tell the NBC show “Meet the Press” that he would run in a wartime presidential election, if one took place. It was the first time he suggested this publicly, after leaving the question open for months.

But he played down the prospect of holding a vote during the war. Russia has repeatedly refused a cease-fire that would allow people to cast ballots, and a vast majority of Ukrainians oppose holding elections in wartime.

The war of words between Mr. Zelensky and Mr. Trump began on Oct. 9, when the American president announced that the United States would buy Russian diesel in an effort to bring down fuel prices before the midterm elections, a deal that could send billions of U. S. dollars into Russia’s economy. He then demanded that Kyiv stop striking Russian refineries, one of its main levers in the war, so that Russian oil could return to the market.

In a social media post on Sunday night, Mr. Trump openly sided with Russia, the aggressor in the conflict, as he explained why he was offering the Kremlin incentives to negotiate a peace deal. He attacked Mr. Zelensky, saying he “doesn’t want to end this war, and probably never did.”

On Monday, the Kremlin spokesman, Dmitri S. Peskov, said that Mr. Putin, Mr. Trump and the Chinese leader, Xi Jinping, could meet next month in Shenzhen, China. The statement fed fears in Ukraine that Mr. Trump is only encouraging Mr. Putin to continue the conflict, and that the two men are conspiring to eventually impose an unfavorable settlement of the war on Kyiv.

Ukraine has accused Washington of restricting the Ukrainian military’s access to a U. S.-provided secure satellite internet network that is important to frontline operations. Ukraine has also complained about what it has described as lapses in U. S. intelligence sharing, which provides early warnings of incoming Russian ballistic missiles.

Ukrainian officials said they received no such warnings on two occasions last week. Mr. Zelensky said it happened again on Sunday night. Ukraine, he wrote in a social media post, got “no early warning from our partners” before missiles struck Kyiv, the Ukrainian capital.

U. S. officials have denied halting the sharing of intelligence with Ukraine on ballistic missiles. Secretary of State Marco Rubio told reporters that the lack of warnings last week resulted from “a software problem involving their early warning system” and that he could not speak to what happened on Sunday night.

Yurii Ihnat, a spokesman for the Ukrainian Air Force, confirmed that no early warning came before a first salvo of missiles struck Kyiv at 11 p. m. local time on Sunday. He noted that early warnings did arrive before the next salvo, around 3 a. m. on Monday.

Ukraine said Russia had launched 16 ballistic missiles at Kyiv and the surrounding region, along with nearly 270 drones. The Air Force said it had brought down more than 240 of the drones. It did not say whether it had shot down any of the missiles, part of a new policy not to release interception rates for ballistic missiles as Kyiv suffers from interceptor shortages.

The depletion of U. S.-made Patriot interceptors, Ukraine’s only reliable defense against Russian ballistic missiles, stems from surging global demand, most notably in the Middle East. Mr. Zelensky told Bloomberg that Washington was delaying deliveries of the interceptors.

The shortage can be heard in the way attacks now unfold. When Kyiv had enough interceptors, residents could hear the thud of air defenses firing at incoming missiles. Now, most of what they hear is the blast of missiles striking their targets, unopposed.

That was the pattern on Sunday night, too. The first salvo sent explosions reverberating across Kyiv’s city center. Then, when the attack ended, the blasts gave way to an eerie hush.

In one part of downtown Kyiv, seconds after the strike, a song rose from an apartment, filling the night. It was “How Can I Not Love You, Kyiv of Mine,” a 1962 lyrical ode to the Ukrainian capital that has become an anthem of the city’s defiance under fire.

Valerie Hopkins contributed reporting from Berlin.

Constant Méheut is a Times correspondent covering the war in Ukraine.
