Connections Coach

As a young actor, she was determined to avoid being typecast as a “sex bomb.” Thirty years later, she’s in total control of the women she plays.

Credit... Paul Kooiker for The New York Times

Supported by

By Marcela Valdes

Marcela Valdes has interviewed Penélope Cruz in three locations over five years, most recently in Toronto.

“There’s nothing that ruins a movie like a bad wig,” the director Olivia Wilde said. So when the actor Penélope Cruz told her, about two weeks before they started shooting “The Invite,” that she wanted to make her character blond, Wilde felt she might have “a full-on heart attack.”

During the 10 days that they rehearsed the film — a comedy involving two couples at a swinging dinner party — Wilde, who also stars in the film, encouraged the actors to be the architects of their characters. She and Seth Rogen took the lead on developing her anxious stay-at-home wife and his embittered music teacher, while Cruz and Edward Norton fleshed out her acerbic sex therapist and his unbuttoned former firefighter. Cruz consulted with the popular psychotherapist Esther Perel to ensure that her character’s marital wisdom rang true. This building phase was over, however, when Cruz told Wilde that she wanted to go blond.

At first, the director tried to persuade Cruz that no changes were needed. Everything was already terrific! But Cruz insisted, Come see it.

“Olivia kind of grabbed me by the elbow and said, Will you come look at something with me?” Norton recalled. “We walked down the hall and we turned the corner and Penélope was sitting there in the wig and our jaws just hit the floor because it was like, Oh, she’s gone, and there’s this thing here — this Spanish Esther Perel.”

“I just watched her shape-shift,” Wilde said. “She took a character that could have simply been alluring and enigmatic and made her surprising and unpredictable.” That shift seeds the movie with a tension that makes viewers eager to laugh.

Creating explosive, original comedy doesn’t just happen, Rogen emphasized. Actors have to make it happen. “And you have to make it happen in a way where it does not look like you are trying to make it happen,” Rogen added. “Penélope is someone who can do that.”

This year Cruz, who is 52, appears in three starkly different roles that showcase her astonishing virtuosity. In this summer’s “The Invite,” she displays cool comic timing and a gift for deadpan delivery. In Javier Calvo and Javier Ambrossi’s historical drama “La Bola Negra” (“The Black Ball”), which arrives in theaters this month, she sings and dances with aplomb. And in Florian Zeller’s upcoming thriller “Bunker,” she smolders as a book editor losing faith in her famous husband. Cruz dialed down her acting schedule for several years after having two children. Now it appears that becoming choosier about when and with whom she works has allowed her to make another leap forward in her capacities.

Late one evening in California, I met Cruz for dinner at the Beverly Hills Hotel. She arrived in a black baseball cap, a leather jacket, jeans, flip-flops and minimal makeup. “I’m like a rag,” she told me as she sat down at our table on the patio. “I came straight from the production.” She’d spent all day and evening shooting a new movie with Nancy Meyers.

In person, among the flowering bougainvillea and fairy lights, Cruz was warm, gentle and watchful. We spoke mostly in Spanish so that she could articulate her thoughts more fully. As we chatted, I could feel her trying to read me, even as I was trying to read her. It reminded me of some of the dinner conversations I’ve had with professional psychologists, when they never quite turned off their powers of observation.

Like Brigitte Bardot and Sophia Loren, Cruz has an iconic look that she deploys in many of her best-known films. Bold eyebrows. Eyeliner and mascara heavily applied and smudged. A radiant smile edged in pink lipstick. Significant cleavage. Big, messy hair. The whole effect suggests beauty that can’t get a rest. The apogee of this look was created by the makeup artist Ana Lozano for Pedro Almodóvar’s 2006 film “Volver,” where Cruz appears as a hard-working single mother. With Lozano’s help, Cruz has reprised versions of this unkempt siren in seven other films, including “Vicky Cristina Barcelona,” “Nine” and “Pirates of the Caribbean: On Stranger Tides.”

Unlike many legendary actresses, however, Cruz loves tossing her glamour aside. She dons a huge auburn wig to play a sadistic film director in the 2021 satire “Official Competition.” She turns into a sleek, stiff blonde to play Donatella Versace in the “American Crime Story” series “The Assassination of Gianni Versace” (2018). She goes bald and appears topless with a mastectomy to play a cancer patient in “Ma Ma” (2015).

“I choose to work with people who will make those decisions from the same place I do: What does that character need?” Cruz told me. “It’s not ‘Does that look good on me?’ That, luckily, doesn’t matter to me.”

Cooking, I learned, is her favorite metaphor for interpreting a character. “It’s like making a soup,” Cruz said. “I have an empty bowl that needs to be filled with things.” Her first ingredient is always a good script. Without one, she noted, it’s tough to work miracles. After that, she keeps adding elements: talking with people who remind her of the character, traveling to a museum to study a painting, listening to particular songs. If the character is based on a real person, she’ll study hours of video. Personal experiences also go into the soup, she said, but their flavors don’t get special preference. Costume decisions, like a wig, help, too. “You keep throwing ingredients into that soup and suddenly, if there’s luck, one day it clicks,” she explained. “You’re located in a spot where that person to whom you’re going to give life is already in you.”

Cruz is such a naturalistic actor that it’s easy to overlook how much intelligence and effort she pours into her performances. She has been nominated for 14 Goya Awards (Spain’s equivalent of the Oscars) and won three. She has been nominated for four Academy Awards and won for best supporting actress in Woody Allen’s “Vicky Cristina Barcelona,” where she plays a temperamental painter totally unlike herself. Yet people still describe Cruz as an intuitive actor, as if a career as varied as hers could be made from gut instincts alone. In fact, Cruz’s training as a performer began at the age of 4, when she began studying ballet, a practice she continued until she shot her first movie at 17. And her training as an actor began when she was 14 and continues to this day.

Her first teacher, Cristina Rota, fled Buenos Aires in 1978, after her partner was disappeared by Argentina’s military dictatorship. Settling in Madrid with her three children, she established an acting school, where Cruz began studying in 1988.

In Argentina, Rota had studied with the renowned acting teacher Hedy Crilla, who had escaped Nazi Germany via France and landed in Buenos Aires in the 1940s with the Comédie Française. “She brought Stanislavsky, Grotowski, Lajos Egri to us firsthand,” Rota recalls in her memoir, describing how Crilla imported naturalistic acting methods to Argentina.

About a year into her studies at Rota’s school, Cruz took on Jean Genet’s play “The Maids.” In it, two sisters take turns playing a scathing game of master-and-servant while their rich, hated mistress is out of the house; one of them ends up dead. “It wasn’t very logical material for someone of that age, but it stirred a lot of things in me,” Cruz said. She spent a year obsessively preparing all three parts. When she performed it in class, Rota’s tears persuaded her to stick with acting as a career. “I’ll never forget that day,” Cruz said. “It was like an injection of self-confidence.”

Her big break arrived in 1992 with the cult director Bigas Luna’s movie “Jamón Jamón.” Nominated for six Goyas, this semi-explicit art house film, in which Cruz plays the daughter of a small-town prostitute, was a sensation in Spain. Cruz was only 17 when she shot the sex scenes. Yet even at that young age, she brought a luminous sadness and vulnerability to the role of a teenager who yearns for love but becomes an object of predation.

Javier Bardem — the handsome scion of a prestigious, left-leaning film family — also stars in the project, as a callous gigolo looking to escape poverty. The two actors were not romantically involved during “Jamón Jamón” and did not become partners for another 16 years, after they worked together on “Vicky Cristina Barcelona.” Yet the scene where Bardem roars up and down a dirt road on a new motorcycle while Cruz walks along its edge, refusing to get on his ride, has become a classic in Spanish cinema. She carries a basket of groceries and wears a short red dress and espadrilles. She smiles only when he can’t see her face.

During the press tour for the film, and for years afterward, male journalists leered at the young Cruz, one speculating about whether she’d added silicone to her breasts. After “Jamón Jamón,” she rejected roles that required her to bare her body. This decision probably saved her career, countering the rush to typecast her as a sex kitten.

“It was really confusing, and there were a lot of people who were like, Are you crazy?” she told me. They predicted that she was ruining her future. “My heart is telling me that right now the noes for the things that I don’t feel are right for this moment are going to actually extend my career,” she recalled. “But it was like betting in a very dangerous casino.”

Fortunately, before “Jamón Jamón” hit theaters, Cruz’s agent, Katrina Bayonas, tricked the director Fernando Trueba into considering Cruz for the part of a girlish virgin in his 1992 comedy, “Belle Époque.” When Bayonas first suggested Cruz, Trueba refused to audition her. Cruz’s early work in television and music videos made her look like a “sex bomb,” he told me, and he needed an innocent.

So Bayonas offered to record a bunch of her young clients performing a scene from his script and to send him the tape. Trueba had never done this before, but it sounded like a smart way to save time casting a small part. Bayonas put Cruz in the middle of the tape. When she appeared, Trueba stopped the video in frustration. He’d told Katrina he didn’t want Penélope!

“Then I hit play and watched the audition,” he told me. “Then I stopped. Rewind. I watched the audition again. I stopped. I watched it three times in a row. You’re an idiot. Why did you have this prejudice? She’s incredible. She’s perfect.”

The sulky teenager trapped in bows, ponytails and Peter Pan collars was a supporting role in Trueba’s film. But for Cruz, it was decisive. It proved she had dramatic range and comic timing. “Belle Époque” won nine Goya Awards and an Oscar for best foreign language film. In 1998, Trueba also brought Cruz her first Goya Award for best actress with another tremendous comedy, “The Girl of Your Dreams.” (Think “The Producers” set in Nazi Germany with Spanish actors.)

Since then, Cruz’s movies often have landed in opposing pairs, as if she’s fighting to never be trapped in one type of role. The outrageous success of her first two films also drew her closer to her family. In her early 20s, as her career took off, she moved back into her mother’s house, where she lived with her two siblings. At that age, she explained, success can really disorient you. “But there, again,” she told me, “family is what saves you.”

The Princess of Wales Theater in Toronto was thick with emotion as “La Bola Negra” ended. In the dress circle, where I sat one night in September, there were tears and gasps and the pressing of hands into faces. People near me stood up and started clapping in the darkness as the credits rolled, even before the theater’s lights came up and the whole audience rose to their feet. Five days later, the film received the Toronto International Film Festival’s People’s Choice Award.

The power and beauty of “La Bola Negra” are hard to overstate. Some of its shots could hang in the Prado Museum next to paintings by Francisco de Goya and Jusepe de Ribera: a truck bed full of gray bodies splattered with red, a man asleep in a hospital bathed in a shaft of golden light. The film is set in three time periods: right before the Spanish Civil War, during the war and 80 years later in contemporary Spain. It is at once a war drama, a romance, a tragedy and a mystery.

Above all, “La Bola Negra” is an ode to the poet and dramatist Federico García Lorca and an examination of the ways in which Spain has punished and hidden loving relationships between men. Early in the film, a father in Andalusia recalls seeing the body of a gay teenager left to rot in public for 100 days, after a group of young men dragged the victim through the streets and drowned him in a trough. “Outside this door,” the father warns his son, “you must be what you must be.”

Cruz’s part in this two-and-a-half-hour masterpiece runs only about 10 minutes — but you feel it like lightning. Ambrossi and Calvo told me they wrote it for her after they received a call from Bayonas last year. By then, the directors — who were once a couple and are fondly known as Los Javis in Spain — had already established themselves as some of the country’s hottest talent with two television series: a sexy biography of the transgender pioneer La Veneno and a surreal musical thriller, “La Mesías” (“The Messiah”). Bayonas knew Cruz wanted to work with them.

“After that, Javi and I turned over everything,” Ambrossi said, “to create a universe, a minifilm for her, so that when she read it, it would be sufficiently rich so that she would say yes.” They were inspired, in part, by a moment Calvo loves in Francis Ford Coppola’s “Apocalypse Now,” when three Playboy models arrive by helicopter and dance for an audience of soldiers, giving them a brief escape from the horrors of the Vietnam War. Cruz’s character, Nené Romero, is a cupletista, one of the bawdy cafe singers popular in Madrid during the 1920s. She performs for an army unit that’s on leave from a military hospital and interrogation site. Sashaying like Mae West, tossing out double entendres, Cruz incites the soldiers with a confident eroticism.

She’s also nearly unrecognizable. Her dark hair is marcelled flat against her head; her eyebrows are drawn pencil thin. Even her voice is different. Cruz loves mastering accents. Over the years, she performed roles in Colombian, Cuban and Andalusian versions of Spanish, as well as in Italian and in English accented by Italian. Altering your speech patterns, she says, is a portal to complete immersion in a character.

“You have months of research and hard work to grasp it and be able to do it even asleep,” she explained, “but then it also creates a distance for you with yourself that makes it easy to fly and step into another’s shoes.” Cruz spent months studying video and audio recordings of cupletistas and practiced her lines with Olga María Ramos, the daughter of a famous cupletista, to learn the high, round and elaborately precise enunciation favored by these singers. She worked with the choreographer Belén Martí Lluch as well to perfect her two song and dance numbers, one of which starts on a moving army tank.

Cruz also appears in a more vulnerable scene. Between acts, Nené turns tricks offstage to survive, and the violence of her last john has left her furious and shaken. A young soldier named Sebastián — played with poignant naïveté by the pop star Guitarricadelafuente — watches her from a stairway. She senses instantly that he isn’t looking for sex. Still recovering from her previous encounter, Nené invites him up and beguiles him with stories about Madrid’s cabaret life and its performers, introducing Sebastián to the existence of a place where men may transform themselves into women and sleep with other men. In Madrid before the war, she explains, “we lived happily in mortal sin.”

Sebastián lights up as if he’s been tapped with a wand. It’s a fairy godmother moment. But for anyone familiar with the history of 20th-century Spain, it’s also tragic, because when Franco and the Spanish fascists won the civil war in 1939, they burned Madrid’s feminist and gay subcultures to the ground.

“This type of woman lived in a world where they believed they would always be free,” Calvo said. “Then came the dictatorships. They were hunted. They were jailed. Some disappeared. So she reminds Sebastián that there exists this possibility, but she also reminds us that there’s a possibility of losing it all.”

Cruz read the entire script when deciding to take the part. “Even if it was only one scene, I needed to be part of something like this,” she told me. “It seems to me that they’ve created something almost revolutionary, something so profound.”

Among the ideas that Rota tried to teach her students is the belief that theater serves an important social function. “The artist is the one responsible for mobilizing and energizing society,” Rota told me. Cruz’s feelings on this topic are complicated. In Toronto, she insisted that she doesn’t go looking for characters who share her opinions. Yet she has a long history of signing on to projects that portray gay relationships sympathetically, or that recall how fascism once dominated Spain. In Trueba’s 2016 film “The Queen of Spain,” she plays a movie star who literally talks back to Franco.

“La Bola Negra” showcases both these issues. The movie’s last line — “Watch out, they’re still stalking us” — is taken from a love poem that García Lorca wrote in the 1930s, not long before he was murdered by Spain’s far right. It is incredible, Cruz noted, that almost a century later the line still resonates. “How true it is,” she told me.

When Nené drags off her brunette wig and stands at the top of the stairs with her shoulders slumped, Cruz makes you feel the devastation that is still to come for Spain. Sebastián doesn’t catch the shift. He’s too smitten with the vision of a liberated life. He’s going to move to Madrid after the war, he declares. “Sure,” Nené says, with a brave smile. “We’ll see each other there.”

The first time I saw Cruz in person, she was on set for Pedro Almodóvar’s 2021 movie, “Parallel Mothers.” Her role, as a single mother who might lose her only child, was harrowing for her, and she was so consumed by it that she couldn’t talk to press. But I watched Almodóvar shoot Cruz’s close-ups as she ran through a tricky bit of dialogue at a kitchen table. She had to move from hope to sorrow and back again in just a few lines, finishing with a smile and eyes that brimmed with tears.

Earlier, when Almodóvar rehearsed Cruz and her co-star Milena Smit, he’d given them directions in a soft voice as they ran through their lines. He said almost nothing to Cruz now as they did three takes. Again and again, Cruz smiled, slipped into the difficult memory, reached the point of moist eyes, and never dropped a tear. It was like watching a ballerina perform fouettés, spinning circle after circle on one leg with perfect control.

“Will you let me do one more?” she asked Almodóvar after the third take.

“Of course.” This time he revised one of her lines, adding three words that gave Cruz one more beat to dig into the sorrow. Action! Her mouth, eyebrows and voice refracted the emotions — joy, grief, hope — like a prism splitting white light into colors. Cut.

Cruz and Almodóvar began working together in 1997. After seeing her in “Jamón Jamón” and “Belle Époque,” he gave her a small part in “Live Flesh” when she was 23. Set in 1970, when Franco declared yet another state of emergency that snatched away citizens’ basic civil rights, the story features Cruz as a sex worker who goes into labor on a bus during a citywide curfew. During her seven minutes onscreen, she doesn’t get to do much more than moan and sweat, but she does it so convincingly that Almodóvar went on to cast her in six more films, assigning her bigger and bigger parts.

“There’s a lot of chemistry between us, as actor and director,” Almodóvar wrote me via email. “When she gives herself, she’s a miracle. To my films, her characters have brought passion and truth.”

Almodóvar’s superb direction and writing helped Cruz develop into a virtuoso who can deliver an octave of emotions in a few beats. But she has not relied on only him to keep extending her prowess; her overall approach to acting is patterned on the dance training she received as a child. In her adolescence, she often danced four hours a day, learning to perform with a smile even when her feet were bleeding. Great ballerinas train ferociously, yet give themselves over to something more soulful when they take the stage. This is Cruz’s method, and her most frequent partner in this process is the acting teacher Juan Carlos Corazza, another émigré to Madrid from Buenos Aires.

In 2008, Cruz approached Corazza, who also taught Bardem, about helping her prepare the role of María Elena for “Vicky Cristina Barcelona.” By then Cruz had already crossed over to Hollywood — starring in both “Vanilla Sky” with Tom Cruise and “Blow” with Johnny Depp in 2001 — and had already won more than a dozen awards in Europe and North America. Yet she was still determined to get better.

Since 2008, Corazza has helped Cruz prepare roughly half her roles. “I think Penélope is always developing a way to embody the character, to capture the physicality of the character,” Corazza told me. “A characteristic of our work, of our creative relationship, is humor. It’s to play and to do the most, let’s say, horrible versions, the most awkward, and also to search for the most refined.”

Defining specific physicality for each character is part of what makes Cruz’s performances so compelling. The brusque, pained movements she found for the suicidal painter María Elena, for example, are nothing like the smooth, assertive gestures she gives the therapist in “The Invite,” who often stands with one hand on her hip — or the depressed walk she adopted for Laura in Michael Mann’s “Ferrari” (2023). Each of her performances is a soup made from scratch, though all her women convey dignity and resilience.

Cruz and Corazza analyze scripts together to identify the contradictions in characters. Corazza honed this approach by studying Anton Chekhov, whose plays, he noted, inspired the revolution in acting that Stanislavsky codified. “He doesn’t condemn the character, but he doesn’t save them either, and that’s difficult,” Corazza explained. “Penélope is always ready for the game of ‘Let’s not save her so much, let’s not idealize her, and let’s not condemn her either.’”

Cruz speaks of Rota, Almodóvar and Corazza with reverence. She keeps growing as an actor, it seems, because she loves assuming the role of protégée. She likes to visit Corazza’s school when they work together. “I often go there with my notes and my backpack to study and I’m happy,” she said. “Happy because you always have the chance to keep being the student in this profession.”

“I know she feels safe when she is protected behind a character,” the director Florian Zeller told me about Cruz. In his new film “Bunker,” however, he wanted her to try a different approach, one that placed a greater emphasis on using emotions derived from lived experiences. As part of that process, he cast Cruz and her husband of 17 years, Javier Bardem, as a book editor and an architect who have also been married 17 years.

“It was not about telling their story, of course,” Zeller clarified. Sofía and Miguel, the couple in “Bunker,” face challenges that are entirely fictional. “What we were trying to catch was something that smells like the truth, you know?”

As Sofía, Cruz gives one of her most restrained performances to date. Her demeanor is gentle, elegant, almost soft, yet even in this subdued mode Cruz performs with an intensity that makes her mesmerizing. She conveys her disappointment in her husband, and her growing attraction to an American author, in micro-expressions. When she gives a small smile to her phone while typing a text message, you feel she’s winked at the camera.

The tension between Sofía and Miguel crystallizes when a tech billionaire asks Miguel to design a palatial end-times bunker. The idea repulses Sofía. “Don’t you think it’s the most disgusting thing of our time?” she says when Miguel describes the project. These tech moguls have destroyed our world, she argues, and rather than use their riches to fix what they’ve smashed, they build fortresses that isolate them further from the conditions of ordinary people. “What’s the point for you as an architect?” she demands.

Zeller might have been interested in slipstreaming behind the emotions of Cruz and Bardem’s marriage, but Cruz herself seemed more interested in a different kind of realism: expressing her own outrage at the way technology has undermined human relationships and professional futures. “When a kid of 18 is now deciding what career he wants, first he has to ask himself: Which ones will be left? Which ones won’t be replaced by robots? By [expletive] robots,” she told me in Toronto. “So my blood boils with these issues.”

Cruz is a deeply private person, so it’s hard to discern the source of her ethics. When I asked, she would say only that her values come from her family. Her maternal grandfather might have been disappeared by Franco’s fascists. Her father was a salesman and loved to sing. Her mother was a hairdresser who played Tchaikovsky for her children. Growing up on the outskirts of Madrid, Cruz loved to spy on the women who frequented her mother’s salon. Camouflaged by schoolbooks, she studied them as they got their hair done and eavesdropped on their conversations. “I think they came, above all, to talk and to tell her their secrets,” Cruz said. She especially liked to listen for what they tried to hide. “I was always trying to figure out, What are they not saying?” Even as a girl she was honing a way of dissecting human behavior, noticing how women communicate not only through words but also through fleeting gestures and facial expressions, though silences, sighs and style.

These days, she says, her own children, Luna and Leonardo, are her top priority. She turns down projects that would require her to leave them for long stretches, preferring to shoot films in Madrid or during their breaks from school, when the family can travel together. She shot “The Invite” mostly during their Easter break, prepared “La Bola Negra” in Madrid while they were in school, and shot “Bunker” in a set that Zeller constructed 20 minutes from their home.

“She’s a very shy and very introverted and extremely un-egotistical person,” said Edward Norton, Cruz’s co-star and friend of more than 20 years. She’s also a disciplined artist who has shrewdly captained her own career. As Corazza would say, contradiction is what makes us human.

While we were in Canada, Cruz received a Special Tribute Award at a gala dinner held by the Toronto International Film Festival. During her acceptance speech, Cruz barely spoke of her work. Instead she paid tribute to Wilde, Zeller, Ambrossi, Calvo and Almodóvar. And she swerved off script to recognize Rogen in the crowd. “Seth, I know you’re there,” she called from the stage in a Garatti diamond necklace and black Chanel gown. “Don’t go without seeing me.”

During the dinner intermission, after the selfie requests and the crush of well-wishers subsided, Cruz made her way to a table Netflix had reserved for the cast of “La Bola Negra.” There she sat for a few minutes with Calvo and Ambrossi, who won the best director award at the Cannes Film Festival in May. The men have long been celebrities in Madrid, but their triumph at Cannes catapulted them to international fame. It was a little overwhelming, Ambrossi told me. He’d need to get away from all the red carpets before he could make sense of it all. But in Toronto they seized the opportunity to ask Cruz for advice. “She’s very discerning,” Calvo explained to me later. “And above all she has golden instincts.”

After hearing their ideas for the future, Cruz reassured them. “Don’t worry,” she said. “You’ll be fine because you’re good people.” She knew what kinds of temptations awaited them. The most important thing was to hold fast to your values. Then Bardem stood up at a table closer to the stage and held a plate of food high beside his head. He and Cruz had operated almost entirely independently at the gala, but the gesture showed he’d been thinking of her nevertheless. She needed to eat before they took away her plate. Ambrossi stood and offered Cruz his arm. They made their way through the concert hall, under the chandeliers, guests turning to admire them as she walked past.

Stylist: Freddy Alonso; Hair and makeup: Pablo Iglesias. Marcela Valdes is a staff writer for the magazine who has also written about the directors Pedro Almodóvar and Alfonso Cuarón.

I first saw Cruz on screen in the 1992 comedy “Belle Epoque,” and I’ve spent the decades since watching her evolve as an actor, eventually tracking down her first film, “Jamón Jamón,” too. So I knew that there was a lot more to Cruz than than the sexy, tempestuous artist that she became famous for playing in “Vicky Cristina Barcelona”. Still I was surprised to find out how modest she can be in real life, and how much dedicated effort she’s poured into becoming the virtuoso she is today. Rewatching her old films, I love noticing haw she gives each character a specific body language.

To Find Criminals and Child Exploitation in Gold Mines, We Just Had to Look

The New York Times October 19, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

Layers of people certify that gold is free from rights abuses and criminality. Nobody makes them leave their desks.

By Justin Scheck

In the past year, I’ve seen toddlers working in gold mines. I’ve met miners who pay a drug cartel for the right to dig, and watched a boy drink from an underground mine’s wastewater pipe. I met workers in Colombia whose hands tremble from mercury poisoning.

One thing they have in common is that they supply gold to the supposedly tightly controlled marketplace of Wall Street financiers, central banks and government mints.

As my colleagues and I unraveled how that was possible, we kept coming back to one key point: The people who are supposed to keep dirty gold out of the legitimate marketplace rarely actually visit the mines.

That’s the gaping hole at the center of the world’s mainstream gold market. The industry has layers of people tasked with certifying that supplies are free from abuse and criminality, but nobody makes them leave their desks in places like London and Geneva.

The Times this week reported that the London Bullion Market Association, the closest thing the industry has to a regulator, has repeatedly allowed gold into the market that has been mined by criminal gangs, a drug cartel and children. In one case, we found the association helped a refiner paper over apparent violations.

Human rights abuses and criminality are often obvious, if you show up and ask. Earlier this year, I visited a mine in Northern Colombia, where miners told us they pay a drug cartel for the right work there. The gold was certified as meeting the industry’s highest standards, and was sold to a supplier of the U. S. Mint.

Similarly, my colleagues revealed that President Trump hurriedly allowed gold imports from Venezuela before independent inspectors could visit the mines and before traders had finished their due diligence.

Venezuelan mines are notoriously linked to corruption and criminality; the national gold company is designated a U. S. security threat. The importer hired one of the world’s top supply-chain experts, who praised the import plan without ever visiting the mines.

A Times reporter visited and quickly found that gangs were profiting from the gold.

I visited mines in Madagascar where children panned for gold in raw sewage and workers hammered rock, with no helmets or shoes, in shafts hundreds of feet deep. Adolescents said the pull of gold is stronger than that of school.

“I’ve already tasted money,” said a 15-year-old boy named Fredo who hauls 20-liter water tanks for miners.

Four decades ago, the Bank of England regulated the gold market, effectively as an arm of the British government. But in 1987, it passed its oversight to the L. B. M. A., an industry group run by the world’s biggest banks and refiners.

For years the L. B. M. A. was mainly concerned with gold purity and weight, not rights abuses and environmental damage. Gold was so much cheaper then. So illegal gold mining, while problematic, was not nearly as profitable, widespread and catastrophic.

But over the past two decades, wealthy investors and governments fueled a price run-up that sent gold to record highs (today’s price is roughly four times what it was in 2010). A destructive illegal-mining boom followed in some of the world’s poorest places.

Miners, and criminals who profit from them, have rushed into areas that are ecologically and politically sensitive, and often dangerous.

Brazilian gangs have moved mining barges hundreds of miles upriver, into some of the Amazon’s most remote corners. Gold mines have dumped millions of tons of waste into Papua New Guinea’s rivers. Close to 200 people have died this year at mines in Uganda, the Central African Republic, Sudan and Sumatra.

In an effort to fight the worst abuses, the United States and the European Union passed laws attempting to exclude so-called “conflict minerals” from the global supply.

In response, the L. B. M. A. issued rules aimed at eliminating money laundering, corruption, organized crime and child abuse from the supply chain. Since 2012, refiners have had to conduct annual audits to show that they followed those rules.

One major requirement: Refiners who process gold from small-scale operations must inspect the mines. This is different from government inspections. Officials in corrupt governments or countries with weak human rights records have an incentive to say that their gold is mined cleanly. The industry inspections are meant to ensure it.

But loopholes and lax enforcement mean inspections don’t always happen. If gold from a high-risk mine passes through a middleman, for example, the refiner can obscure its source. That’s how drug cartel gold ended up at the U. S. Mint and the Royal Canadian Mint. The drug connections melted away in a cauldron of gold in Texas.

In Madagascar, gold from unlicensed mines sailed into the legitimate marketplace. Despite the L. B. M. A.’s written rules, the refiner said it did not need to inspect the mines itself. The gold was certified as meeting the highest levels in the industry.

Justin Scheck is a London-based reporter for The Times.

There are gifts for men. And then there are manly men gifts. Countless gift guides for the men in your life offer up the same neckties and tool sets and tasteful leather belts. And don't get us wrong: We're classy people, too. We like only the finest T-shirt a Savile Row tailor recommends, and anything themed for whiskey.

But this is a guide to the manliest gifts made for man men, menly objects ranging from the most classic of man totems to the most ridiculously hypermasculinized. Welcome to the red-hot tropics of the manosphere. Mere regular soap will not do when soap with the word “men” on it also exists. No mere shaving for us, when shaving can be aggressive. Enjoy.

For more men-themed gifts for man-themed men, check out our Gifts for Outdoorsy People, our Gifts for Dads Who Don't Need Anything, and Gifts for Golfers.

Updated October 2026: We've added a toiletry bag from SPC/LST, a pressure washer, a head shaver, and a giant flashlight; removed a couple sold-out options; and ensured up-to-date links and prices.

Männkitchen

Shop

MÄNNKITCHEN

Shaking isn't manly. Grinding is manly. Cannons are manly. Grinding so dominantly that your pepper grinder can plausibly be called a cannon is manly. So is deftly tooled precision of any kind. But Männkitchen’s Pepper Cannon isn't an expensive gimmick for the insecure. Its stainless steel burrs will grind peppercorns to the exact right size, among 50 settings, and this will end up mattering to anybody who spends a lot of time seasoning meat or building a rub. The all-metal construction will last decades. And it'll grind your pepper so fast it'll feel like the Dust Bowl got spicy.

Every man needs a good knife. Probably two. One for his pocket. One for the kitchen. If you're going to get a good knife, why not Anthony Bourdain's? Maybe it's me, but I pretty much don't know a dude who doesn't have a tattered copy of Kitchen Confidential somewhere in his house. This Global 8-inch chef's knife is Bourdain's knife, the one he recommended to starting chefs. The one he recommended as a baseline good chef's knife for those at home. It is Japanese-made stainless steel, ice-hardened, lightweight. Seamless from its handle to its convex edge. The Global chef knife is economy itself. It is a knife that most chefs own eventually. Maybe the man in your life would also do with a good knife.

Mileseey

Amazon

You know what men like? Knowing how long something is, or how far away it is. Know what they (I) don't like? Stretching out a dinky tape measure that keeps shimmying or bending or snapping back into the roll. The solution to everything is always lasers. Lasers can do anything. Just ask Elon Musk.

Anyway, just point this Mileseey S50 at anything, press the button, set your starting measuring point, and it'll tell you how far away it is. (It measures to 1/32 of an inch, but I wouldn't trust it past 1/16 of an inch.) Get a tripod for it and you can also do point-to-point measurements from a distance. I've measured windows for fittings. Door jambs. Most of the rooms and spaces in my house. I've barely used tape for four months. Why use tape when you can use lasers? Mileseey says the green laser light on this S50 is more visible than red light during the daytime. Maybe this is true. There are also a whole lot of trigonometric functions I haven't figured out, and the included instructions are only half helpful. But mostly I just want to know: How big is that thing? How far away?

The military-inspired System Kit from SPC/LST features two sections that can snap together (one zips flat and has three internal pockets, while the other zips only on the top and has just one zippered pocket), along with a 20-mm side strap with a clip in case you need to attach it to your pack, truck, or parachute. —Kat Merck

These Hell Hands grill gloves from Big Green Egg are rated up to 900 degrees Fahrenheit. They're made with thick cowhide that goes most of the way up to your elbows—and look like something you'd wear for the zombie apocalypse. The pads are made with thick, puncture-resistant Armortex fabric and stitched with Kevlar.

I don't know if this makes these gloves bulletproof. But what I do know is that I have placed my palm flat onto a scalding 500-degree cast-iron pan while wearing one of these Hell Hands. They are stretch canvas, svelte, sturdy. They have pockets inside other pockets, pockets that remove traces of being pockets. If you're the sort of guy who wants to look good, without looking like you want to look good, these pants are your pants.

Suck it up, and embrace the steely, Vader-esque manliness of this Ultra-Tough cooler from RTIC. It's roto-molded, natch, but it's also filled with 2.8 inches of foam. I have tested the 45-quart version while tailgating in temps where the cooler was actually helping keep our seltzers from exploding.

The Ultra-Tough is a beast to carry by yourself (the manly way, the way John Wayne would carry a cooler) because it weighs almost 30 pounds empty. The first butcher became a butcher after he got in a fistfight outside a butcher shop. This is Naples, Italy, we're talking about, where you sell meat or you are the meat. (We made this proverb up, but it seems right.) Anyway, this is not just good but actually great beef in a box. Pat LaFrieda beef is the beef served at some of the most famous restaurants in New York. It will also come in the mail, wherever you are: fresh, never frozen. And then it goes on the fire. Data Centers Have a New PR Plan: Your Kid’s Field Trip

Wired October 18, 2026

Welcome back to Power Play! Each week, senior writer Molly Taft tackles a topic around this midterm season’s biggest issue: data centers. They’re out this week, so Caroline Haskins is reporting for duty. If you’ve got a question or thought for the column, feel free to shoot Caroline an email at caroline_haskins@wired. com or reach her securely on Signal at carolinehaskins.61.

The nonprofit 7x24 Exchange International wants to promote data centers, which they believe are "mission critical” infrastructure. As part of this work, the group recommends a children’s story, “What is a Data Center?,” which follows a honey badger named Honey who gets a guided tour of a data center from a worker named Oliver. Oliver explains that the job of data center employees is to make sure that the “functions supported by the data center” are available to anybody, “no matter what time it is.”

"Like when my mom shops online late at night because my dad is sleeping and won't know about it?" Honey asks.

The story is part of a broader pattern across the data center industry. In addition to lobbying, job creation programs, tax breaks, companies and interest groups are trying something a bit more creative: winning over the youth. As pushback to massive data center build-outs and energy-guzzling campuses intensifies, the industry is apparently taking a softer approach to community building using a tactic other industries with a public relations problem have tried.

Alex Molnar, a research professor at the University of Colorado Boulder and the director of the National Education Policy Center, tells WIRED that, for over a century, industries with an image problem—fast food, tobacco, oil and gas—have brought their messaging to schools.

“A very, very big reason why corporations get involved in the schools is, quite simply, corporate propaganda—for the purpose not necessarily of selling a product, but of telling their ‘story,’” Molnar says.

In May, the Potomac chapter of the Association for Computer Operations Management (AFCOM), a trade group for the data center industry, sponsored Memorial Day-themed flag-making kits to be distributed to 3,100 first graders across 37 schools in Loudoun County, Virginia, also known as Data Center Alley. In addition to the flag kits, kids received an informational card with statistics about “the positive impact” that the data center industry has on the local economy.

Besides promoting heartwarming tales about how women can shop, 7x24 Exchange is also the brains behind a holiday it calls “International Data Center Day,” which is “designed to create awareness of the data center industry and inspire the next generation of talent.”

The nonprofit encourages people to pitch the holiday to school administrators. For participating high schools, it offers a celebratory crossword puzzle and information about data center training programs. For elementary schools, it offers data center-themed coloring pages, instructions for an evaporation-themed science project, and print-out activities like “Draw a picture of the cloud" and “Draw a data superhero.” It also promotes several data center-themed books for young readers, including one in which two sisters visit a data center and meet a robot named JB and another that features two brothers who visit a "vibrant digital world" and save the internet. Then there’s “Polly Packet's Precious Payload,” which follows a mother who teaches her daughter about data centers.

7x24 Exchange has also visited or organized at least a half-dozen K-12 events at schools across the country this year. In Minnesota, it brought Fridley High School students on a field trip to a local Cummins diesel power generation facility in order to learn about the “generators that power data centers worldwide.” (7x24 Exchange, Cummins, and Fridley High School did not respond to WIRED’s request for comment.)

The nonprofit is far from the only organization sponsoring school activities that are friendly to data centers. WIRED’s tally of public blogs and social media posts found that, since 2025, at least eleven companies and industry groups have hosted student field trips to local data centers.

Sabey, a company that runs seven US data centers, has hosted a number of field trips for Washington-based high schoolers, including one in May for Eastmont High School students, one in January for Manson School District students, and another last October for Quincy High School students.

Manson School District publicized the trip in a blog post showing what appears to be adults and students in a conference room. The image labeled us “AI-generated content,” though, and several people in the photo have missing limbs. The blog says that students learned about “the role data centers play in storing, processing, and protecting information” and “the wide range of careers” in the data center industry.

Quincy School District communications coordinator Jessica Blancas tells WIRED that the district “has organized data center visits for many years” at the facilities of companies like Microsoft, Vantage, Yahoo, and Sabey. She described the latter company as a “long-standing” district partner, citing its consistent work offering “guest speakers,” “mock interviews,” and “internship opportunities.”

Blancas adds that the district has organized “all-girls visits to Sabey,” as well as tours for students who intend to go into specific fields like construction or engineering. (Manson School District and Sabey did not respond for comment.)

Amazon, meanwhile, hosted a field trip last February at its Arlington, Virginia, “Skills Center,” a free community space for anyone “curious about cloud computing and future job possibilities.” It was open to any high school in the DC metro area, though Jackson-Reed High School was the only one to attend.

Molnar says he doesn’t get what’s in it for kids. “Why would a third grader be interested in a data center?” he says.

“You're going to see miles after miles of the most boring things imaginable,” he adds. “Lines after lines of these servers generating enormous volumes of heat. You're also going to hear some fair amount of noise. And you're not going to see many people because not many people work there when they're built.”

It’s common for companies to sow goodwill through public outreach, and as tech companies have reckoned with the backlash to data centers, these field trips are taking place in an increasingly fraught environment.

A Pew Research poll conducted over the summer found that about half of the 10,000 Americans surveyed see data centers as “mostly bad” for the environment and quality of life, and across the country, an ideologically diverse cohort has started rallying against them. In some places, the negative sentiment toward local data centers has been amplified by their proximity to local schools.

Providing educational materials and offering field trips are ways that industries can maintain their social license to operate in a community. The data center sector is, in many ways, following the playbook other industries have to sow goodwill with children as well as their parents. The oil and gas industry has sponsored university research projects and STEM programs in K-12 schools. The tech world has similarly funded STEM programs, as well as advocated for in-school coding programs while lobbying to make computer science count as a science credit.

Fossil fuel companies have also spent millions of dollars developing K-12 lessons with pro-industry talking points, particularly in states like Oklahoma and Texas.

Molnar believes this kind of corporate influence shouldn’t be allowed because kids are “in an absolutely powerless position.” Kids “need to be protected” by their school districts and communities, he says.

“As an adult, I have access to alternative information—I have a critical ability to assess what I'm hearing, and to render some kind of judgments,” Molnar says. “None of that is true of children.”

Data centers may be for kids, but some of the products that rely on their server racks sure aren’t. When Meta launched Muse, it looked like a cute little AI agent for the masses. But my colleague Reece Rogers recently discovered that Muse has a naughty side. When Reece asked Muse if it was able to sext, it told him to “shoot your shot.” Reece did, and Muse was receptive. Enthusiastic, even! We published the chat logs—well, the PG-13 ones since WIRED is a family site, after all—and Reece spoke to consumer advocates who were alarmed at Muse’s sexy demeanor.

Meta, for its part, says this is all part of the plan. “Muse is an app for people 18 and over that allows them to engage in adult conversations, if they choose, using a private and secure VM only accessible to them,” company spokesperson Daniel Roberts told Reece. So if that’s your thing, have at it!

OnlyFans Creators Are Pissed That Meta Lets Muse Talk Dirty

Wired October 18, 2026

The generative AI revolution hasn’t been kind to Vanniall, an OnlyFans creator who lives in New York City. She now constantly finds hyperrealistic deepfakes—AI-generated images and videos that copy everything about her—circulating online and often isn’t able to get them removed.

On top of that, Vanniall struggles to build an audience on popular social media platforms, like Instagram, without getting in trouble. “There’s always some sort of report or appeal that I'm going through with them,” she tells WIRED. Vanniall’s Instagram account, which has over 100,000 followers, is currently restricted and cannot be viewed without logging in.

So, when I tell her that Meta allows its AI agent, called Muse, to engage in explicit sexting with adult users, she seems frustrated by the decision: “It's not fair that they get to pull money out of people with their sexually active AI agent, but they won't let real people, real adults, engage in any sort of sensuality or sexuality.”

It’s a common refrain I heard from other adult content creators, who questioned why their accounts on Meta platforms often seem restricted, while Meta’s AI agent is now allowed to talk dirty with millions of adult users.

“A private, one-to-one conversation between an adult and an individualized AI agent on a platform restricted to people 18 and over is very different from the marketing and promotion of services on a social media platform,” Meta spokesperson Tracy Clayton tells WIRED.

Meta’s Muse is the first always-on AI agent to break out of early adopter circles in San Francisco. The Muse app is like a message thread; text the digital assistant, give it access to your personal data, like calendar and email, and have it proactively find ways to help, like canceling a workout class that overlaps with your dinner reservation. Meta’s large distribution network, through platforms like Instagram and Facebook, helped catapult the app to the top of the download charts during its first month, as millions of new users experimented with an agent for the first time.

In addition to having it organize your calendar, Meta says, it’s OK for users of the adults-only app to engage in X-rated AI conversations with Muse. A Meta spokesperson previously told WIRED the company wouldn’t “block legal adult behavior.” Meta’s Muse generates explicit text but not images or videos.

While Meta takes a different approach to moderation on Instagram, other social media platforms in the United States do allow sexually explicit content. X remains one of the most popular platforms for many OnlyFans creators to draw in new subscribers and connect with fans. Many adult performers have also migrated to Bluesky after Elon Musk took over the platform formerly known as Twitter, where users can also share adult content.

“I think we're already seeing AI being allowed to do more than humans would get away with,” says Jiz Lee, who runs an OnlyFans account and has worked for years behind the scenes in queer porn. Meta has previously flagged Lee’s Instagram posts for removal. Lee feels like queer and trans people are often treated unfairly by large social media companies, whether or not the person is an adult content creator.

Lee traces many online censorship issues back to FOSTA-SESTA, a law signed by President Trump in 2018 that impacted Section 230 protections for platforms, and many websites responded by censoring adult content. “If sex work was decriminalized, then a lot of these issues wouldn't be happening, a lot of the censorship wouldn't be happening,” they say.

Lee also wants to know more about how Muse was trained and who, if anyone, was compensated by Meta for their data. “We've been slow to react industry-wise,” they say. But Lee is starting to see more adult content companies clarify AI usage stances in official contracts. They want to protect performers from being gobbled up into AI training data.

“When we're at award shows, and companies do advertisements for AI agents, they literally get booed like crazy,” says Tony Genius, who also has an OnlyFans account and appears in adult films. He has concerns about fully AI-generated porn in the future potentially displacing human performers. He also sees current AI tools as helpful for some marketing tasks independent creators do, like using automations to clip video segments for social media.

For many OnlyFans creators, navigating Meta platforms is frustrating but critical to remaining visible online. Genius claims to be on his seventh Instagram account in the past five years.

When asked about Muse’s sexting ability, he questioned why Meta made one of its apps, Muse, gated for those 18 and over but doesn’t seem interested in creating another adults-only space on social media. “It could be: Instacam,” he says.

Muse generating adult content could offer explicit AI interactions to a wider audience. Genius says he would be open to collaborating with a tech company to create an AI-version of himself that fans could message. He wants to find ways for humans to keep making money as adult performers, ensuring they aren’t cut out or unfairly trained on. Right now, he sees his human-ness and authenticity as central to connecting with audiences.

Meanwhile, Vanniall is fervently against using any AI agent. Well, at least, Meta’s Muse. “Stop downloading that app,” she says. “You do not need to give Meta any more money or any more of your personal information. They have enough.”

Review: Valerion VisionMaster Max 4K Projector

Wired October 18, 2026

All products featured on WIRED are independently selected by our editors. However, when you buy something through our retail links, we may earn an affiliate commission.

8/10

Valerion’s VisionMaster Kickstarter campaign raised more than $8 million in 2024, making it the most-funded campaign on the platform that year. After spending the past few weeks with the flagship VisionMaster Max, I’m confident there are plenty of satisfied backers.

At $3,999, it costs far more than excellent point-and-play rivals, such as the Nebula X1 (9/10 WIRED Recommends), but considerably less than native 4K home-theater projectors from brands like Sony and JVC. That leaves the Max straddling two very different camps.

Its compact design, built-in Google TV, and automated setup suggest the classification of a premium lifestyle projector, while optical zoom, vertical lens shift, a mechanical iris, and sophisticated black-level processing point toward something far more capable. It’s easy to use and almost too pretty to ceiling-mount, but arguably too sophisticated to spend its life propped up on a side table. So the question remains: Who is the VisionMaster Max actually for?

The 16.5-pound VisionMaster Max is simple to get up and running. Google TV grants instant access to many streaming services, while auto-keystone and autofocus make positioning a frictionless process. (However, because keystone correction digitally reshapes the image, when used heavily, it can reduce resolution—but that’s true for all devices with the feature.) Optical zoom, with a 0.9 to 1.5:1 throw ratio, lets you resize the picture without moving the projector. There’s also vertical lens shift, which moves the image up or down without needing to resort to digital correction. All of this means that if you’ve got a blank wall and five minutes, you can stream Emily in Paris on a 90-inch screen in no time.

Valerion VisionMaster Max 4K Projector

Rating: 8/10

All products featured on WIRED are independently selected by our editors. However, we may receive compensation from retailers and/or from purchases of products through these links. Learn more.

It’s clever tech, though not fully unique, with the XGIMI Horizon range and Nebula X1 offering similar optical-image manipulation. Even so, the VisionMaster Max offers considerably more control than most point-and-play designs. Praise is also due for the remote, which looks and feels great. Many brands scrimp on details like accessories, but Valerion maintains its premium feel throughout.

The VisionMaster Max produces a seriously bright image. Its 3,500 ISO lumen RGB triple-laser light source easily projected a 75-inch picture I could happily watch during the day in a bright room. Valerion says it’s good for images between 40 and 300 inches. I maxed out at 130 inches but was impressed by how even the detail remained right to the edges at that size.

Valerion VisionMaster Max 4K Projector

Rating: 8/10

All products featured on WIRED are independently selected by our editors. However, we may receive compensation from retailers and/or from purchases of products through these links. Learn more.

While I watched during the day, the colors appeared a bit washed out in this environment, but much less so than I expected. Once I watched in the dark, however, I enjoyed punchy high-dynamic-range (HDR) highlights, excellent detail, and smooth motion.

In terms of color, the Max has 110 percent Rec.2020 coverage, meaning the lasers can reproduce an exceptionally wide range of colors, far exceeding the needs for ultra-high-definition (UHD) and HDR video. In my living room, colors looked rich without becoming cartoonish, while the combination of brightness, detail, and contrast gave movies cinematic quality.

Black levels with most home projectors are good, but not brilliant. Here, however, the proprietary six-stage iris self-adjusts the aperture from scene to scene, closing for darker images to deepen blacks, and opening up when a scene calls for more brightness. Enhanced Black Level (EBL) works alongside the iris, electronically reducing laser output in darker scenes, adjusting the image curve to maintain details. Together, these features dramatically reduce the charcoal-gray blacks common with this type of projector. I was astonished by the depth and shadow detail it produced without losing brighter details. Even the film The Dark Knight, with its muted color grading, looked good.

Valerion VisionMaster Max 4K Projector

Rating: 8/10

All products featured on WIRED are independently selected by our editors. However, we may receive compensation from retailers and/or from purchases of products through these links. Learn more.

Though I didn’t put the VisionMaster Max through its paces for video-game testing (I’m not much of a gamer, unless you count Mario Kart battles on the Nintendo Switch), the projector’s specifications are nonetheless impressive. It supports refresh rates up to 240 Hz at 1080p, with claimed input lag as low as 4 milliseconds (ms); for 4K, 60-Hz gaming, that input lag is rated at 15 ms. Two HDMI 2.1 inputs and auto low-latency mode further strengthen its gaming credentials, although it lacks a variable refresh rate (VRR) to dynamically smooth out delays.

Less impressive than its picture is its sound: The VisionMaster Max has two 12-watt speakers, and audio is clean, detailed, with effects neatly separated from dialog. But it still suffers from its box form factor. To be fair, with the exception of Anker’s removable satellite speaker designs like the Nebula X1, audio fails to keep up with image quality in many lifestyle projectors. I’d contend that at this price, an all-in-one projector should provide audio that matches the pixel-perfect picture. The Max’s speakers are fine, but push it beyond level 25 of 100, and it just sounds loud.

Thankfully, since the projector supports both DTS and Dolby Atmos, you can connect it to a decent 5.1/7.1 home theater audio system. You can also wirelessly link to a Bluetooth speaker, which makes for a clean living-room setup, although latency can be an issue. For reliable synchronization and true surround sound, HDMI eARC remains the better audio option.

Valerion is not without stiff competition, and that includes against itself. The Nebula X1 offers a similarly simple Google TV setup and 3,500-lumen brightness, with optional wireless surround sound making it better suited to casual living-room or outdoor use. The Leica Cine Play 1 (9/10, WIRED Recommends) combines superb optics with a more lifestyle-friendly design. Valerion’s cheaper VisionMaster Pro 2 ($2,999) retains key features, including Google TV, RGB triple-laser projection, optical zoom, and EBL, but it loses the Max’s iris and vertical lens shift. For casual movie nights, I’d be happy with this compromise that keeps extra money in my pocket.

While not necessarily casual, the Max is great and likely best suited for the viewer who wants to enjoy its capabilities. Its weight, extensive picture controls, and exceptional brightness encourage a proper screen, external sound, and careful setup, where its superb black levels and cinematic image can be fully exploited.

The brand seems to agree, as it’s strongly encouraging customers to go all-in with its baffling array of deals. At the time of publication, you can opt to bundle the $3,999 Max with a choice of screens and four stands—including a tripod and ceiling mount—without paying any additional fee.

It may be overkill for occasional big-screen streaming, but as a compact projector at the heart of a home theater, I highly recommend it.

Climate Change Has It In for the World’s Best Surfing

Wired October 18, 2026

This story originally appeared on The Guardian and is part of the Climate Desk collaboration.

The climate crisis is coming for some of the world’s greatest surf breaks, submerging some as sea level rises and wiping out others as classic breaks get crushed against coastal developments.

Analysis of dozens of famous waves in World Surfing Reserves (WSR) found that more than three-quarters were at high risk because of changing tide levels, hardened shorelines, and shifting sands.

The impacts matter not only to the surfers catching the waves but also to the communities that depend on the multibillion-dollar surf economy, often located in places with little else.

The waves rated at most risk in the study include the “bombing barrels” of Croyde Beach in North Devon, UK; the point breaks at Noosa in Australia and Oriente Salvaje, El Salvador; and Santa Cruz reefs of California such as Sewer Peak and Wind and Sea.

The best surfing waves are created by intricate combinations of seafloor shape, swell direction, and tide. “Surf breaks are incredibly unique oceanographic phenomena—a confluence of all these factors that fit together just right to make the wave happen—and so those processes are really sensitive,” said Dan Reineman, an associate professor at California State University Channel Islands and a coauthor of the study.

Global heating is pushing up sea level and changing rainfall patterns that affect sediment movement, which can upset the delicate balance and destroy the wave. However, the researchers said the expert local knowledge of surfers could be tapped to help protect the waves.

Trent Hodges, a coauthor of the study and a senior programs manager at Save the Waves Coalition, which launched the WSR program in 2009, said: “Climate change will impact surf breaks all over the world in different ways, depending on their unique geographies. We learned directly from the local surfers how they are seeing their waves change. It’s a canary in the coal mine too—when a wave changes, that often means the beach is changing, and everybody enjoys the beach.”

The study, published in the journal Climatic Change, concludes: “Climate change and coastal management both have significant negative implications for the future viability of multiple surf breaks of global significance and, therefore, the myriad distinct local communities, cultures and economies they support.”

Almost 200 local experts analyzed 57 surf breaks in all but two of the 13 WSRs, spread across eight countries. The researchers said thousands of other surf waves around the world faced similar peril.

A key finding was that where coastlines were more natural, they could adapt better to the changes brought by the climate crisis, by shifting inland and relocating sediments. Development such as sea walls, jetties, and groynes made the beaches and waves less resilient, Reineman said.

Adam Hall, a cofounder of the North Devon WSR, was one of the local surfers who contributed to the study. He said: “North Devon is so special. We have Saunton Sands, a world-renowned longboarding wave with really long, mellow rides, and the UK’s best beach break at Croyde. We’ve got left- and right-hand point breaks and a sheltered spot for when it gets too windy and too big. Whatever you want to do, we’ve got it.”

He said surfing was very important for the local economy, and not just in summer. “Surfers will come throughout the year. They fill up the pubs, restaurants, and car parks when the swells are good in January, February, and March, where if you go to any other tourist destination that doesn’t have surf, they’re dead on their knees.”

Bellroy has stepped in to become my accessories maker of choice, and I love the luxe leather feel of the Pod Jacket, and it's a great alternative to our leather pick above. It includes a corded lanyard, which I don't use since I prefer to keep it in my pocket, and the lanyard just gets in the way. I like that I can still charge it wirelessly. If leather is not your thing, the Pod Jacket is available in other materials. —Les Shu

Compatible with AirPods Pro (2nd and 3rd generation).

Spigen Classic LS Case: This case makes your AirPods Pro look like the classic Macintosh mouse, but the aesthetics don't outweigh its mediocre functionality. The lid constantly pops off, and while I appreciate that Spigen includes extra adhesive, I don't want to have to deal with it. It was also annoying to open and too bulky to fit conveniently in my purse or pocket.

How Can I Tell Which AirPods I Have?

How do you know which case to buy? Apple has several generations of its AirPods, whether you have the standard AirPods or the AirPods Pro, so be sure the case you select works with your model. (Some cases are interchangeable, particularly the first- and second-generation AirPods and the first- and second-generation AirPods Pro.) To find what you have, go to Settings > Bluetooth on the Apple device you paired them with. Tap the “i” icon next to your AirPods' name to see the model number. If your AirPods aren't connected to an Apple device, you can find the model number on the device itself. It's on the underside of each earbud—you may need to use your smartphone's zoom feature to read it.

Once you have the model number, you can cross-reference it with this tool to identify the generation. You can also just check the receipt in your order history if you purchased them online.

You probably know if you bought a different case for your AirPods, but it's worth checking the case's model number, too, as Apple has released stand-alone models with wireless charging and MagSafe support. You can find those details here.

How We Test AirPods Cases

I make sure these cases provide adequate protection in day-to-day life. I keep my AirPods in most of the time and always tote them around, so these cases get a lot of field testing. I also make sure they allow the full use of AirPods' features, like hearing the Find My tone or allowing wireless charging. I tested most of these cases with my AirPods Pro 3, but am hoping to check out more options for the AirPods 4 and the AirPods Max soon.

Encryption Is Getting Squeezed From All Sides

Wired October 17, 2026

Welcome to Kernel Panic, a weekly newsletter by Lily Hay Newman and Matt Burgess from inside the new world of privacy and digital security. To receive this newsletter in your inbox each week, sign up here.

Oh, Canada. The Great White North is the latest country to contemplate legislation that could essentially mandate backdoors and increase data retention in encrypted services. The proposed changes have prompted the Canadian anti-censorship company Psiphon VPN—which keeps millions of Iranians online during repressive internet shutdowns—to say it will leave the country if the bill passes. And Psiphon is not the only one.

Encrypted messaging app Signal has said it would exit the Canadian market because the legislation would require unacceptable changes to its open source projects. Apple and Meta have criticized the bill, and DuckDuckGo and NordVPN say they would consider pulling their services, too. But as countries around the world contemplate similar legislation, even larger questions begin to emerge about which states or regions could differentiate themselves as being safe havens for privacy services if global hostility to encryption continues to rise.

It’s been maddening and disturbing to see more and more democratic countries around the world propose changes to their surveillance and data collection laws, with the aim of giving cops and intelligence agencies greater powers to access people’s information. Governments already have broad digital surveillance powers and investigative tactics to solve crimes that involve encrypted data, but legislative proposals almost inevitably include provisions to expand this access even more—mandating additional logging and what amounts to backdoors or intentional flaws in encrypted products, which cryptographers and security engineers have consistently said cannot be built safely. Truly everyone who understands the issue has said it as much for decades. Yet policymakers return again and again to the idea, somehow expecting a different conclusion or a new breakthrough that will make it all possible.

“There have always been some officials within certain agencies that tend to view technology as a crime scene in and of itself, and it becomes a myopic point of fixation where access is desired,” says Kate Robertson, a senior research associate at the University of Toronto’s Citizen Lab. “But that type of siloed thinking forgets that technology needs to be the secure operating platform for hospitals, for banks, for national security agencies, for police services themselves to protect victims who report private information to them.”

In recent years, the UK and Australia have introduced sweeping surveillance reforms that can compel companies to break their encryption. Other encryption-threatening proposals have also emerged in the EU, France, India, Ireland, Spain, Sweden, Switzerland, and others. While not all measures have passed into law or been enacted, the hostility is clear.

First proposed in 2025, and partially revised due to blistering criticism from tech companies and civil society, Canada’s C-22 bill can broadly place requirements on tech companies, including those outside of Canada, to introduce “technical capabilities” that allow data to be accessed for law enforcement purposes. Like many such bills, C-22 says that companies will not have to introduce a “systemic vulnerability” into their systems. But opponents have pointed out that any capability to access end-to-end encrypted data amounts to a backdoor that could be discovered and abused by anyone. And this risk is only heightened even more by the ease with which anyone can now use AI tools for reverse engineering and system mapping.

“Companies could be asked to introduce vulnerabilities, build backdoors, bypass, weaken or otherwise defeat encryption,” members of the US House Judiciary and Foreign Affairs committee said in a May letter to Canadian officials.

In addition to potential impacts on encryption, C-22 also includes provisions that could require companies to retain metadata about user activity, something that many privacy focused services (including VPN services from Psiphon and DuckDuckGo) intentionally avoid. As a result, these companies say, they would be forced to change their business models to collect data they do not need or want to collect about their users. And researchers say that such product changes would diminish user trust while increasing the potential for widespread surveillance.

“If you are asking and requiring for this infrastructural change—that they retain metadata by default—it is creating a surveillance capability within a tool that didn’t have it,” says Afsaneh Rigot, the founder of the De|Center, a research organization that aims to reduce the risk of technological harms. “There are contexts like Iran and other contexts globally, who all of this has a trickle effect on. It's not going to stay in Canada because these types of laws always get copy pasted around the world.”

As more countries contemplate such laws, developers focused on privacy and anti-censorship tools are increasingly casting around for safe jurisdictions to operate in. But this still doesn’t solve the problem of reaching users in all countries around the world and for now, there are no sure bets.

“Changing your headquarters isn’t much of a plan B when the law follows your users, as C-22 would,” says Joseph Lorenzo-Hall, security portfolio lead at the Internet Society. “The strongest protection is holding as little user data as possible, but ‘we don’t have it’ is no defense if governments can force you to start collecting it. A safe haven needs more than favorable winds in strong encryption. It needs laws that let companies keep their privacy promises and defend them against foreign threats to confidentiality and integrity.”

Spotted something we should include next week? Let us know at kernelpanic@wired. com. And stay safe out there.

The Best LED Grow Lights to Keep Your Plants Thriving All Winter

Wired October 17, 2026

All products featured on WIRED are independently selected by our editors. However, we may receive compensation from retailers and/or from purchases of products through these links. Learn more.

Summer is officially over, along with its allotment of free sunlight. You might be sad about this, but your indoor plants might be even sadder. A good LED grow light can replicate sunlight with full-spectrum light and day/night cycles, keeping plants lush and thriving even in a dark, windowless corner or basement.

I have no fewer than 40 houseplants in my home at any given time, as well as a fair number of grow lights, and what I've found to be important for a general consumer (i. e., someone not doing that kind of indoor grow) isn't necessarily certain colored light wavelengths but whether a grow light is easy to live with in your house.

Many grow lights are more or less going to serve the same purpose, so what you really need to know is this: Is the light so bright that it's disruptive? Does it require complicated installation? Is it easy for kids or pets to knock over? The grow lights recommended below are ones that WIRED staffers have lived with for months, if not years, and have found them both effective and easy to integrate into our lives.

Also be sure to check out our guides to the Best Indoor Gardening Systems, Best Gifts for Plant Lovers, and Best Kitchen Composters.

Amazon

Amazon

Amazon

Amazon

What Is PPFD?

Photosynthetic photon flux Ddensity, or PPFD, expressed in micromoles per square meter per second (μmol/m²/s), is a measurement of how much light reaches your plant that's usable for photosynthesis. In general, the higher the plant's energy needs, such as producing a flower or a fruit, the higher the PPFD number you want. Though different lights have different height requirements given the plants they're made for, for standardization purposes, I measured the PPFD of each grow light at 18 inches with the Photone app and a light diffuser. Keep in mind these measurements are general and approximate.

How I Test Grow Lights

Some of these grow lights I bought myself, with my own money, before I even began working at WIRED. Others were owned by staffers and recommended to me. I also have press samples from other guides I worked on, which I liked so much I ended up keeping around.

For the traditional grow lights, I tested them at home under normal-life conditions. I put them where they'd fit, tested their timers, and noted whether or not they were dimmable. I also measured each light's PPFD (see above) and noted whether certain lights could be daisy-chained for more extensive coverage.

There are a lot of options out there for starting seeds and helping houseplants along in the winter, and many of them are bulky, fussy, or require elaborate hanging setups. WIRED commerce SEO director Stewart Savin used these lights to start her garden earlier this year and had 138 successful germinations across 144 seedling cells. ("The vast majority of those plants went on to have long lives in my garden after I hardened them off," she says.) Note that because this light can only go beneath a rack, shelf, or cabinet, it’s not inherently adjustable, and therefore is best for small plants (like seedlings) that aren’t going to grow especially tall.
